div.p: Octopuses have voracious appetites and will fight to eat anything whatever. Often they do not even spare one another, but the smaller, caught by the larger and falling into the more powerful creature's hunting-snares — what are called the fish's tentacles — then becomes its dinner. The octopuses lie in wait for fish in this way as well. They settle beneath the rocks and transform their own colour to match them, so that they seem to be the very thing the rocks naturally are. The fish then swim up to the octopuses as if to the rock, and the octopuses, finding them off their guard, throw their own arms about them like nets.

Here too is something Socrates said to Alcibiades. The young man was in great anxiety and dread of coming forward before the people. Heartening and rousing him, Socrates said, "Do you not despise that cobbler?" naming him. When Alcibiades agreed, Socrates went on, "And what of that man who cries his wares in the markets, or that tent-maker?" When the young man assented, Socrates said, "Well then, the people of the Athenians is gathered together out of such men; and if you despise them one by one, you must despise them when assembled as well." So nobly did the son of Sophroniscus and Phaenarete instruct the son of Cleinias and Deinomache.

Come then, let us also describe in words and shape forth the famous Thessalian Tempe; for it is agreed that speech too, if it has the power of description, can show whatever it wishes no less effectively than men skilled in handiwork. There is, then, a place lying between Olympus and Ossa. These are very lofty mountains, cleft apart as if by some divine design, and between them they receive a region whose length extends to forty stades, while its breadth is in one place a plethron, and in another a little more. Through the middle of it flows the river called Peneus. Into this the other rivers too flow together, and share their water with it, and make Peneus great. The place has resorts of many and various kinds, not the works of human hands, but the spontaneous handiwork of Nature, which took pains for beauty at the time when the region came into being. For ivy, abundant and very thick, is in its prime and flourishes, and after the manner of noble vines creeps up the lofty trees and grows together with them; and much bindweed runs up to the very crag and overshadows the rock; and the rock is hidden beneath, while all the green is seen, and it is a festival for the eyes. On the smooth and level ground there are varied groves and continuous shady retreats, most pleasant lodgings for travellers to flee to in the summer season, which gladly afford them coolness. And many springs flow through it, and streams of cold water run, most pleasant to drink. These waters are said to be good for those who bathe in them and to contribute to their health. And birds sing, scattered here and there, especially the musical ones, and they feast the ears right well, and escort the passers-by without effort and with pleasure, through their song banishing the weariness of those who go by. On either side of the river are the resorts and the resting-places already mentioned. Through the middle of Tempe the river Peneus goes, advancing slowly and gently like oil; and much shade is cast over it by the trees that grow alongside and the boughs that hang above, so that for the greater part of the day it shuts out the sunbeam as it comes on, and allows those who sail to sail in the cool. And all the people who dwell around come together, one with another, and sacrifice and hold gatherings and drink together. So, since there are many who sacrifice and who make burnt offerings continually, it is natural that most pleasant fragrances accompany those who walk and those who sail; thus does the constant honour paid to the higher powers make the place divine. There, indeed, the Thessalians say that Pythian Apollo was purified at the command of Zeus, when he had shot down with his arrows the dragon Python, who guarded Delphi, while Earth still held the oracle. Crowned, then, with a wreath of this Tempean bay, and taking a branch of the same bay into his right hand, the son of Zeus and Leto came to Delphi and took over the oracle. And there is an altar in that very place, where he both crowned himself and broke off the branch. And even now, every ninth year, the Delphians send well-born boys and one of their own number as chief delegate. These, coming there and sacrificing magnificently at Tempe, go back again, having plaited crowns of the same bay from which the god then crowned himself. And they go by that road which is called the Pythian, leading through Thessaly and Pelasgia and Oeta and the country of the Aenianes and that of the Malians and Dorians and the Western Locrians. These too escort them with reverence and honour, no less than do those who honour the men who bring the sacred things from the Hyperboreans to this same god. And indeed at the Pythian games they give the victors crowns of this bay. So much let me too now have said about Tempe in Thessaly.

Socrates used to speak of the divine sign that accompanied him to Theages and Demodocus and to many others. He said that often, by a heavenly dispensation, a voice came to him; "and whenever it comes," he said, "it always signals to me a turning-away from what I am about to do, but it never urges me on. And again, if one of my friends consults me about something, and that voice comes, once more it turns me away. In this way it advises me, and I in turn advise the one who consults me; and I do not let him act, following the divine forewarning." He offered as a witness Charmides the son of Glaucon: for Charmides told him that he intended to train for the foot-race at Nemea, and the moment he began to speak the voice came. Socrates tried to keep Charmides from holding to his purpose, but Charmides was not persuaded; and indeed his effort did not come out as it should.

They say that Hiero of Syracuse was a lover of Greek culture and honoured learning most manfully. And they tell how ready he was to do good turns; for they say that he was more eager to give than those who asked were to receive. He was also most courageous in spirit. He lived in harmony with his three brothers, untroubled by jealousy, loving them very greatly and being loved by them in turn. With him, they say, lived both Simonides and Pindar; and Simonides did not shrink, heavy though he was with age, from coming to him; for the Cean was by nature fond of money, and Hiero's generosity, they say, drew him on all the more.

Pherenice brought her son to Olympia to compete. When the Hellanodicae forbade her to watch the contest, she came forward and pleaded her case, saying that she had a father who was an Olympic victor, and three brothers, and that she herself had a son competing at Olympia; and she prevailed over the people and the law that barred women from the spectacle, and she watched the Olympic games.
Oricadmus became a lawgiver of wrestling, having devised by himself the style of wrestling called the Sicel manner.

Aspasia, the daughter of Hermotimus, the Phocaean, was reared in orphanhood, her mother having died in childbirth. So Aspasia was brought up in poverty, yet temperately and with endurance. A dream came to her often and foretold good things, hinting at her future fortune, that she would live with a man of nobility and worth. While she was still a child, there appeared on her face, just below the chin, a tumour, ugly to see, and it grieved both her father and the girl. So her father showed her to a physician; and he promised to heal it if he received three staters. The father said he had not the money, and the physician said that he himself had no remedy at hand. Aspasia was distressed, as was natural, at this, and going out of doors she wept; and holding a mirror on her knees and seeing herself in it, she was greatly pained. As she had eaten no dinner because of her grief, a very timely sleep came upon her, and with the sleep a dove appeared, and turning into a woman it said: "Take heart, and bid a long farewell to physicians and their remedies; take of the rose-garlands of Aphrodite, however dry they may now be, and rubbing them fine sprinkle them on the tumour." When the girl had heard this and done it, the tumour vanished; and Aspasia was again the fairest of her companions, having received back her beauty from the fairest of the goddesses. And she had an abundance of graces, as no other maiden of that time; her hair was golden and lightly curling, her eyes were very large, her nose a little hooked, and her ears very small. Her skin was tender, and the colour of her face was like roses. For this reason the Phocaeans, while she was still a child, called her Milto. Her lips too showed red, and her teeth were whiter than snow. Her ankles were fine, of the kind that Homer, in his own speech, gives to the most beautiful women, calling them "fair-ankled." Her voice was sweet and tender: one would have said, hearing her speak, that he was hearing a Siren. From all the busyness and fussiness of women she was free. For wealth tends to supply such things; but she, being poor and reared by a father who was himself poor, contributed nothing fussy or superfluous to her appearance. Now Aspasia once came to Cyrus, the son of Darius and Parysatis, the brother of Artaxerxes — not willingly, nor with her father's consent, but by force, such as often befalls when cities are captured or tyrants or satraps use violence. One of Cyrus's satraps, then, brought her up to Cyrus along with other maidens, and very quickly she was preferred above the other concubines for the simplicity of her character and the modesty of her manner and because she was beautiful without artifice. There helped her too, toward being loved beyond measure, the fact that she had understanding. Often, indeed, Cyrus used her as an adviser even in pressing matters, and when persuaded he did not repent of it. When Aspasia first came to Cyrus, he happened to have just risen from dinner and was about to drink in the Persian manner; for after they have eaten their fill, the Persians give themselves up zealously to wine and to toasts, as though stripping for a contest with the drink as their rival. In the middle of the drinking, then, four Greek maidens were brought before Cyrus, among them Aspasia of Phocaea. They were most finely got up; for three of them had had their hair plaited and their faces painted with cosmetics and pigments by their own attendant women, who happened to have come up with them. They had also been taught by their nurses how they must approach Cyrus and how to flatter him, and not to turn away when he came near, nor to be displeased at his touch, nor to refuse his kiss — courtesan's lessons indeed, and the practices of women who trade hucksterishly on their beauty. So they vied with one another to surpass each other in beauty. But Aspasia would not put on a costly tunic, nor consented to wrap herself in an embroidered robe, nor would she submit to bathe, but calling on all the Greek and Liberating gods, she cried aloud her father's name, and cursed herself and her father, believing that the dress and elaborate adornment of her body, contrary to her habit, was a plain and confessed slavery. When struck, she put it on by compulsion, and yielded to the orders, grieving nonetheless that she was forced to do not maidenly but courtesan's things. So the others, coming forward, looked Cyrus in the face and smiled and assumed a cheerful air; but Aspasia looked down, and her face was filled with deep flushes of fiery red, and her eyes brimmed with tears, and in every way she was plainly ashamed. When he bade the women sit near him, the rest obeyed quite readily, but the Phocaean paid no heed to the command, until the satrap who had brought her sat her down by force. And when Cyrus touched them and examined their eyes and their cheeks and their fingers, the others bore it, but she would not endure it; for when Cyrus merely touched her with the tip of his hand, she cried out and said he would weep for doing such things. Cyrus was greatly delighted at this. And when she rose up and tried to flee, because he had touched her breasts, then indeed the son of Darius admired her nobility in a manner not Persian, and looking at the man who had bought her he said: "This one alone you have brought me free and undefiled; the rest are hucksterish both in appearance and still more in manner." From this Cyrus loved her more than any human being with whom he had ever consorted. Some time later Cyrus was deeply in love with her, and was loved in return by her, and their love advanced to such a point that it was near to equality of honour, and not out of tune with the concord and temperance of a Greek marriage. So the fame of his love for Aspasia spread even to Ionia and to all Greece. The Peloponnese too was filled with talk about Cyrus and her, and the report came even to the Great King; for it was believed that Cyrus, after her, would not deign to make trial of any other woman. From this there came back to Aspasia the memory of the old visions, of that dove and of its words and of all that the goddess had foretold; and she believed that the goddess had been her guardian from the beginning, and she offered to Aphrodite rites of initiation and thank-offerings. First, then, she had an image of gold made for her, of sufficient size. She supposed this image to be Aphrodite, and she set beside it a dove studded with jewels; and every day she propitiated the goddess with sacrifices and words of good omen. She sent also to her father Hermotimus many fine gifts, and made him rich. And she lived in temperance, as the Greek and Persian women say. A necklace was once brought to Cyrus from Thessaly, the younger Scopas having sent it; and the gift had been brought to Scopas from Sicily, and the necklace seemed wrought with marvellous art and intricacy. So when all to whom Cyrus showed it were full of wonder, he, greatly pleased with the treasure, went at once to Aspasia's, at midday, and finding her asleep, he slipped under her cloak and lay quietly beside her, and waited without a sound, keeping still himself; and she slept on. When she awoke and saw Cyrus, she embraced him in her wonted way and showed him affection. He, taking the necklace from its little box, showed it, saying that it was worthy either of a king's daughter or of a king's mother. When she agreed, he said: "See, then, I give it to you to have as your own; and put it on, as you are, and show me your neck." But she was not overcome by the gift, but answered very wisely and learnedly: "And how," she said, "shall I dare to put on myself a gift worthy of Parysatis, your mother? Rather send it to her, Cyrus; and I will provide you a fair neck even without it." So Aspasia, high-mindedly and in a manner royal beyond what women do, acted the opposite of what women are wont to do; for they are terribly fond of finery. But Cyrus, pleased with the answer, kissed Aspasia, and writing down each thing that had been done and said in a letter, he sent it to his mother together with the necklace. And Parysatis, receiving the gift, was no less pleased with what was written than with the gold; and in return for this she rewarded Aspasia with great and royal gifts. For this above all delighted her, that although Aspasia stood in very high favour with her son, yet in being loved by Cyrus she wished to be surpassed by Cyrus's mother. So Aspasia praised the gifts, but said she did not need them, since money too had come to her with the gifts, very much of it; and she sent it to Cyrus, saying: "To you, who feed many men, this might be useful; but to me you suffice, being loved, and you are my adornment." By this, as was natural, she astonished Cyrus, and beyond dispute this woman was admired both for the beauty of her body and still more for the nobility of her soul. When Cyrus was killed in the battle against his brother, and Cyrus's camp was taken, she too was captured along with the other spoils — not falling into the enemy's hands at random and by chance, but King Artaxerxes sought her out with much care; for he knew her fame and her excellence. When they brought her to him in bonds, he was indignant, and threw those who had done this into prison, and ordered that costly adornment be given her. But she, unwilling and lamenting and weeping over many things, was forced to put on the king's dress; for she mourned bitterly for Cyrus. Having put it on, she appeared the fairest of women, and at once Artaxerxes was inflamed and consumed, and held her first of his women, and honoured her beyond measure by his eagerness to please her, trusting that he would persuade her to forget Cyrus and would teach her to love him no less than that man. And he attained his hope, but late and slowly; for the goodwill toward Cyrus that had melted into Aspasia had wrought in her, more than anything, a love-charm hard to wash away. Some time later Tiridates the eunuch died, the fairest and most beautiful youth in Asia; he ended his life while still in his bloom and just emerging from boyhood, and the king was said to love him most ardently. From this the king mourned most grievously and grieved most bitterly, and there was public mourning throughout all Asia, all men gratifying the king in this. And no one dared approach him or console him; for they believed that he was incurably affected by what had happened. When three days had passed, Aspasia, putting on a mourning dress, as the king was going off to his bath, stood weeping and looking at the ground; and he, seeing her, was astonished and asked the reason of her coming. And she said: "I have come, O king, to console you in your grief and pain, if it is your wish; but if you are angry, I will go back again." The Persian was greatly pleased at her care, and bade her go up to the chamber and await him; and she did so. When he returned, he put the eunuch's robe over Aspasia's black dress; and somehow the youth's garb suited her, and her beauty shone out all the more to her lover. When once he was won over by this, he begged her, until the keenness of his grief should fade, to come to him dressed thus. And she, to please him, was persuaded; and she alone of all in Asia — not of the women only, they say, but of the king's sons and kinsmen — consoled Artaxerxes and healed the affliction of his grief, the king yielding to her care and wisely persuaded by her consolation.

This is an Arcadian tale about Atalanta the daughter of Iasion. Her father, when she was born, exposed her; for he said that he had need not of daughters but of sons. But the man who took her to expose her did not kill her, and going to Mount Parthenium he laid her near a spring; and there was a hollow rock there, and above it lay a thick-covered thicket. Death had been decreed for the infant, but she was not betrayed by fortune; for a little later a bear, robbed of her own cubs by hunters, came, her teats swollen and heavy with milk. Then, by some divine guidance, taking pleasure in the infant, she suckled it, and at once the beast was relieved of its pain and gave nourishment to the infant. And so, again pouring out her milk and giving suck, since she had not remained a mother to her own, she became nurse to one who was nothing to her. The hunters who from the first had plotted against the beast over her offspring kept watch on her, and having observed each thing that was done, when the bear had gone off as usual to hunt and graze, they carried off Atalanta — though she was not yet so called, for they themselves gave her the name. And she was reared by them on a mountain diet. Little by little her body grew with her age; and she loved virginity and shunned the company of men and longed for solitude, taking the highest of the Arcadian mountains, where there was a well-watered glen and great oaks, and also pines and the deep shade they cast. For what harm does it do us to hear of Atalanta's cave too, as of Calypso's in Homer? In the hollow ravine there was a cave, one and very deep, and in front it was guarded by a deep precipice. Ivy crept around it, and the ivy twined with soft trees and crept up through them. Crocuses too grew about the place in the soft and deep grass. And with them sprang up the hyacinth and many another colour of flowers, able not only to furnish a feast for the eyes, but the scents from them filled the air all around; and one could keep festival both in other ways and feast upon the fragrance. There were many laurels too, the sweet foliage of a plant ever in its bloom to look upon; and vines, flourishing with very plentiful clusters before the cave, displayed the industry of Atalanta. And waters perpetual and ever-flowing, clear to see and cold, as far as one could judge by touch and tell by drinking, flowed in abundance and without stint; and these same waters were also fit for the watering of the trees aforesaid, flowing continually and helping toward their life. So the place was full of graces, and showed at once a most venerable and a chaste maiden's chamber. Atalanta's bedding was the hides of the beasts she had hunted, her food their flesh, her drink the water. She wore a plain dress, of a kind not out of tune with Artemis; for she said that she emulated the goddess both in this and in wishing to be a virgin throughout. She was very swift of foot, and neither beast nor man plotting against her could escape her; and when she wished to flee, no one could overtake her. And not only those who saw her loved her, but already from report men loved her too. Come, let me describe her appearance too, if it does no harm; and it does none, since from this too may be gained both experience and art of words. In height, while still a child, she was beyond grown women; and she was beautiful, as no other of the maidens then in the Peloponnese. Her look was masculine and fierce, this both from her wild rearing and now too from her exercises in the mountains. She had nothing girlish or delicate; for she did not come forth from a bridal chamber, nor was she of those reared under mothers and nurses. Nor did she have the over-plump body either, and that quite naturally, since in the hunts and at the very exercises she worked her whole body hard. Her hair was golden, in no way by womanly fussiness and dyes and cosmetics, but the colour was the work of nature. Her face was reddened too by the suns, and looked like a flush outright. And what flower could be so beautiful as the face of a maiden trained to modesty? She had two startling things: matchless beauty, and with it the power to frighten too. No idle man would have loved her at the sight, nor would he even have dared to look her in the face at first; so great was the radiance that shone, with her beauty, on those who saw her. She was hard to meet, both in other ways and for her rarity. For one could not easily see her; but unexpectedly and unforeseen she would appear, chasing a beast or defending herself against someone, darting like a star, then she would hide herself, running through a thicket or a copse or some other dense growth in the mountain. Once, at midnight, those who dwelt near her — bold lovers and most tiresome revellers — came in revel, two of the Centaurs, Hylaeus and Rhoecus. Their revel was no flute-girls nor indeed the doings of the young men of the city, but pine-torches, and lighting and kindling these, by the first appearance of the fire they would have startled even a whole people, let alone a single maiden. Breaking off fresh-cut boughs of pines, then plaiting them together, they made themselves crowns. Continually and frequently clashing their weapons through the mountains, setting fire to the trees as well, they pressed on toward the girl, evil suitors, with insolence and frenzy paying beforehand the wedding-gifts of their marriage. But the plot did not escape her; seeing the fire from the cave and recognizing who these revellers were, in no way dismayed nor cowering at the sight, she bent her bow, let fly her arrow, and hit the first very opportunely. And he lay there, while the second came on, no longer in revel-fashion but now in war-fashion, wishing to defend his comrade and to glut his own onset. But to him too the girl's other arrow came as avenger. So much, then, for Atalanta the daughter of Iasion.

Aristotle the son of Nicomachus, a wise man both in being so and in seeming so, when someone took from him the honours that had been decreed him at Delphi, wrote to Antipater about these matters thus: "Concerning the honours decreed me at Delphi and of which I have now been deprived, I am so disposed as neither to care greatly about them nor to care nothing at all." This would not be love of glory, nor would I myself condemn any such thing in Aristotle, but, being right-minded, he thought it was not the same thing not to receive some honour and, having received it, to be deprived of it. For the one, not to attain it, is no great matter; but the painful thing is to attain it and then to be robbed of it.

Weaving and the loom, gifts of the goddess Ergane, the spiders neither know nor wish to know. For what use would such a creature have for a garment of that kind? Their web is rather a trap, a kind of fish-basket for whatever falls into it. The spider keeps her watch over the snare entirely motionless, and seems lifeless; and once something — whatever it may be — has fallen in, she has her feast. Only so much falls in as the web can hold, and that is enough to make her a meal.

Once, when Megabyzus was praising poor and unskilful paintings and finding fault with others laboriously and well executed, the boys of Zeuxis who were grinding the ochre laughed at him. Zeuxis therefore said: "While you keep silent, Megabyzus, these boys admire you, for they see your clothing and the attendants about you; but whenever you wish to say something about art, they despise you. Guard yourself, then, among those who are praised, by keeping a hold on your tongue and not playing the connoisseur about matters that are none of your concern."

To Anaxagoras of Clazomenae, while he was earnestly conversing with his friends, someone came and said that his two sons had died — the only sons Anaxagoras had. And he, in no way disturbed, said: "I knew, when I begot them, that I had begotten mortals."

Hipparchus, the eldest of the sons of Pisistratus, was the wisest of the Athenians. He was the first to bring the verses of Homer to Athens, and he compelled the rhapsodes to sing them at the Panathenaea. He also sent a fifty-oared ship to fetch Anacreon of Teos to him. And Simonides of Ceos he kept always near him with great eagerness, winning him over, as one would expect, with great gifts and fees; for that Simonides was fond of money, no one will deny. The care of educated men was indeed this Hipparchus's chief concern. He wished the Athenians to be educated under his own patronage, and he was eager to rule over them while they grew better men; for he thought one ought to envy no man his wisdom, being himself a man of nobility and worth. So Plato says, if indeed the Hipparchus is truly Plato's.

In Aegina the victory of Taurosthenes at Olympia was announced to his father on the very same day by an apparition, so they say. Others say that Taurosthenes had brought a dove with him, taking it from its young, which were still wet and unfledged, and that on winning he released the dove, having fastened purple to it; and the bird, hastening to its young, made the journey from Pisa to Aegina in a single day.

Lais, when she saw Eubotas of Cyrene, fell most ardently in love with him, and made proposals of marriage. He, fearing some plot from her, promised that he would do so; yet Eubotas did not consort with her, living a temperate life. His promise was to be fulfilled after the contest. Having won, then, that he might not seem to have broken his agreements with the woman, he had a portrait of Lais painted and carried it to Cyrene, saying that he was bringing Lais and not breaking the compact. In return for this the wife whom he married lawfully set up for him a most enormous statue in Cyrene, rewarding him for his self-restraint.

There were the verses of Oroebantius of Troezen before Homer, as the Troezenian accounts say. And Dares the Phrygian, whose Phrygian Iliad is still preserved even now, as I know, they say lived before Homer too. Melesander of Miletus wrote of the battle of the Lapiths and Centaurs.

There was a man of Mytilene, Macareus by name, a priest of Dionysus, who, so far as appearance went, was gentle and fair, but most impious of men above all. A stranger came to him and gave him a great quantity of gold for safekeeping; and Macareus, digging up the ground in the innermost part of the temple, buried the gold. In time the stranger came and demanded the gold back. He, leading him inside as though to give it back, cut his throat, dug up the gold, and put the stranger in its place; and he thought that, as he had escaped men's notice, so he would escape the god's too. But this turned out not so; how could it? When a little time had passed, the god's triennial festival came, and he sacrificed magnificently. And while he was occupied with the Bacchic rites, his children, two in number, were left behind inside the house, and imitating their father's sacred rite they came to the ancestral altar while the offerings were still burning; and the younger offered his neck, and the elder, finding a sacrificial knife that had been left lying, killed his brother like a victim. Those in the house, seeing it, cried out. The mother, hearing the cry, rushed out, and seeing the one dead and the other still holding the bloody knife, snatched up a half-burnt billet from the altar and with it killed the boy. News came to Macareus, and leaving the rite, just as he was, with wrath and fury he rushed into the house, and with the thyrsus he was holding killed his own wife. So his deeds became known to all, and Macareus, arrested and tortured, confessed all that he had done in the temple; and amid the very tortures he gave up his life. And the man unlawfully slain came to public honour, and was buried at the god's command. So Macareus paid no slight penalty — to use the poet's phrase — with his own head and his wife's and, moreover, his children's too.
Agesilaus praised those of the barbarians who broke their oaths, because, having made the gods their enemies by their perjuries, they made them friends and allies to himself.

The Egyptian frogs are a clever sort of creature, and far surpass the rest of their kind. For if a frog meets with a water-snake, a creature bred of the Nile, it bites crosswise on a piece of reed and carries it, holding fast and not letting go by main force. The snake then is unable to swallow the frog along with the reed, for it cannot open its mouth wide enough to take in what the reed holds apart. And so by their cleverness the frogs prevail over the strength of the water-snakes.

Alexander, when he beheld the portrait of himself at Ephesus painted by Apelles, did not praise it as the work deserved. But when the horse was led in and neighed at the horse in the picture as though at a real and living one, Apelles said: "O king, the horse seems to be a far better judge of painting than you."

To Xenophon, as he was sacrificing, a messenger came from Mantinea, saying that his son Gryllus was dead. He laid aside his crown, but went on sacrificing. But when the messenger added to his former words this also, that he had died victorious, Xenophon set the crown again upon his head. These things are commonly known and have gone out to many.

There is this Attic custom: when the ox has been slaughtered, they acquit all the others, judging each in turn for the killing; but they condemn the knife, and say that it killed the animal. And the day on which they do this they call the festival of the Dipolia, and also the Bouphonia.

Alexander indulged his companions, allowing them to live in luxury, seeing that even Hagnon wore golden nails in his boots. Cleitus, whenever he was about to give audience to anyone, would receive his petitioners while walking upon purple cloths. Perdiccas and Craterus, being fond of exercise, were followed by hides a stade in size, beneath which they would enclose a large space in their encampments and take their exercise. Much dust too followed them, brought on pack-animals, useful for their wrestling-grounds. Leonnatus and Menelaus, being fond of hunting, were followed by hunting-nets a hundred stades long. As for Alexander himself, his tent held a hundred couches, and fifty golden columns divided it and held up its roof; the roof itself was gilded throughout and wrought with costly embroideries. And first, within, stood five hundred Persians called the apple-bearers, dressed in robes of purple and quince-yellow; above them a thousand archers, clothed in flame-colour and scarlet; before these, five hundred Macedonians with silver shields. In the middle of the tent a golden throne was set, and seated upon it Alexander gave audience, with his bodyguards standing about him on every side. Around the tent ran an enclosure, where there were a thousand Macedonians and ten thousand Persians. And no one dared approach him easily; for great was the fear of him, lifted up as he was by pride and fortune into tyranny.

The chicks of partridges, as soon as they get their feet out of the shell, are from that moment most swift of foot. The chicks of ducks swim the very moment they come from the womb. And the cubs of lions claw the wombs of their mothers, eager to come to the light.
Iccus of Tarentum was the first to take up wrestling, having lived the period of his training most temperately, passing his life on a strict diet, and remaining ignorant of love throughout.

Epaminondas, when he was mortally wounded at Mantinea, was carried to his tent still breathing, and called for Daiphantus, that he might appoint him general; but they said the man was dead. Then he asked that Iolaidas be called quickly. When he too was said to be dead, he advised them to make terms with the enemy and form a friendship, since no general was left in Thebes.

Xerxes the son of Darius, digging up the tomb of the ancient Belus, found a glass coffin, where the corpse lay in oil. The coffin was not full, but fell short of the rim by about a hand's breadth. Beside the coffin lay a short pillar, on which was written: "For him who opens the tomb and does not fill up the coffin, it shall not be better." Reading this, Xerxes was afraid, and ordered oil to be poured in as quickly as possible; yet it was not filled. He ordered more to be poured in. But it took no increase, until he gave up, spending in vain what he poured. Shutting up the tomb, he went away in distress. And the pillar did not lie in what it had foretold; for having gathered seven hundred thousand men against the Greeks, he fared ill, then returning home died the most shameful of deaths, slain by night in his bed by his son.

Timotheus the son of Conon said the best thing of all against Aristophon of the deme Azenia. For since Aristophon was a spendthrift, Timotheus touched him most bitterly, saying: "He for whom nothing is enough — for that man nothing is shameful."

Here too is a clever thing about the Egyptian dog. They do not drink from the river all at once, nor without restraint, nor freely, stooping down and lapping up as much as their thirst demands; for they are wary of the beasts in the water. Instead they run along the bank, and stealthily drink as much as they can snatch, again and again. So, drinking at intervals, they satisfy themselves; yet they do not perish, and they cure their thirst all the same.

I wish to tell you of a deed of Phalaris not at all in keeping with his usual character; for the deed proclaims an irresistible humanity, and on that account seems foreign to him. Chariton was a man of Acragas, a lover of beauty and passionately devoted to the bloom of youth; and he loved with the fiercest ardour Melanippus, a man of Acragas, excellent in soul and outstanding in beauty. This Melanippus was wronged in something by Phalaris; for when he was at law with one of the tyrant's own friends, Phalaris ordered him to drop the suit. When he would not obey, the tyrant threatened to do the worst to him if he did not yield. So the friend, by the necessity Phalaris imposed, won the case against justice, and the magistrates destroyed the record of the trial. The young man bore this grievously, saying he had been outraged, and confessed his anger to his lover, and begged him to share in the attack upon the tyrant; and he was eager to take in others among the young men whom he knew to be hottest for such an undertaking. Chariton, seeing him in a frenzy and inflamed with anger, and knowing that none of the citizens would join them for fear of the tyrant, said that he too had long desired this and was zealous by every means to deliver his country from the slavery that had overtaken it; but that it was not safe to make such matters known to many. He asked Melanippus, then, to let him consider these things more carefully, and to allow him to watch for the right moment for the deed. The youth agreed. So Chariton, taking the whole hazard upon himself, and unwilling to take his beloved as a partner — so that, if he were caught, he alone might suffer the penalty and not drag the other into the same — when it seemed to him the time was right, took a dagger and set out against the tyrant. He did not, however, escape notice, for the bodyguards kept watch over such things very strictly. Thrown into prison by Phalaris and racked to make him name his accomplices, he endured it and bore up under the tortures. But when this dragged on, Melanippus came to Phalaris and confessed that he was not only an accomplice of Chariton, but had himself begun the plot. When Phalaris asked the reason, he told the whole story from the beginning and the suppression of the record, and confessed that he had been deeply aggrieved by it. Phalaris, then, marvelling at them both, released them from punishment, ordering them to leave that very day not only the city of Acragas but Sicily itself; yet he allowed them to enjoy their own rightful property. These men the Pythia afterward celebrated, and their love, in these verses: "Guides divine of love to mortal men, blessed were Chariton and Melanippus born" — the god calling their love a divine friendship.

Dion, the son of Hipparinus and the disciple of Plato, happened to be conducting some public and common business, when his son, falling from the roof into the courtyard, ended his life. He changed nothing at this, but continued doing what he had been doing from the first.

They say that Poliarchus the Athenian went so far in luxury that he had even those dogs and cocks in which he delighted carried out to public burial when they died. He invited his friends to their funeral, buried them lavishly, and set up monuments over them, carving epitaphs upon them.

Polycrates of Samos dwelt among the Muses, and he honoured Anacreon of Teos and held him in esteem, and delighted in him and in his songs. But I do not praise his luxury. Anacreon praised Smerdies, Polycrates's favourite, rather too warmly, and the youth took pleasure in the praise, and embraced Anacreon with great dignity, since the poet loved his soul, not his body. For let no one, in the gods' name, slander the poet of Teos to us, nor say that he was a man without restraint. But Polycrates grew jealous because Anacreon honoured Smerdies, and saw that the poet was loved by the boy in return; and Polycrates sheared the boy's hair, to disgrace him, thinking thereby to grieve Anacreon. But Anacreon, with self-command and restraint, made no pretence of blaming Polycrates, but turned the reproach upon the youth, charging him with rashness and folly for arming himself against his own hair. As for the song upon the cutting of the hair, let Anacreon sing it; for he will sing it better than I.
Alexander son of Philip, having marched four hundred stades three times in succession under arms, joined battle with the enemy and, before he had let his army rest, mastered his foes.

They say that Agathocles the tyrant of Sicily had a most ludicrous disfigurement of the head. For as it grew bald, his hair gradually falling out, he, ashamed of it, made a covering for his hair, a crown of myrtle; and it was a screen for his baldness. The Syracusans, however, knew of the baldness, and were not ignorant of the plot of the hair against him, but kept silent because of the madness of his audacities and impieties.
The Egyptians say that Sesostris was instructed in the laws by Hermes.

King Archelaus prepared a costly feast for his companions. As the drinking went on, Euripides, having drunk rather strong wine, was somehow drawn little by little into intoxication; then, embracing Agathon the tragic poet, who was reclining beside him, he kissed him, though he was about forty years old. When Archelaus asked whether he still seemed to him to be a beloved, he answered: "Yes, by Zeus; for not only the spring of the beautiful is fairest, but the autumn too."

Aristides the Locrian, bitten by a Tartessian weasel and dying, said that it would have been much more pleasant to him to die bitten by a lion or a leopard, if indeed death needed some pretext, and that by such a beast — bearing, as it seems to me, the disgrace of the bite much harder than death itself.

There is a law of the Lucanians, so I am told, that if a stranger arrives after sunset and wishes to enter someone's house for shelter, and the man does not receive him, he is fined and made to answer for his inhospitality — to the visitor himself, I suppose, and to Zeus the protector of strangers. I am told that the Dardanians from Illyria bathe only three times in the whole of their lives: at birth, at marriage, and at death. The Indians neither lend at interest nor know how to borrow; indeed it is not lawful for an Indian either to wrong another or to be wronged, and for this reason they make no written contract and accept no deposit. There is a Sardinian law by which sons would beat their fathers to death with clubs once they had grown old, and bury them, holding it disgraceful for a man far advanced in age to go on living, since the body, worn out by age, errs in many ways. There is another law of the same people: there were prosecutions for idleness, and the man who lived aimlessly had to stand trial and render account, showing the source of his living. The Assyrians gather their maidens of marriageable age into some city and put them up for public auction, and each man leads home as his bride the one he has bought. A man of Byblos who comes upon anything on the road that he did not himself set down takes nothing of it, for he regards such a find not as a windfall but as an act of injustice. The Derbices put to death those who have lived beyond seventy years, slaughtering the men as sacrifices and strangling the women. The Colchians bury their dead in hides and, having sewn them up, hang them from trees. Among the Lydians it was the custom that women should be courtesans before marriage, but once joined in wedlock to live chastely; and for a woman who erred with another man there was no possibility of pardon.

There is a story in circulation about Nicostratus the cithara-player, that in a dispute about music with Laodocus the singer to the cithara he said that the other was a small man in a great art, while he himself was a great man in a small one. It seems, then, that it is a fine thing not only to increase a household and wealth, but an art as well — if one ought to give any weight to Nicostratus, who put this so well and gracefully.

Polygnotus of Thasos and Dionysius of Colophon were painters. Polygnotus painted on the grand scale and worked out his subjects in figures of full size; the work of Dionysius, except in scale, imitated the art of Polygnotus down to the last detail — feeling, character, the disposition of the figures, the fineness of the drapery, and all the rest.

I am told there is a law in force at Thebes ordering craftsmen, both painters and sculptors, to render their likenesses toward the better. The law threatens with a fine — a fixed penalty in money — anyone who ever models or paints toward the worse.

Men have remembered benefits and repaid gratitude for them. Theseus did so to Heracles. For when Aïdoneus, king of the Molossians, had bound Theseus — at the time when he came with Pirithous to carry off the king's wife, not seeking the marriage for himself but doing it to oblige Pirithous — Heracles came among the Molossians and rescued Theseus; and on this account Theseus set up an altar to him. The Seven against Thebes too repaid gratitude to Pronax. For when Pronax had died on their account, they founded the contest in his honour, which most people suppose was first held in honour of Archemorus. Heracles also repaid gratitude to Nestor. For when Neleus refused to purify him, his other sons sided with Neleus, but Nestor did not; and for this reason, when Heracles took Pylos, he killed Neleus and his other sons, but not only spared Nestor: he granted him to hold his father's kingdom. The Athenians too, as a whole people, repaid gratitude to the descendants of Heracles. Since their forefather had been a benefactor to Theseus, the Athenians on this account brought them back into the Peloponnese. Heracles also repaid gratitude to the three hundred and sixty men of Cleonae. For when they had marched with him against the Molionidae and died nobly and well, he handed over to them the honours he had received at Nemea from the Nemeans, which they had given him when he overcame the lion that haunted their land and ruined their crops. Menestheus, the son of Peteos, too was not ungrateful toward the sons of Tyndareus. For when they had expelled the sons of Theseus and taken captive Aethra, the mother of Theseus, they gave the kingdom to Menestheus; and on this account Menestheus was the first to name them Lords and Saviours. Darius too, the son of Hystaspes, having received a cloak from Syloson while he was still a private man, gave him, when he came into possession of the kingdom, the rule of his own homeland Samos — gold for bronze, one might say.
When the Lacedaemonians wished to destroy the city of the Athenians, they consulted the god; and he answered that they should not stir the common hearth of Greece.

There was no profit, then, even in death for the wicked, since not even then do they find rest, but either they are wholly deprived of burial, or, even if they manage to be buried, they are nonetheless cast out from this last honour and from the common anchorage of all bodies. The Lacedaemonians, at any rate, when Pausanias took the side of the Medes, not only put him to death by starvation, but also cast his corpse outside their borders — so Epitimides says.

And then, who does not know how sudden and swift are the reversals of fortune? The Lacedaemonians, at any rate, who once ruled over the Thebans, were themselves in turn so mastered by them that the Thebans not only reached the Peloponnese but crossed the Eurotas and ravaged the territory of the Lacedaemonians. They very nearly took the city itself, had not Epaminondas feared that all the Peloponnesians might join in common cause and fight on behalf of Sparta. Dionysius the tyrant, when he was reduced to a siege by the Carthaginians and no hope of safety appeared, was himself disheartened and was contemplating flight. But one of his companions, a man named Ellopides, came to him and said: "Dionysius, tyranny is a fine shroud." Shamed by this, he regained his resolve, and with a few men overcame many tens of thousands, and even enlarged his rule. Amyntas the Macedonian too, when he had been defeated by the neighbouring barbarians and had lost his rule, was minded to abandon the country entirely; he would have been content if only he could save himself alone. But while he was in this state, someone repeated to him the words of Ellopides. And seizing a small piece of ground and gathering a few soldiers, he recovered his rule. The Egyptians called Ochus, in their native tongue, "the Ass," reproaching the sluggishness of his mind by reference to the dullness of that animal. In return for this he forcibly sacrificed Apis to an ass. Dion the son of Hipparinus, an exile under Dionysius, came back to war against him with two thousand soldiers, and made him what he had himself formerly been — an exile. And the Syracusans, drawing up nine triremes against the hundred and fifty of the Carthaginians, were greatly victorious.

Plato the son of Ariston once shared a tent at Olympia with men he did not know, and to whom he himself was unknown. So thoroughly did he win them over and bind them to him by his company — dining with them simply and spending his whole days with them in everything — that the strangers were delighted by their meeting with the man. He made no mention of the Academy or of Socrates; he revealed this one thing only to them, that his name was Plato. When they came to Athens, he received them very warmly and kindly. And the strangers said: "Come now, Plato, show us your namesake too, the associate of Socrates; lead us to his Academy and introduce us to the man, so that we too may gain something from him." But he, smiling gently, as was his way, said: "But I am that very man." They were astonished that, having so great a man among them, they had failed to recognize him — since he had kept their company without pretension and unaffectedly, and had shown that he could win over his companions even without his usual discourses. Plato used to call Aristotle "the Colt." What did he mean by that name? Clearly it is agreed that a colt, when it has had its fill of its mother's milk, kicks its mother. Plato was hinting, then, at a certain ingratitude in Aristotle. For Aristotle, having received from Plato the greatest seeds and provisions for philosophy, then, glutted with the best of them and breaking the bit, built a rival school against him and led a rival band of companions and associates about in the walkway, eager to be Plato's antagonist.

And then, was not Pericles, the son of Xanthippus, attentive to the Athenian people? So it seems to me. As often, at any rate, as he was about to come before the assembly, he prayed that no such word might rise to his lips as would tend to exasperate the people, proving offensive to them and giving an impression he did not intend.
Diogenes used to say that even Socrates himself lived in luxury; for he had taken needless trouble over his little house, his little couch, and the sandals which Socrates would sometimes wear.

Zeuxis of Heraclea, when he painted his Helen, made a great deal of money from that picture. For he did not allow those who wished it to look at her freely, at random and as chance permitted, but a fixed sum of silver had to be paid down, and only then might one view her. Since, then, the man of Heraclea took a fee for the painting, the Greeks of that time called that Helen of his "the Courtesan."

Epicurus of Gargettus used to cry aloud, saying: "He for whom a little is not enough — for him nothing is enough." He also said he was ready to contend even with Zeus for happiness, having a barley-cake and water. What Epicurus had in mind in praising pleasure, while thinking such thoughts as these, we shall learn another time.

Often money gathered penny by penny with much toil drains away, as Archilochus says, into the belly of a harlot woman. For just as a sea-urchin is easy to grasp but hard to hold, so it is with money too. And Anaxagoras, in his work On Kingship, says that it is hard to gather money together, but harder to set a guard around it.

They say that Hieron, the tyrant of Sicily, was at first a private man and the most unmusical of men, and that in his boorishness he differed not in the least from his brother Gelon; but when it happened that he fell ill, he became the most cultivated of men, devoting the leisure that came of his sickness to refined entertainments. So when Hieron had recovered his strength, he kept company with Simonides of Ceos and Pindar of Thebes and Bacchylides of Iulis. But Gelon was an unmusical man. They say that Ptolemy the Second too became most cultivated, having himself also fallen ill. And Plato says that Theages took up philosophy for no other reason than the care of his sickness; for it, keeping him from public affairs, drove him into the love of wisdom. And what man of sense would not have wished sickness also upon Alcibiades and Critias and Pausanias the Lacedaemonian and others? Upon Alcibiades and Critias, so that they might not run away from Socrates — the one to become insolent and at one time a lover of Sparta, at another to ape the Boeotian character, and then again the Thessalian, and to take pleasure in the ways of the Medes and Persians when he was at the court of Pharnabazus; while Critias became most tyrannical and bloodthirsty, grieved his country much, and, hated himself, ended his life. Strato too, the son of Corragus, seems to have fallen ill at the right moment; for, though well born and well off in wealth, he did not exercise. Suffering from his spleen and needing the treatment that comes from the gymnasium, he at first used it only so far as to recover his health; but advancing in the art and making it his business, he won at Olympia in a single day both wrestling and the pancratium, and again at the next Olympiad, and at Nemea, and at Pytho, and at the Isthmus. Democrates the wrestler, when he himself had fallen ill in the feet, would go to the contests and stand in the stadium, draw a circle round himself, and bid his opponents drag him outside the line; but they were defeated, unable to do it. He, standing firm and steadfast in his stance, would go off crowned.

If a man attaches himself to Callias, Callias will make him a lover of drink; if to Ismenias, a flute-player; a braggart, if to Alcibiades; a cook, if to Crobylus; a clever speaker, if to Demosthenes; a good general, if to Epaminondas; high-minded, if to Agesilaus; honest, if to Phocion; just, if to Aristides; wise, if to Socrates.

Pythagoras taught men that he had sprung from better seed than belongs to mortal nature; for on the same day and at the same hour, they say, he was seen both at Metapontum and at Croton. At Olympia, too, he displayed that one of his thighs was of gold. And he reminded Myllias of Croton that he was Midas the son of Gordius, the Phrygian. He stroked the white eagle, which submitted to him. He was also greeted as he was crossing the river Cosa, the river saying to him: "Greetings, Pythagoras." He used to say that the leaf of the mallow was the most sacred of things. He said that number was the wisest of all things, and second to it the man who gave things their names. He explained earthquakes as nothing other than a gathering of the dead. The rainbow, he said, was a beam of the sun. And the sound that often falls upon the ears was the voice of higher beings. It was not possible to raise a question with him about anything, or to ask anything further about what he had said; instead, the men of that time attended to his words as to a divine oracle. As he made his way about the cities, the report went round that Pythagoras had come not to teach but to heal. This same Pythagoras enjoined men to abstain from the heart, and from a white cock, and above all from things that have died of themselves, and not to use the public bath nor to walk the highways; for it is unclear whether those very things are clean.

When Plato came down to Sicily at the summons of Dionysius, who had sent him many invitations one after another, and Dionysius brought him up onto his chariot — himself driving, and making the son of Ariston his fellow-rider — then, they say, a Syracusan, a man of charm and not unschooled in Homer, delighted at the sight, recited those lines from the Iliad, slightly altered: "And loudly groaned the oaken axle under the weight; for it bore a mortal man, and the best of men." Though suspicious of everyone, Dionysius nevertheless had so much respect for Plato that he alone entered his presence without being searched, even though Dionysius knew him to be a friend of Dion to the last degree.

Philip the Macedonian was said to be not only good at war and a clever speaker, but to honour education most manfully. By furnishing Aristotle with abundant wealth, at all events, he was the cause of much wide experience besides — and in particular of the knowledge concerning animals; for the son of Nicomachus reaped the fruit of his Inquiry into Animals through the resources provided by Philip. He honoured Plato too, and Theophrastus.

The story goes that Democritus of Abdera, wise in other respects as well, desired in particular to escape notice, and set about this very thing in earnest. For this reason he travelled over much of the earth. He came to the Chaldaeans at Babylon, and to the Magi, and to the sages of the Indians. When his father Damasippus's estate was divided into three parts among his three sons, he took only the silver as provision for his journey and left the rest to his brothers. For this very reason Theophrastus praised him, that he travelled about gathering a better harvest than Menelaus and Odysseus. For those men wandered, differing in nothing from Phoenician traders; they amassed wealth, and this was the pretext for their voyaging and sailing about. The Abderites used to call Democritus "Philosophy," and Protagoras "Argument." Democritus laughed at everyone and said they were mad; whence his fellow-citizens called him "the Laugher." These same people say that Hippocrates, at their first meeting, took Democritus for a madman, but as their conversation went on, came to admire the man beyond measure. And they say that Hippocrates, though a Dorian, nevertheless wrote his treatises in the Ionic dialect for Democritus's sake.
The beloved of Socrates was Alcibiades, and of Plato, Dion. Dion, indeed, profited something from his lover.

The Athenians of old wore purple cloaks and put on embroidered tunics. They bound up the hair on their heads in topknots, threading golden cicadas into it, and went about decked with other added ornaments of gold. Their slaves carried folding stools behind them, so that they should not seat themselves at random and as chance allowed. Such were the men who won the battle at Marathon.

Pericles, and Callias the son of Hipponicus, and Nicias of Pergase were brought to poverty by prodigality and a life of pleasure. For when their money failed them, the three drank hemlock to one another as a final toast, and so took their leave, as if from a banquet.

Leoprepes of Ceos, the father of Simonides, once happened to be sitting in a wrestling-school; then some young men, intimate with one another, asked the man how their friendship might best be made to last. He said: "If you give way to each other's anger and do not, by coming to grips with your passion, then provoke one another against each other."

Thrasyllus of Aexone fell ill of a strange and novel madness. For leaving the city and going down to the Piraeus and living there, he believed that all the ships putting in there were his own; he registered them and sent them off again, and rejoiced over those that came safe and entered the harbour; and he continued for many years dwelling with this affliction. When his brother arrived from Sicily, he handed him over to a physician to be cured, and the physician stopped him of his disease. But Thrasyllus often recalled his time in madness, and said that he had never taken such pleasure as he then took in the ships that came safe to harbour, though none of them belonged to him at all.

Xanthus the lyric poet — and he was older than Stesichorus of Himera — says that Electra, the daughter of Agamemnon, did not have this name at first, but was called Laodice. But when Agamemnon was slain, and Aegisthus married Clytemnestra and reigned, since she remained unbedded and was growing old a virgin, the Argives called her Electra because she had no share of a husband and had had no experience of the marriage-bed.

Pamphaes of Priene presented Croesus the Lydian with thirty minae while his father was still alive. And when Croesus succeeded to the kingdom, he sent him a wagon full of silver. Diogenes, having received a small coin from Diotimus of Carystus, said: "May the gods grant you all that your heart desires — a husband and a household." For Diotimus seemed somewhat effeminate.

Pherecydes of Syros ended his life most painfully of all men, his whole body being consumed by lice; and as his appearance grew loathsome, he avoided the company of his acquaintances. Whenever anyone came and asked how he was faring, he would put his finger, stripped bare of its flesh, through the hole in the door, and say that his whole body was in such a state. The people of Delos say that the god at Delos, in anger, brought this upon him. For sitting in Delos with his disciples, he said, among much else about his own wisdom, this in particular: that he had sacrificed to none of the gods, and yet had lived no less pleasantly and free of pain than those who offer up whole hecatombs. For this idle boasting he paid the heaviest penalty.

For indeed I cannot persuade myself not to laugh at Alexander the son of Philip, if it is true that, hearing Democritus say in his writings that there are countless worlds, he was distressed that he was not master even of the one and common world. How greatly would Democritus himself have laughed at him — what need is there even to say it, when this was his very business?

The fox: not only is the land creature cunning, but the sea-fox too is full of craft. It is not wary of the bait, nor on its guard against it, because of its greed; yet it utterly despises the hook. For before the angler can draw up his rod, the fish leaps up, bites through the line, and swims off again. Often it has swallowed two or three hooks, and the fisherman has not dined upon it as it makes its way off through the sea.

The Lacedaemonians practised a remarkable economy of time, husbanding it from every quarter for pressing needs, and allowing none of the citizens either to take their ease or be idle with it, lest, being spent on things outside virtue, it should be wasted to no purpose. A proof of this, among others, is the following. When the ephors of the Lacedaemonians heard that those who had seized Decelea were taking an afternoon walk, they sent word to them: "Do not take walks" — implying that they were living softly rather than training the body. For the Lacedaemonians must procure their health not through walking but through the exercises of the gymnasium.

They say that Antigonus the Second, when some men brought to him his son's corpse from the battle-line, looked at him, but did not change colour, nor did he weep over him; rather, praising him as a good soldier, he ordered him to be buried.

Neleus son of Codrus, having no share in the kingship, left Athens because the Pythia had bestowed the rule on Medon; and he set out to found a colony. He put in at Naxos, not by choice but forced by a storm; and when he wished to sail away, contrary winds blowing against him prevented him. As he was at a loss what to do in his straits, the seers said that the camp must be purified, since many sailed with him whose hands were not clean. So he himself pretended to have killed a child and to need purification; and he withdrew, and persuaded the others who shared the same guilt to do likewise. When this had happened and those men had been found out, he abandoned them, and they settled Naxos. But Neleus came to Ionia, and first founded Miletus, having driven out the Carians and the Mygdonians and the Leleges and other barbarians, from whom the twelve cities in Ionia took their name. These are they: Miletus, Ephesus, Erythrae, Clazomenae, Priene, Lebedos, Teos, Colophon, Myus, Phocaea, Samos, and Chios. And later he founded many other cities on the mainland.

When Hiero came to Olympia at the holding of the Olympic games, bringing horses, Themistocles barred him from the contest, saying that one who had not taken part in the greatest of dangers ought not to take part in the festival; and Themistocles was praised for it.

This is a Phrygian tale, for it belongs to Aesop the Phrygian. The tale says that the sow, if anyone touches her, squeals, and with good reason; for the sow has neither wool nor milk nor anything else but her flesh. So at once she dreams of death, knowing for what purpose she is by nature useful to those who will use her. And tyrants are like Aesop's sow, suspecting and fearing everything; for they know that, just as the sows do, they too owe their lives to all.

Some men were sacrificing at Delphi. The Delphians, plotting against them, secretly put some of the sacred treasures into their baskets, where they had their frankincense and cakes. So, having seized them as temple-robbers, they led them off to the rock and hurled them down according to the Delphic law.
Lais the courtesan, as Aristophanes of Byzantium says, was also called "the Axe." This surname convicted her of the savagery of her character.

They say that Laius was the first to fall in love with noble youths, having carried off Chrysippus the son of Pelops. And from this it seemed to the Thebans one of the fine things to love youths in their bloom.

The Athenians did not make use only of those of their own citizens who were fit for office and command, but they chose foreigners too and entrusted public affairs to them, if indeed they judged them to be good men and fit for such things. Apollodorus of Cyzicus they often chose as general, though he was a foreigner, and Heracleides of Clazomenae; for having shown that they were men worth mentioning, they were then not deemed unworthy to rule the Athenians. And for these things one must praise the city, which did not sacrifice the truth to its citizens, but gave honour even to those who did not belong by birth, but through virtue were worthy to be honoured.

Tachos the Egyptian, so long as he kept to his native diet and lived frugally, passed his life in the best of health; but when he came to the Persians and fell into their luxury, he could not bear the unaccustomed food, and ended his life of dysentery, exchanging luxury for death.

Pherecydes, the teacher of Pythagoras, when he fell into his sickness, first sweated a warm, sticky sweat like slime, and afterward a foul one, and then he became infested with lice. As his flesh dissolved away into the lice, a wasting set in, and so he passed from life.

Aristotle says that what are now called the Pillars of Heracles were, before they were so named, called the Pillars of Briareos; but when Heracles had purged land and sea and become beyond dispute the benefactor of mankind, men, honouring him, set the memory of Briareos at naught and named them the Pillars of Heracles.
There is a Delian tale of two plants that sprang up in Delos, an olive and a palm, which Leto grasped and at once gave birth, though till then she had been unable to do so.

Epaminondas had a single cloak, and that a dirty one; and whenever he gave it to the fuller, he himself stayed at home for want of another. While he was thus circumstanced, when the king of the Persians sent him much gold, he would not accept it; and, if I judge rightly, the man who did not take it was higher-minded than the man who offered it.

It is right to praise the end of Calanus the Indian as well — another might say to marvel at it. It came about thus. Calanus, the Indian sage, having bidden a long farewell to Alexander and the Macedonians and to life, when he wished to release himself from the bonds of the body, had a pyre heaped up in the fairest suburb of Babylon; and the wood was dry and choicely selected for fragrance — cedar and citron-wood and cypress and myrtle and bay. Then, having exercised in his accustomed exercise — which was running — he went up and stood in the middle of the pyre, crowned with a wreath of reed. The sun struck him, and he made obeisance to it; and this was the signal for the Macedonians to kindle the pyre. This was done, and he, enveloped by the flame, stood unflinching, and did not fall until he was wholly consumed. At this, they say, even Alexander was astonished, and said that Calanus had overcome greater adversaries than himself; for he had striven against Porus and Taxiles and Darius, but Calanus against pain and death.
The Scythians wander about their own land; but Anacharsis, being a wise man, carried his wandering farther still. He came, at any rate, to Greece, and Solon admired him.

Mockery and abuse seem to me to have no power. For if abuse meets with a firm character, it is dissolved; but if with a base and abject one, it prevails, and often not only grieves but kills. Let these be the proof of it: Socrates, when mocked in comedy, laughed; but Poliagrus hanged himself.

Aristotle, having squandered the money he had from his father, set out on military service, and then, faring badly in it, turned up as a seller of drugs. Slipping into the Peripatos and listening at the edge of the lectures, being by nature better endowed than many, he then took on the disposition which he afterward acquired.

The Athenians were always toiling to build themselves a fleet. Over the years, succeeding at times and failing at others, they lost two hundred triremes with their crews in Egypt, a hundred and fifty off Cyprus, two hundred and forty in Sicily, and two hundred in the Hellespont. Of hoplites they lost forty thousand in Sicily, and a thousand at Chaeronea.

The king of the Thracians — let someone else tell his name — when Xerxes marched against Greece, fled to Mount Rhodope, and advised his six sons not to make war on Greece. But they were not persuaded; and when they returned, he blinded them all, doing no Hellenic deed.

I cannot help loving these things in the Athenians. When the assembly was in session, Demades came forward and proposed by decree that Alexander be made the thirteenth god. But the people, not bearing the excess of impiety, fined Demades a hundred talents, because he had enrolled Alexander, a mortal, among the Olympians.

The Athenians were terribly versatile in their constitutions and ready for changes beyond all others. For they bore monarchy with moderation under Cecrops and Erechtheus and Theseus and the Codrids down the line; they made trial of tyranny under the Pisistratids; they practised aristocracy down to the time of the Four Hundred; then later ten of the citizens ruled the city each year; and finally there came anarchy at the time of the establishment of the Thirty. Whether one ought to praise so abrupt a turning of their character, I for my part do not know.

This too is an Attic law. Whoever comes upon the unburied body of a man must by all means cast earth upon it, burying it facing toward the west. This also was observed among them: a plough-ox that has laboured under the yoke with the plough, or even with the wagon, must not be sacrificed, since it too would be a farmer and a sharer in the labours of men.

There were Attic courts: for those who killed with deliberate intent, on the Areopagus; for those who killed unintentionally, at the Palladium; and for those who admitted the killing but disputed that it was just, the inquiries were held at the Delphinium.

A child picked up a golden leaf that had fallen from the crown of Artemis, and did not escape notice. So the judges set before the child toys and knucklebones and the golden leaf; and again it was drawn to the gold. For this they put it to death as a temple-robber, granting no pardon to its age, but exacting punishment for the deed.

So great was the superstition of the Athenians that if anyone cut a small holm-oak out of a hero's shrine, they would put him to death. Indeed, when Atarbes killed the sacred sparrow of Asclepius by striking it, the Athenians did not overlook this idly, but put Atarbes to death; and they granted pardon neither for ignorance nor for madness, holding the things of the god above both. For it was said that he did it unwillingly — others say, in a fit of madness.

When the council of the Areopagus had arrested a certain sorceress and was about to put her to death, they did not kill her until she had given birth; for when she was seized, she was with child. Releasing the innocent infant from the sentence, they justly assigned the death to the guilty woman alone.

Aeschylus the tragic poet was being tried for impiety over one of his plays. When the Athenians were ready to stone him, Amynias, his younger brother, drew aside his cloak and showed his forearm stripped of its hand. Now it happened that Amynias had won distinction at Salamis where he lost his hand, and was the first of the Athenians to receive the prize for valour. When the judges saw the man's affliction, they remembered his deeds and acquitted Aeschylus.

When the Tarentines were besieged by the Athenians and about to be taken by famine, the people of Rhegium voted to fast one day in every ten and to give over the food of that day to the Tarentines. So when the Athenians withdrew, they were saved; and remembering their distress, the Tarentines keep a festival called the Fast.

There is a story that the report about Medea is false: that she did not kill her children, but the Corinthians did. This tale about the woman of Colchis, and the play, they say Euripides composed at the request of the Corinthians, and the falsehood prevailed over the truth through the poet's excellence. And on account of the daring deed against the children, the Corinthians to this day make offerings to the children, as if paying them a tribute.

The sea-turtles lay their eggs on land, and having laid them they at once bury the eggs in the earth; then they turn back and swim away to their own haunts. They are so far given to reckoning that they count up on their own the forty days in which their offspring, the eggs being formed, become living creatures. Then they turn back again to the place where they laid and hid their young, dig up the earth they had heaped over them, and lead away the hatchlings, who are already stirring and able to follow them.

They say that Hippomachus the trainer, when the athlete he was training had managed a certain wrestling-throw, and the whole crowd standing round shouted out, struck him with his rod and said: "But you did badly, and not as you ought, what should have been done better; for these men would not have praised you had you done something skilful" — hinting that those who do each thing well and finely ought to please not the many, but those who have an understanding eye for what is done. Socrates too seems to have made light of the judgement of the many in his conversation with Crito, when Crito came to the prison and tried to persuade him to run away and so frustrate the Athenians' verdict against him.

Crates the Theban is found to have been high-minded in other respects too, and contemptuous of the things admired by the multitude — and so also of money and of country. Now that he gave up his property to the Thebans, this has gone out to all; but the other thing about him is not known to all. It is this. As he was departing from Thebes after it had been refounded, he said: "I have no need of a city which some other Alexander will raze."

They say that none of the ancient Thracians knew letters; indeed all the barbarians who dwell in Europe held it most shameful to use writing. But those in Asia, as the story goes, used them more. Hence some even dare to say that Orpheus, being a Thracian, was no wise man, but that the legends about him are otherwise false. This Androtion says, if anyone is to be trusted on the illiteracy and want of culture of the Thracians.
Pericles, when in the plague he lost his sons, bore their death most manfully, and persuaded all the Athenians to bear with better spirit the deaths of their dearest.

They were mocked in comedy for their thinness: Sannyrion the comic poet, and Meletus the tragic poet, and Cinesias the writer of dithyrambic choruses, and Philetas the poet of hexameters. And Archestratus the seer, when captured by the enemy and placed on a scale, was found to weigh the weight of an obol, so they say. And Panaretus too was very thin; yet he continued free of sickness. They say that Hipponax the poet was not only small of body but also thin. And Philippides too, against whom there is a speech by Hyperides, was very thin. Hence to grow very lean of body they used to call "to be Philippidized," they say. Alexis is the witness.

It happened that an adulterer was caught in Thespiae; and then he was led through the marketplace in bonds. His companions, however, rescued him. So a faction-fight broke out, and it came about that many murders were committed.

One may laugh at those who are proud because of their fathers, seeing that among the Romans we do not know the father of Marius, yet we admire him for his deeds; and of Cato the Elder too the father must be sought out.

In Heraea in Arcadia, I hear, there grow vines from which comes a wine that turns men's reason aside and makes the Arcadians frenzied, but makes the women fruitful. In Thasos, they say, two kinds of wine are produced; and the one, when drunk, brings on a very deep and therefore pleasant sleep, but the other is an enemy to life and produces wakefulness and gives distress. And in Achaea, near Ceryneia, a wine is produced that helps the women who wish to miscarry.

Aristippus seemed to speak very forcibly in counselling men neither to be distressed over things past nor to be anxious beforehand over things to come; for such conduct is a sign of cheerfulness and a proof of a serene mind. He bade them keep their thought on the day, and again on that part of the day in which each man is either doing something or planning it. For he said that the present alone is ours, and neither what is past nor what is expected; for the one has perished, and the other is uncertain whether it will be.

The Athenians, having mastered the Chalcidians, parcelled out their land into two thousand lots, the region called Hippobotos; they set aside sacred precincts for Athena in the place named Lelantos, and the rest they let out according to the inscribed pillars that stood by the Royal Stoa, which held the records of the leases. The captives they put in chains, and not even thus did they quench their wrath against the Chalcidians. The Lacedaemonians, having mastered the Messenians, took for themselves half of everything produced in Messenia, and compelled the free women to go to their funerals and to mourn the dead who were strangers and no kin to them; of the men, some they left to till the soil, others they sold, and others they killed. The Athenians too committed that outrage: for, taking hold of prosperity, they did not bear their good fortune with moderation. They compelled the daughters of the resident aliens to carry parasols in the processions for their own girls, and the wives to do so for their wives, and the men to carry water-vessels. The Sicyonians, having taken Pellene, set up the wives and daughters of the Pellenians in a brothel. Most savage are these deeds, O gods of the Greeks, and not honourable even among barbarians, so far as my memory reaches.
