When Philip won the battle at Chaeronea, both he and all the Macedonians were exalted at what they had done. The Greeks were terribly cowed by him, and surrendered themselves to him city by city. This the Thebans did, and the Megarians, and the Corinthians, and the Achaeans, and the Eleans, and the Euboeans, and all those in the Acte. Yet Philip did not keep the agreements he made with them, but enslaved them all, doing what was lawless and against right.

The son of Harmatides the Thespian, having come as an ally to the Athenians along with other citizens, at first fought well and nobly; but when his weapons were used up and he was contending bare-handed against armed men, he ended his life gloriously. So I have addressed the young man by his father's name, honouring him in Homeric fashion. But his own name, if anyone is concerned to know it, he will learn from another source.

The Lacedaemonians, when Isadas was still a boy and the law had not yet called him to arms, since he had leapt out of the gymnasium and won distinction, crowned him; but because he had rushed against the enemy before the required age and without his native arms, they fined him.

Lysander had died, and the man who had betrothed his daughter while he was still alive, when the girl was left fatherless and Lysander after the close of his life proved to be poor, drew back from the betrothal and said he would not take her to wife. For this the ephors fined the man; for he was minded neither as a Laconian nor in any way as a Greek, since he forgot a friend who had died and valued wealth above his agreements.
The Athenians put to death the envoys sent to Arcadia, because they had taken another road and not the one appointed, even though they had succeeded.

Are not these too Laconian customs? It is a law among the Spartiates that the man who has provided three sons should be free of garrison duty, and the man with five exempt from all public services. They marry without dowries. A Lacedaemonian man was not permitted to know a mechanical trade. They were obliged to wear a scarlet cloak in battle, both because the colour has something of dignity, and because the flow of blood from wounds upon it would all the more startle their opponents, the sight becoming deeper and more fearful. It was not permitted to a Laconian man even to strip the slain enemy. Those who fought nobly and died were wreathed with olive sprays and other branches, and were brought forth amid praises; and those who showed the highest valour had the scarlet cloak laid upon them and were buried with honour.

When the Lacedaemonians, breaking their oaths, raised up and put to death the suppliants from Taenarum — and the suppliants were among the helots — by the wrath of Poseidon an earthquake fell upon Sparta and shook the city most violently, so that only five houses out of the whole city were left standing.

Artaxerxes, also surnamed Ochus, when Bagoas the eunuch, who was an Egyptian, plotted against him, was, they say, killed and cut to pieces and thrown to the cats; another man was buried in his stead and given to the royal tombs. But it did not satisfy Bagoas to have killed Ochus: he even made handles for daggers out of his thighbones, showing his bloodthirstiness by this. He hated him because Ochus too, while tasting Egypt, had killed the Apis, as Cambyses had done before him.

Since from the poems of Homer a report came to Delphi that the precinct of Apollo was rich with ancient wealth — in those lines, "not all that the stone threshold of the Archer holds within, of Phoebus Apollo in rocky Pytho" — the story goes that the Delphians set about digging up the ground around the hearth and the tripod; but when manly earthquakes came about the oracle, they came to their senses and stopped.

Pericles, while general of the Athenians, framed a law that whoever did not happen to be born of two citizen parents should have no share in the citizenship. But the retribution of the law overtook him. For his two sons, Paralus and Xanthippus, both died in the public plague, and Pericles was left with his bastard children, who, under their father's own law, had no share in the citizenship.

Gelon, having defeated the Carthaginians at Himera, brought all Sicily under his power. Then, coming into the assembly stripped naked, he declared that he was giving back the rule to the citizens; but they would not have it, having found him by experience more democratic than the power of monarchs allows. For this reason there stands in the temple of Sicilian Hera a statue of him showing him naked, and the inscription confirmed Gelon's deed.

Dionysius the Second held his rule very well fortified, in this manner. He possessed ships no fewer than four hundred, of six and five banks of oars; a force of infantry up to a hundred thousand, and nine thousand cavalry. The city of the Syracusans was adorned with very great harbours, and a very high wall was thrown round it; it had gear ready for another five hundred ships, and there was stored up in it grain to the amount of a million bushels. There was an armoury heaped with shields and swords and spears and greaves and breastplates and catapults — and the catapult was an invention of Dionysius himself. He had a great many allies besides. Trusting in these, Dionysius supposed that he held his rule bound fast with adamant. Yet this very man first killed his brothers; he saw his sons too slaughtered by violence, and his daughters dishonoured and then slaughtered naked. None of his line met with customary burial: some were burned alive, others cut to pieces and flung into the sea. This befell him when Dion the son of Hipparinus attacked his rule. He himself, living in utter poverty, ended his life an old man. Theopompus says that through excessive unmixed drinking his eyesight was ruined, so that he saw dimly; and that he sat in the barbershops and played the buffoon. And in the very midst of Greece he continued in his unseemliness, draining out a most painful life. The change of Dionysius from such great heights to such low estate was no ordinary lesson to men in moderation and order of conduct.

The divine power does well in not letting tyrannies pass to a third generation, but either wiping out the tyrants at once like a pine, or robbing them of children. These tyrannies are remembered by the Greeks as having lasted from of old down to descendants: that of Hieron in Sicily, that of the Leuconidae about the Bosporus, and that of the Cypselidae in Corinth.

This deed of Darius the son of Hystaspes I am told was most humane. Aribazus the Hyrcanian plotted against him, together with other men of no obscure standing among the Persians; and the plot was to be carried out on a hunt. Learning of this beforehand, Darius did not cower, but bidding them take up their weapons and their horses, ordered

them to make ready their javelins; and looking at them sharply, he said, "Why, then, do you not do that for which you set out?" But they, seeing the man's unflinching gaze, checked their impulse. Fear so gripped them that they threw down their spear-points, leapt from their horses, made obeisance to Darius, and gave themselves up to him to do with as he pleased. He scattered them to different places, sending some to the borders of India, others to the Scythian lands. And those men remained faithful to him, holding in memory the kindness shown them.

Wild boars, then, are not untrained in medicine and self-treatment. Whenever they have eaten henbane unawares, they drag their hindquarters behind them, their bodies grown slack; then, though convulsed, they nevertheless make their way to water, and there gather up crabs and eat them with the greatest eagerness. These become for them a remedy for their affliction, and restore them to health again.

This is a Theban law, rightly and humanely laid down above most: that it is not permitted to a Theban to expose a child or to cast it out into a wilderness, condemning it to death; but if the child's father is poor in the extreme, whether the child be male or female, he is to bring it, fresh from its mother's pains and still in its swaddling-clothes, to the magistrates; and they, receiving the infant, hand it over to whoever offers the smallest price. There is an agreement and a contract with him, that in return he shall rear the child, and when it is grown have it as his slave, male or female, taking its service as the recompense for its upbringing.

Demochares, the nephew of Demosthenes, wishing to show that he despised the evil-speaking of the many, when he saw some censorious fellows sitting in a surgery, eager by every means to speak ill, said: "What do you say, you Dysmenidae?" — at once unmasking their character by this name.

When Alexander took Darius, he held a wedding feast for himself and for his companions. The bridegrooms were ninety, and the bridal chambers equal in number to them. The hall that received and entertained them held a hundred couches; and each couch had silver feet, but his own had golden feet, and all were adorned with purple and embroidered coverings of barbarian weave, very costly. He also brought into the banquet his personal guest-friends, and seated them facing himself. In the courtyard the other forces feasted, the infantry and the navy and the cavalry, and the embassies too and the Greeks who were visiting. The meals were held to the trumpet: it sounded the assembling note when they were to come in to the feast, and the recall note when it signalled them to depart. For five days running he celebrated the weddings with sacrifices. Musicians and actors came too, some of comedy and some of tragedy, very many of them. There were also from India conjurers of distinction, and they were thought to surpass all the others from elsewhere.

Xanthippe said that, though countless changes of fortune befell the city and themselves, in all of them the face of Socrates was the same, whether he was going out of the house or returning to it; for he was fitly disposed toward all things, and was ever serene in mind, above all grief and stronger than every fear.

Oenopides of Chios the astronomer dedicated at Olympia a bronze tablet, inscribing upon it the astronomy of fifty-nine years, saying that this was the Great Year. And Meton of Leuconoe the astronomer set up pillars, and recorded the solstices of the sun, and discovered the Great Year, as he said, and declared it to be nineteen years.

Eteocles the Laconian used to say that Sparta could not endure two Lysanders. And Archestratus the Athenian used to say that the city of the Athenians could not endure two Alcibiadeses. So intolerable, then, was each of them.
Alexander crowned the tomb of Achilles, and Hephaestion that of Patroclus, hinting that he too was the beloved of Alexander, as Patroclus was of Achilles.

When Alexander took the city of the Thebans, he sold all the free men except the priests. He exempted from sale also his father's guest-friends — for Philip had been a hostage among them while still a boy — and he released their kinsmen too. He honoured the descendants of Pindar, and allowed his house alone to stand. He killed about six thousand of the Thebans, and thirty thousand were taken captive.

This is a Lacedaemonian law, and the law says these things. That no Lacedaemonian should be seen more unmanly in colour, or have more bulk of body than the exercises warrant; for the one was taken to confess idleness, the other not to confess a man. It was added to the law that every ten days, without fail, the youths should present themselves naked before the ephors in public. And if they were well-knit and vigorous, and as it were carved and chiselled by their exercises, they were praised; but if any of their limbs was flabby or too soft, with fat swelling and growing on them through indolence, then they were beaten and chastised. And the ephors made it their care each day to busy themselves about their dress, whether every part of it fell short of the fitting order. And there had to be cooks in Lacedaemon of meat only; but whoever knew anything beyond this was driven out of Sparta, like the purgings of the sick. These same men brought down Naucleides the son of Polybiades, who had grown over-fleshed and over-fat in body through luxury, into the assembly of the spectators, and threatened him with the penalty of exile, unless he should reform for the future the life he then lived, which was blameworthy and Ionian rather than Laconian; for they said that his appearance and the condition of his body brought shame both on Lacedaemon and on the laws.

Of Semiramis the Assyrian, different men sing different tales, but she was the fairest of women, though she used her beauty rather plainly. Coming to the king of the Assyrians, summoned for the renown of her beauty, he, when he met the woman, fell in love with her. She asked of the king that she might take the royal robe and rule Asia for five days, and that whatever she commanded should be done. Nor did she fail of her request. When the king had seated her upon the throne, and she knew that she held all things in her hand and at her will, she ordered the guards to kill the king himself; and so she took possession of the Assyrian empire. This is what Dinon relates.

Strato of Sidon is said to have been eager to surpass all men in luxury and extravagance. Theopompus of Chios compares his life to the manner of living of the Phaeacians, which Homer too, in keeping with his greatness of mind, dramatized as was his wont. With Strato, indeed, there was not one singer alone, charming his dinner and bewitching him, but many women were present, musicians and flute-girls and courtesans surpassing in beauty, and dancing-girls. He vied vigorously, moreover, with Nicocles the Cyprian, since that man too vied with him. And the contest was over nothing serious, but over the things just mentioned. Learning from those who came to them what passed in each other's houses, each then strove in rivalry to outdo the other. They did not, however, continue to the end in these pursuits; for both became the work of a violent death.

When some of his companions were grieving most heavily, Aristippus said many other things to console their sorrow, and this in particular by way of preface: "But I have come to you not to share your grief, but to put a stop to your grieving."
Pittacus very greatly praised the hand-mill, adding this praise of it, that in a small space one may exercise in a variety of ways. There was a song, too, called the Mill-song.

Laertes too is found working with his own hands by his son, scraping a plant, though he was very deep in age. And Odysseus himself admits that he knows many crafts and is skilled in them: "In handiwork no other mortal could rival me — to lay a fire well, and to split dry wood." And the raft, too, he made for himself in the quickest time, without needing shipwrights. And Achilles also, third in descent from Zeus, himself carves the meat, hastening to prepare a meal for the envoys who had come from the Achaeans.

Once, when snow was falling, the king of the Scythians asked one of them who was enduring it naked whether he was cold. And he asked the king in return whether his forehead was cold. When the king said no, "Well then," he said, "neither am I; for I am all forehead."

Demosthenes the son of Demosthenes, if there was to be an assembly the next day, would lie awake the whole night through, plainly thinking out and learning by heart what he meant to say. And so Pytheas, it seems to me, used to mock him on this account, saying that his arguments smelled of lamp-wicks.

When Hephaestion died, Alexander cast weapons upon his pyre, and melted down gold and silver with the corpse, and the robe most prized among the Persians. He cut off too his own locks, doing a Homeric deed and imitating his own Achilles. But he did it more violently and more hotly than Achilles, shearing the citadel of Ecbatana of its battlements. So far, then, as concerned his own hair, he seemed to me to be acting in the Greek manner; but when he laid hands on the walls — there Alexander was already mourning in barbarian fashion, and he changed his dress too, giving over everything to passion and love and tears. Hephaestion died at Ecbatana. There is a report current that these things had been prepared for Hephaestion as a corpse, but that Alexander, dying, made use of them himself; for the mourning fulfilled over the youth did not come first, but the death of Alexander overtook it.

And then, is not great self-restraint a fine thing — so it seems to me — if indeed even the wife of Phocion wore Phocion's cloak, and needed neither saffron robe nor Tarentine gown nor mantle nor flounced dress nor hairnet nor veil nor dyed tunics? She was clothed first in self-restraint, and second in what was at hand.
To Xanthippe, who did not wish to put on his cloak and so to go to see the procession, Socrates said: "Do you see that you go not to look on, but rather to be looked at?"
Among the Romans most of the women are accustomed to wear the same shoes as their men.

"One must deceive children with knucklebones, but men with oaths." Some say the saying is Lysander's, others Philip the Macedonian's. Whichever it may be, it is not rightly said, in my judgment. And perhaps it is no wonder if the same things do not please me and Lysander; for he was a tyrant, while I — how I am minded is plain from the fact that the saying does not please me.

Agesilaus the Lacedaemonian, when he was already an old man, would often go out unshod and without a tunic, wrapped only in his cloak, and this in the early morning in wintry weather. Someone reproached him for attempting things too youthful for his age; but he said: "Why, the young men of the citizens look to me, just as colts look to the full-grown horse."

And what then? Were not the philosophers good at war as well? So they seem to me, if indeed the Tarentines chose Archytas general six times, and Melissus commanded a fleet, and Socrates served three campaigns, and Plato himself went to Tanagra and to Corinth. The campaign and generalship of Xenophon many others sing, and he himself admits it in his account of Cyrus. Dion the son of Hipparinus overthrew the tyranny of Dionysius. And Epaminondas, as Boeotarch, conquered the Lacedaemonians at Leuctra, and became first among the Thebans and the Greeks. Zeno too did much in public life on behalf of the Athenians against Antigonus. For it makes no difference whether a man benefits others by counsel or by arms.

When the Mytilenaeans ruled the sea, they hung this punishment over those of their allies who revolted: that their children should not learn letters nor be taught music, judging this the heaviest of all chastisements — to pass their lives in want of culture and in ignorance.
Rome was founded by Romus and Romulus, the sons of Ares and Silvia. And she was one of the descendants of Aeneas.

When Eudoxus came to Sicily, Dionysius was very grateful to him for his coming. But he, neither flattering this in any way nor fawning, said: "I have come as if to a good innkeeper, with whom Plato lodged" — confessing that he had come not for Dionysius's sake but for Plato's.

They say that the Egyptians endure tortures terribly well, and that an Egyptian man will die under the rack sooner than confess the truth. Among the Indians the women, when their husbands die, submit to the same fire. And the women vie over this honour of the husband; and the one who wins by lot is burned together with him.

Solon was general in the battle for Salamis, and, having captured two Megarian ships, he transferred Attic commanders into them, and clad his own men in the enemy's arms, and shifting his moorings, by this stratagem cut down many of the Megarians as they sailed in. He prevailed over them also in argument — not by cleverness of speech, but by carrying his point chiefly through the proofs themselves. For opening ancient tombs, he showed that all the Athenians were laid facing the west, according to their ancestral custom, but the Megarians were buried at random and as chance had it. And the Lacedaemonians judged the case.

A man came to Lacedaemon, a Chian, already an old man, in other respects a braggart, but ashamed of his old age, and trying to hide his grey hair by dyeing it. So he came forward and said the things for which he had come. Then Archidamus stood up and said: "What sound thing could this man say, who carries falsehood about not only on his soul, but on his head as well?" And he threw out what the man had said, discrediting the Chian's character by what was plain to see.

Caesar did not think it beneath him to frequent the doors of Ariston, nor Pompey those of Cratippus. For though they had great power, they did not despise those who could benefit them in the greatest things, but had need of them, great as they were in dignity. For it was not to rule, it seems, but to rule well, that they wished.

The venomous spider is as great an evil to deer as it is to men, and they are in danger of perishing quickly. If, however, they taste ivy, the bite does them no harm. But the ivy must be of the wild kind.

In the ninety-first Olympiad, in which Exaenetus of Acragas won the foot-race, Xenocles and Euripides competed against each other. And first was Xenocles — whoever he may be — with his Oedipus, Lycaon, Bacchae, and the satyr-play Athamas. Second to him was Euripides with his Alexander, Palamedes, Trojan Women, and the satyr-play Sisyphus. It is absurd — is it not? — that Xenocles should win and Euripides be beaten, and that with such dramas. One of two things, then: either the judges who held the vote were senseless and ignorant and far from a right judgement, or they were bribed. Either is monstrous, and least of all worthy of the Athenians.

The Athenians chose Phrynichus general, neither for his political zeal nor for the worth of his family, nor yet because he was rich; for often men were admired at Athens for these things and were preferred to others. But because he had composed for the war-dancers in a certain tragedy melodies suitable and warlike, in this way he so won over the theatre and prevailed upon those present that at once they chose him to be general, trusting that he would lead in the works of war well and as need required, since the melodies and verses he had made in his drama were not out of keeping with men in arms.

Cimon of Cleonae, they say, perfected the art of painting while it was still in its infancy and was being practised without skill and without experience by those before him, in a manner still, so to speak, in swaddling-clothes and at the breast. For this reason he was the first to receive larger fees than his predecessors.

The younger Dionysius, when he came to the city of the Locrians — for his mother Doris was a Locrian — took for himself the greatest house in the city, and strewing it with roses and thyme and other flowers, he sent for the daughters of the Locrians and lay with them most licentiously. For this he paid the penalty; for when his tyranny was overthrown by Dion, then the Locrians prostituted the wife and daughters of Dionysius, and all men outraged them without restraint, especially the kinsmen of the maidens whom Dionysius had ruined. And when they were sated with outraging them, they killed them by piercing them under the nails of their hands with needles. Their bones they pounded in mortars, and stripping the flesh from the bones they laid a curse on any who would not taste of them; and whatever was left of them they sank in the sea. As for Dionysius, after passing through many and various changes of life in Corinth, through his extreme poverty, he at last ended his days as a begging-priest of the Mother of the gods, beating drums and accompanied by the flute.
Aristotle of Cyrene used to say that one should not accept a benefit from anyone; for either, trying to repay it, one would have trouble, or, not repaying it, one would seem ungrateful.

Hipparchus was killed by Harmodius and Aristogiton, because at the Panathenaea he did not allow the sister of Harmodius to carry the basket for the goddess according to the local custom, though she was perhaps worthy of it.

Cleomenes the Laconian, taking Archonides as a partner from among his companions, made him a sharer in his affairs. So he swore that, if he gained power, he would do everything with his head. Having gained the rule, then, he killed his companion and cut off his head and put it in honey, and whenever he was about to do anything, he would stoop over the vessel and tell all that he was doing, saying that he was not breaking faith nor perjuring himself, but taking counsel with the head of Archonides.
They say that Lysander the Lacedaemonian, while spending time in Ionia, cast aside the ordinances of Lycurgus, since they were toilsome, and dissolved his life in luxury.

Polyclitus made two statues at the same time, the one to please the crowd, the other according to the rule of his art. He pleased the many in this way. For each of those who came in, he changed and reshaped something, yielding to each man's suggestion. So he set out both; and the one was praised by all, but the other was laughed at. Taking them up, then, Polyclitus said: "But this one, which you blame, you made; and this one, which you admire, I made." Hippomachus the flute-teacher, when a pupil of his playing the flute made a mistake in his playing but was praised by those present, struck him with his rod and said: "You played badly; for these men would not have praised you otherwise."
When a lion is sick, nothing else does it any good, but its remedy for the illness is to eat an ape.

Consider what the Athenians decreed, and that under a democracy: of the Aeginetans, to cut off the great thumb of the right hand of each, that they might not be able to wield a spear but might pull an oar; of the Mytilenaeans, to slaughter all of military age — this too they decreed, on the proposal of Cleon, son of Cleaenetus. As for the captives taken of the Samians, they were to be branded on the face, and the brand was to be an owl — and this too was an Attic decree. I would not have wished these things either to have been ratified at Athens or to be told of the Athenians — O Athena of the City, and Zeus the Deliverer, and all the gods of the Greeks.

With a man in love a man not in love would not join in the ranks when the battle presses and the war draws together. For the man who knows no love flees and runs away from the lover, as one profane and uninitiated to the god, and brave only so far as his soul goes and his body has strength; but he dreads the other, as one possessed and inspired by a god, and, by Zeus, maddened not with this common madness from Ares, but from Eros. For those who are seized by the other of these gods — one of whom Homer says rages like Ares — these, encompassed by a single divinity, contend well and finely only so far as they are once inspired; but the bacchants of Eros, fighting and enduring a double servitude, both from the onset of Ares and from the kindling of Eros, naturally, according to the Cretans' notion, succeed doubly. So no one could blame the man who, bent on slaughter from Ares and Eros together, will not stand to fight against a hoplite who is ranged under one god only, and not under the two.

Archelaus the tyrant of the Macedonians — for so Plato names him, and not "king" — had a favourite, Crateuas, who fell in love with the tyranny no less than Archelaus had loved the boy, and he killed his lover, expecting that he would become a tyrant and a man of fortune. But having held the tyranny three or four days, he in turn was plotted against by others and met his end. It would be most fitting to apply to this Macedonian drama that verse: "He who contrives evil for another contrives it for his own heart." They say that Archelaus had broken faith with him, having promised to give him one of his daughters; and when he married the girl to another, Crateuas in his rage destroyed Archelaus.

Demetrius Poliorcetes took cities, and indulging his own luxury, he procured for himself a revenue of twelve hundred talents each year, and of these he spent little on his army, but the rest on his own debauchery. His floor was sprinkled with perfumes, and at every season of the year the choicest flowers in bloom were strewn beneath him, that he might walk upon them. He was licentious with women too, and attempted youthful loves. He took care also to be handsome, arranging his hair and dyeing it golden and anointing his face with rouge. He used other unguents besides, taking pride in his self-indulgence.

Philoxenus was a glutton and a slave to his belly. Once, when a dish was being cooked in a tavern, for a while he enjoyed himself and feasted on the smell; but when his appetite grew stronger and he was overcome by his nature — a bad one, ye gods — then, unable to bear it, he ordered his slave to buy the dish. When the slave said that the tavern-keeper was selling it for a high price, he said: "It will be all the more pleasant to me, if I buy it for more." One must remember such things too, not to emulate them, but to flee from them.

The best of the Greeks lived in poverty all their lives long. Let some, then, praise wealth still, after the best of the Greeks, to whom poverty was allotted throughout their lives. These are they: for instance, Aristides son of Lysimachus, a man who achieved many things in war, and who fixed the tribute for the Greeks. Yet this man, such as he was, did not even leave behind enough for his own burial. And Phocion too was poor. When Alexander sent him a hundred talents, he asked: "For what reason does he give it to me?" When they said that Alexander considered him alone among the Athenians a man of nobility and worth, he said: "Then let him allow me to remain such." And Epaminondas son of Polymnis was poor. When Jason sent him fifty gold pieces, he said: "You are beginning an unjust act." And borrowing fifty drachmas from one of his fellow-citizens for travelling-money, he invaded the Peloponnese. Learning that his shield-bearer had taken money from one of the captives, he said: "Give me back my shield, and buy yourself a tavern, where you will live out your days; for you will no longer be willing to risk yourself, now that you have become rich." When his friends reproached Pelopidas for neglecting money, a thing useful for life, he said: "By Zeus, useful — but to this Nicomedes," pointing to a certain lame and crippled man. Scipio, who lived fifty-four years, neither bought nor sold anything: so few were his needs. When someone showed him a finely adorned shield, he said: "But it befits a Roman man to have his hopes in his right hand, not in his left." Ephialtes son of Sophonides was very poor. When his companions offered him ten talents, he did not accept them, saying: "These will compel me, out of respect for you, to grant away something of justice; and if I do not respect you and grant you the favour, I shall seem ungrateful."

Timesias of Clazomenae governed the Clazomenians well; for he was one of the good men. But envy, which is wont to prevail against such men, prevailed against Timesias too. At first he cared little for being envied, but the following thing, they say, drove him from his country. He was passing by a school; and the boys, having been let out by their teacher, were playing. A dispute arose between two boys over a line, and one of them swore: "So may I dash out the brains of Timesias!" Hearing this, and supposing that envy of him was unrestrained and that he was terribly hated by his citizens, since even the boys hated him — let alone the men — he willingly departed from his country.
Lamia the Attic courtesan said: "The lions from Greece have become foxes in Ephesus."

Xenocrates of Chalcedon, when mocked unkindly by Plato, never grew indignant, they say; and to the man who urged him on about it, that he might answer Plato something, he very sensibly silenced the man, saying: "But this is good for me."

The Cretans are good archers, and indeed they shoot the wild goats grazing on the mountain peaks. But the goats, once struck, at once chew the herb dittany, and the moment they have tasted it all the arrows drop out of them.

I hear of Timotheus, son of Conon, the general of the Athenians, that when he was at the height of his good fortune and was taking the cities with the greatest ease, and the Athenians did not know where to place him out of their wonder at the man — that he, meeting Plato, son of Ariston, walking outside the walls with some of his acquaintances, and seeing him grand to look upon in his breadth, gracious in countenance, and discoursing not about the levying of money nor about triremes, nor about naval needs nor about crews, nor about the necessity of sending help nor about the tribute of the allies, nor about the islanders or any other such trifle, but about those matters of which Plato spoke and was wont to take seriously — the son of Conon, standing still, said: "What a life, and what true happiness!" From this it is plain that Timotheus did not declare himself to be very happy at all, since his happiness lay not in these things, but in his reputation and honour among the Athenians.

About the ephors at Lacedaemon I have many other fine things to tell, but what I have chosen, this I will now relate. When one of the handsome youths among them preferred a rich lover to a worthy poor one, they laid a fine upon him, punishing, as it seems, his love of money with a penalty in money. And another, a fine and good man who loved none of the well-formed youths, him too they fined, because, being worthy, he loved no one; for plainly he would have made that youth like himself, and perhaps another too. For the goodwill of lovers toward their beloveds is powerful to work virtues in them, when they themselves are upright. And indeed this too is a Laconian law: when a youth errs, they pardon the simplicity of his character and the youthfulness of his age, but punish the lover on his behalf, bidding the lovers be judges and examiners of what the youths do.

The Athenians chose Solon to rule them by election, for they did not choose him by lot. When he had been chosen, he set the city in order in other respects, and in particular he drew up for them the laws that are still kept to this day. And then the Athenians ceased to use the laws of Draco; those laws were called "ordinances." Only his homicide laws did they keep.

Plato, when the Academy was said to be an unhealthy spot, and the physicians advised him to move to the Lyceum, would not consent, saying: "But I would not move even to the heights of Athos for the sake of living longer."

When the art of painting was just beginning, and was, so to speak, at the breast and in swaddling-clothes, painters represented animals so unskilfully that they had to write over them: "This is an ox, that a horse, this a tree."

Zoilus of Amphipolis, who wrote against Homer and against Plato and against others, was a pupil of Polycrates; and this Polycrates also wrote the accusation against Socrates. This Zoilus was called "the rhetorical Dog." He was of this sort. His beard hung down, his head was shaved to the skin, and his cloak was above the knee. He loved to speak ill of people, and had leisure to make himself hateful to many, and the wretch was full of blame. So one of the learned men asked him why he spoke ill of all; and he said: "Because, wishing to do harm, I cannot."

The Aeginetans once were the most powerful among the Greeks, having obtained a certain abundance of wealth and good fortune; for they had a naval force and were very great. In the Persian wars too they proved brave, and for this were judged worthy of the prizes of valour. And they first struck coinage, the coin called after them the Aeginetan.

On one day Dionysius married two wives, Doris the Locrian and Aristomache the daughter of Hipparinus, the sister of Dion; and he slept with each in turn. And the one followed him when he campaigned, the other received him on his return.

The Athenians chose Demades to be general in preference to Phocion. He, preferred and proud of it, came to Phocion and said: "Lend me the dirty cloak you used to wear during your generalship." And Phocion said: "You will never lack for anything dirty, so long as you are such as you are."

Mice too, it seems, are the most prophetic of animals. For when a house is already growing old and about to collapse, they are the first to perceive it, and abandoning their holes and their former dwellings, they flee as fast as their feet will carry them and change their lodging.

Socrates, seeing at the beginning of the Thirty the men of distinction put to death and the very wealthy plotted against by the tyrants, is said to have met Antisthenes and said: "Have you any regret that we became nothing great or august in our lives, and not such as we see the monarchs in tragedy — those Atreuses and Thyesteses and Agamemnons and Aegisthuses? For these are exposed to view, slaughtered and made the stuff of tragedy and eating their wicked feasts every time; but no poet of tragedy was ever so bold or shameless as to bring a slaughtered chorus onto the stage in a drama."

The Peripatetics say that by day the soul, in bondage to the body, is entangled with it and cannot purely behold the truth; but by night, released from this service and gathered into a sphere in the region about the chest, it becomes more prophetic, whence come dreams.

We shall no longer wonder if human nature, being mortal and short-lived, compels men to perish, when we see even rivers failing, and hear that even the highest of the mountains are diminishing. The voyagers, at any rate, say that Etna is seen to be smaller than it was before; and they say that Parnassus and Pierian Olympus have suffered the same thing. And those who think they have observed the nature of the universe still more closely say that even the cosmos itself is perishing.

That Parrhasius the painter wore a purple robe and a golden crown is attested both by others and by the epigrams on many of his pictures. He once competed in Samos, and met with a rival not much inferior to himself, and then was defeated. His picture was Ajax contending against Odysseus for the arms of Achilles. Having been defeated, Parrhasius answered very wittily to the companion who grieved with him; for he said that he himself cared little for the defeat, but that he grieved for the son of Telamon, who had now been defeated a second time over the same thing. He carried also a staff with golden spirals winding round it, and he fastened the straps of his sandals with golden buckles. They say that he plied his art neither unwillingly nor laboriously, but with great cheer and ease; for he would sing, and softly humming would try to lighten the toil of his craft. So Theophrastus says.

Diogenes had a pain in his shoulder, either, I suppose, from a wound or from some other cause. When he seemed to be in great pain, one of those who were vexed with him jeered at him, saying: "Why, then, do you not die, Diogenes, and free yourself from your troubles?" And he said: "Those who know what one must do in life and what one must say — these it is fitting should live," and he admitted that he himself was of their number. "For you, then," he said, "who do not know what should be said and done, it is well to die; but for me, who have knowledge of these things, it is fitting to live."
Dionysius the Sicilian was himself devoted to the art of medicine, and would heal and cut and cauterize and the rest.
The Romans, beneath the Palatine hill, set up a temple and an altar to Fever.

An account has come to me saying that Isocrates the orator was the cause to the Persians of the enslavement by which the Macedonians enslaved them. For when the fame of the panegyric speech which Isocrates delivered among the Greeks came to Macedonia, it first roused Philip against Asia; and when he died, it prepared Alexander his son, the heir of his father's possessions, to take up the impulse of Philip.

Philiscus once said to Alexander: "Care for your reputation, but do not be a plague and a great disease, but health." He meant that to rule by force and harshly, and to take cities and destroy peoples, is the work of a plague, but to take thought for the health and safety of one's subjects is the good work of peace.

Ants too, as I hear, have a kind of prophetic sense. For when a famine is to come, they are remarkably industrious in laying up stores and hoarding for themselves wheat and the other seeds that make an ant's dinner.

As for Themistocles, son of Neocles, I do not know whether one should praise this. When Themistocles had ceased from his prodigality — having been disowned by his father — and began to live soberly, and had given up his courtesans, and was seized with another love, the love of the public life of the Athenians, and set himself most ardently to office and was eager to be first, he said, they tell us, to his acquaintances: "What would you give for a man like me, who am not yet envied?" Now one who longs to be envied is striving for that which Euripides calls "being stared at." But that this is empty, the same Euripides declares.

The handsome youths at Lacedaemon are not coy toward their lovers, nor arrogant, since one may learn from them the opposite of what is found among other young men in their bloom. They themselves, indeed, beg their lovers to "breathe into" them; and this is a Lacedaemonian expression, meaning that one ought to love. A Spartan love knows nothing shameful; for if a youth has dared to submit to outrage, or a lover to commit it, it has profited neither to remain in Sparta; for either they were banished from their country, or, what is yet harsher, deprived of life itself.

Strange, is it not? Yet true. When Demosthenes failed in Macedonia, Aeschines son of Atrometus, of the deme Cothocidae, both stood in high repute with the Macedonians and far surpassed the other envoys in spirit. The cause of this for Aeschines was his friendship with Philip and the gifts he had from him, and the fact that Philip listened to him gently and gladly, regarding him with a kindly look and showing the goodwill he bore him. All this drew Aeschines on to free speech and to a ready flow of words. Demosthenes was not the only one to suffer this in Macedonia, clever as he was at speaking; Theophrastus of Eresus did the same. For he too broke down while speaking before the Council of the Areopagus, and offered this excuse, that he had been overawed by the dignity of the council. Most bitterly and most readily, then, did Demochares meet this speech of his, saying: "Theophrastus, they were Athenians who sat in judgment, not the twelve gods."
The Romans expelled from the city Alcaeus and Philiscus the Epicureans, because they introduced the young to many strange pleasures. And the Messenians too drove out the Epicureans.
Archytas used to say: "Just as it is hard work to find a fish without a bone, so too a man who possesses nothing deceitful and thorny."

Alcibiades sent Socrates a large and most finely prepared cake. Xanthippe, then, taking it as a gift sent by a beloved to a lover, and inflamed with jealousy after her own fashion, threw the cake out of the basket and trampled it underfoot. Socrates laughed and said: "Then you too will have no share of it." And if anyone thinks that I am speaking of small matters in saying these things, he does not know that even by such things the man of worth is tested, in despising the very things that the many call the ornament of the table and the adornments of the feast.

An adulterer caught in Gortyn was brought before the magistrates; then, convicted, he was crowned with wool. This crowning signified that he was unmanly and womanish and lustful after women. And he was sold publicly and was most dishonoured and had no share in public affairs.

Meton the astronomer, when the Athenians were about to sail against Sicily, was himself already one of the levy. But knowing clearly the fortunes that were to come, he tried to avoid the voyage, fearing it and eager to free himself from the expedition. When he could accomplish nothing, he feigned madness; and he did many other things, wishing to confirm the belief in his sickness, and among them he burned down his own dwelling, which was near the Stoa Poikile. From this the magistrates released him. And it seems to me that Meton feigned madness better than Odysseus of Ithaca; for Palamedes detected that man, but no one of the Athenians detected this one.

The king of the Persians, when travelling, that he might not be idle, used to carry a little linden-wood board and a little knife, that he might whittle it. And these the royal hands made; for he had neither book nor thought, that he might read something serious and worthy, or plan something noble and worth mention.

Gelon of Syracuse dreamed that he was struck by a thunderbolt, and because of this he cried out, not faintly or weakly as one does in a dream, but like a man, in his great terror at the fright. His dog, which was sleeping beside him, was thrown into confusion by the cry, and standing over him barked very fiercely, threateningly and intently. By this Gelon both woke from sleep and was released from his fear.

Anytus and his party set upon Socrates and plotted against him, for what reasons and on what grounds has been told long ago. But, suspicious of the Athenians and afraid how they would stand toward the accusation of the man — for great was the name of Socrates, both for other reasons and because he refuted the sophists as men with nothing sound about them, who neither knew nor said anything worth the trouble — on these grounds, then, they wished to make trial regarding the slander against him. For they did not think it advisable to bring an indictment against him outright at once, for the reasons I have stated, and for these as well: lest the friends of Socrates, growing savage, should set the judges against them, and they themselves should suffer some incurable harm, as men who falsely accused one who was not only the cause of no evil to the city, but on the contrary an ornament to Athens. What, then, do they devise? They persuade Aristophanes, the comic poet — a buffoon, a man absurd and eager to be so — to make a comedy of Socrates, doubtless the things that go about: that he was a babbler, and that he made the weaker argument appear the stronger, and brought in strange divinities, and neither revered nor honoured the gods, and taught these same things to those who came to him and persuaded them to hold them. Aristophanes, taking a thoroughly bold subject, and sowing in laughter and the charm of his verses, and taking the best of the Greeks for his subject — for the drama was not against Cleon, nor was he making comedy of the Lacedaemonians or Thebans or Pericles himself, but of a man dear to the other gods and especially to Apollo — since, then, it was an unaccustomed thing and a paradoxical spectacle on the stage and in comedy, Socrates, the comedy first of all astonished the Athenians by its unexpectedness; and then, being by nature envious and disposed to begrudge the best — not only those in public life and office, but still more those who were well thought of for fine speech or for the dignity of their lives — they reckoned these Clouds a most delightful entertainment, and applauded the poet as never before, and shouted that he had won, and bade the judges write down Aristophanes above and no other. So much for the drama. As for Socrates, he rarely frequented the theatres; but if ever Euripides, the poet of tragedy, was competing with new tragedies, then he would come. And when Euripides was competing at the Piraeus, Socrates went down there too; for he delighted in the man, both for his wisdom and for his excellence in verse. And once, when Alcibiades, son of Cleinias, and Critias, son of Callaeschrus, were teasing him and forced him to go into the theatre to hear the comedy, he was not pleased with them, but utterly despised — being a man temperate and just and good, and besides wise — men who were mockers and insolent and said nothing sound; which grieved them terribly. So these too were the seeds of the comedy against him, and not only those that are admitted to have come from Anytus and Meletus. It is likely too that Aristophanes was paid for these things. For since they wished — or rather were eager by every means to slander Socrates — and since he himself was poor and accursed, what was strange in his taking money for no good end? But of these things he himself knows; at any rate his drama was well thought of. And indeed it happened then, if ever, as Cratinus says, that the theatre was sick in its wits. And since it was the festival of Dionysus, a very great multitude of the Greeks came in their eagerness for the spectacle. So, when Socrates was being paraded on the stage and named many times — and I would not wonder if he was even seen among the actors, for plainly the mask-makers fashioned him as like as could be — the strangers, who did not know who was being made fun of, raised a murmur and kept asking who this Socrates might be. Perceiving this — for he was present, not idly nor by chance, but knowing they were making a comedy of him, and indeed he sat in a conspicuous place in the theatre — in order to resolve the strangers' perplexity, he stood up and remained standing throughout the whole drama while the actors performed, and so was seen. So far did Socrates carry his disdain of comedy and of the Athenians.

The nation of the Tapyri is so very fond of wine that they live in wine, and spend the greater part of their lives in their intercourse with it. And they do not only use it for drinking, but wine is for them an ointment as well, as oil is for others.
They say that Anaxagoras of Clazomenae was never seen laughing, nor smiling at all. They say too that Aristoxenus was a mighty enemy of laughter; and that Heraclitus wept over everything in life.

Dionysius of Heracleia, the son of the tyrant Clearchus, I hear, from his daily gluttony and luxury grew, before he knew it, exceedingly fat and gross of body. The reward, then, of his bodily bulk and the mass of his flesh that he reaped was difficulty in breathing. As a remedy for this affliction, they say, the physicians prescribed that very long fine needles be made, and that these be driven through his ribs and belly whenever he chanced to fall into a deeper sleep. This it was their task to do, until the needle passed entirely through the callused and, as it were, alien flesh of him; but he lay there no different from a stone. If, however, the needle reached the place where his body was still sound and his own — not made alien by excessive fat — then he too felt it, and woke from sleep. He gave audience to those who wished to approach him by setting a chest before his body. Others say it was not a chest but a little tower, so that the rest of his parts might be hidden, and only his face, showing above it, might converse — clothing himself, ye gods, in this miserable garb, the cage of a beast rather than the dress of a man.

Critias blames Archilochus for having spoken most ill of himself. "For if," he says, "that man had not put about such a reputation of himself among the Greeks, we should not have learned that he was the son of Enipo the slave-woman, nor that, leaving Paros because of poverty and want, he came to Thasos, nor that, having come, he became hateful to those there, nor indeed that he spoke ill of friends and enemies alike. And besides this," he says, "we should not know either that he was an adulterer, had we not learned it from him, nor that he was lecherous and insolent, and — what is still more shameful than these — that he threw away his shield. Archilochus, then, was no good witness for himself, leaving behind such a glory and such a report of himself." These things I do not charge against Archilochus, but Critias does.

They say that a certain Sicilian became so keen of sight in Sicily that, fixing his eye from Lilybaeum to Carthage, his vision was in no way deceived. And they say that he could report the number of ships putting out from Carthage, and was not wrong about a single one."

There came from the Hellespont to the Attic courtesan Gnathaena a man as a lover, drawn by her fame. So over the wine he talked much, and seemed tiresome. Gnathaena, taking him up, said to him: "So you say you have come from the Hellespont?" When he agreed, she said: "And how is it you do not know the first of the cities there?" When he said, "And which is this?" she answered, "Sigeum." And by means of the name she fittingly silenced him.
They say that Ptolemy the son of Lagus took great delight in enriching his friends. And he used to say that it was better to make others rich than to be rich oneself.

Agathon used many antitheses often. When someone, as if correcting him, wished to remove them from his dramas, he said: "But you, my good man, do not realize that you are obliterating Agathon out of Agathon." So proud was he of these, and he thought that this was his tragedy.

Aristotle says that the swan has fine and numerous offspring, but also has spirit. Often, indeed, swans have come to anger and to battle and killed one another. The same writer says that swans fight with eagles; yet they defend themselves and do not begin unjust attacks. That they are fond of song has already been told and retold. For my part I have never heard a swan sing, and perhaps no one else has either; yet it is believed that it does sing. And they say that it is most musical and tuneful precisely at that time when it is near the end of its life. They cross the open sea as well, and fly low over the water, and their wing does not grow weary.

That Xerxes was a laughable man, if indeed he despised the sea and the land, the work of Zeus, and made for himself new roads and an unwonted voyage, yet was a slave to a plane-tree and admired the tree. In Lydia, at any rate, they say that, seeing a fine large plane-tree, he stayed there that day with no need to, and used the desert about the tree for his halting-place. Moreover he hung costly ornament upon it, honouring its branches with collars and bracelets, and left a keeper for it, as a guard and warden over a beloved. And from this what good came to the tree? The borrowed adornment, which in no way belonged to it, hung there idly and added nothing to its beauty; since the beauty of a tree is this — noble branches, abundant foliage, a firm trunk, deep roots, winds that toss it, far-spreading shade from it, the seasons turning, and water, some nourishing it through channels, some watering it from heaven; but Xerxes' robes and the barbarian's gold and the rest of the gifts were worthy neither of the plane-tree nor of any other noble tree.

The Byzantines, being terrible drunkards, have a reputation for living in the taverns, having moved out of their own houses and chambers, and let them out to the strangers who sojourn in the city; and not only their houses, but they gave up their wives to them as well, so that the Byzantines bear at once a double charge, of drunkenness and of pandering. And, dissolving as they do under drunkenness and wine, they rejoice to hear the flute, and being played to is their whole business; but a trumpet they cannot endure at all. And from this one may understand that the Byzantines are most ill-disposed toward arms and wars. For this reason indeed Leonidas, their general, in a hard siege, when the enemy had assaulted the walls and the Byzantines, deserting their posts, were passing the day in their usual haunts, ordered the taverns to be set up for them upon the walls. And this stratagem persuaded them, late and slowly, not to leave their station, since their pretext had been taken away from them. Damon tells these things of them. And Menander too seems to agree with these, when he says: "Byzantium makes the merchants drunkards; we drank the whole night through."

Diogenes of Sinope, when at last he lay sick unto death, dragged himself along alone and threw himself down beside a little bridge near a gymnasium, and ordered the keeper of the wrestling-school, when he perceived that he had breathed his last, to throw him into the Ilissus. So little did Diogenes care for either death or burial.

They say that Philetas of Cos was very slight of body. Since, then, he was easily upset by any cause, they say he had soles of lead made for his shoes, that he might not be overturned by the winds, if ever hard gusts blew. But if he was so weak that he could not stand against a gust of wind, how could he have carried so great a burden? For my part, the tale does not convince me; but what I have learned about the man, that I have told.

Socrates used to say that idleness is the sister of freedom. And as proof he cited the Indians and the Persians, the bravest and most free of men, both of them most idle when it comes to money-making; whereas the Phrygians and Lydians are most industrious, but slaves.

The most beautiful and lovable of men, they say, were, among the Greeks Alcibiades, and among the Romans Scipio. They say too that Demetrius Poliorcetes laid claim to beauty. And Alexander son of Philip, they say, was beautiful without effort; for his hair was swept back and was golden, and there shone forth from his appearance, they say, something awe-inspiring in Alexander.

The verses of Homer the ancients formerly sang divided into parts. For instance, they spoke of "The Battle at the Ships" and a certain "Doloneia" and "The Aristeia of Agamemnon" and "The Catalogue of Ships" and "The Patrocleia" and "The Ransom" and "The Games over Patroclus" and "The Breaking of the Oaths." These for the Iliad. And for the other: "The Events in Pylos" and "The Events in Lacedaemon" and "Calypso's Cave" and "The Affair of the Raft" and "The Tales told to Alcinous" and "The Cyclops" and "The Descent to the Dead" and "The Affairs of Circe" and "The Washing of the Feet" and "The Slaying of the Suitors" and "The Events in the Country" and "The Events at Laertes'." Late, Lycurgus the Lacedaemonian was the first to bring the poetry of Homer in a body to Greece; and he brought this freight from Ionia, when he was abroad. Later Pisistratus gathered it together and produced the Iliad and the Odyssey.

Someone gave Stratonicus the harper a lavish welcome; and he was overjoyed at the invitation, for he happened to have no lodging, having come to a foreign land. So he warmly embraced the man for the readiness of his sharing his roof. But when he saw one man coming in, and another, and that the man's house was in a manner open and unclosed to all who chose to lodge there, then Stratonicus said to his attendant: "Let us go away from here, boy; for it seems we have a wood-pigeon instead of a dove, having found an inn instead of a house."

They say that doves brood on their eggs by turns. Then, when the young are hatched, the male spits upon them, that they may not be bewitched. The female lays two eggs, of which the first is always made male, the second female. Doves lay throughout every season of the year; and so they breed ten times in the year. There is a story current among the Egyptians that those in Egypt lay twelve times. Aristotle says too that the rock-dove differs from the pigeon: the pigeon is the larger, the rock-dove the smaller, and the pigeon becomes tame, but the other does not. The same writer says that the male does not mount the female before he has kissed her; for the females will not endure the company of the males without a kiss. And he adds this too, that the females mount one another when they fail of union with a male; and they emit nothing into one another, but lay eggs from which no young come to them. If one should give any heed to Callimachus, he says that the ring-dove, the turtle-dove, the pigeon, and the wood-pigeon resemble one another in nothing. Indian reports say that in India there are doves the colour of quinces. Charon of Lampsacus says that white doves appeared about Athos at the time when the Persian triremes were destroyed there as they were rounding Athos. At Eryx in Sicily, where there is the august and holy temple of Aphrodite, the people of Eryx at a certain season celebrate the festival of the Departure, and they say that Aphrodite is then carried over from Sicily to Libya. At that time the doves vanish from the place, as though travelling abroad together with the goddess. But for the rest of the time a very great multitude of these birds is agreed to throng about the goddess's temple. Achaean stories, on the other hand, say that Zeus himself changed his shape into a dove out of love for a maiden named Phthia. This Phthia lived at Aegium.

Some men of Clazomenae, coming to Sparta and behaving with insolence and arrogance, smeared with soot the thrones of the ephors, where they are accustomed to sit and conduct business and arrange each of the city's affairs. When the ephors learned of it, they were not angry, but, summoning the public herald, ordered him to proclaim publicly this admired pronouncement: "Let it be permitted to the Clazomenians to behave indecently."

The Argives and Tirynthians too have been made a subject of comedy, as approaching wine too intemperately. As for the Thracians, this indeed is already noised abroad and made common talk, that they are most terrible drinkers. Nor have the Illyrians escaped this charge, but they have taken on besides that further reproach, that it is permitted to the strangers present at a banquet to drink to the wives, each to whichever he wishes, even if the woman is no relation to him at all.

When Philip conquered the Athenians at Chaeronea, though elated by his success, he nonetheless kept his reason in check and did not grow insolent; and for this reason he thought he ought to be reminded each morning by one of his pages that he was a man, and he gave the boy this duty to perform. And they say that he would neither go out himself, nor would any of those who had business with him be admitted to him, until the boy had called this out to him three times.

The Argives gave Homer the first place in all poetry, and ranked all others second to him. When they made sacrifice, they invited Apollo and Homer to the feast. It is said too, besides this, that being at a loss to provide a dowry for his daughter, he gave her the Cypria as her marriage portion. And Pindar agrees with this.

The daughters of Aristides, while he was still alive, were courted by those among the Greeks who seemed to be of distinction. But they were looking, in fact, not to the life of Aristides, nor did they admire his justice; for if they had been emulators of these, they would have persisted in their suit afterward as well. As it was, when he died, they thought there was no common concern with the girls; for at his death the son of Lysimachus was found to be poor. This it was that turned those wretched men away from a marriage at once glorious and most honourable, in my judgment. Much the same happened in the case of Lysander too; for when they learned that he was poor, they ran away from the marriage.

They say that Heracles rested his labours in the contests with play. The son of Zeus and Alcmene was very fond of playing with children. This Euripides too hints at to us, making this same god say: "I play; for I ever love changes from toil." He says this while holding a child. And Socrates was once caught by Alcibiades playing with Lamprocles, who was still an infant. And Agesilaus, bestriding a reed, rode it with his son, who was a boy, and to the one who laughed he said: "For now be silent, but when you become a father yourself, then you will tell of it." And Archytas of Tarentum too, a statesman and a philosopher, having many household slaves, took great delight in playing with their children, the home-bred slaves; and most of all he liked to delight in them at his banquets.

The comic poets say that a certain Polydorus was the dullest of mind, and another one named Coecylion, who counted the waves out of excessive folly. There is a story too that Sannyrion was such a man, who looked for a ladder in an oil-flask. And Coroebus and Melitides too they call those fools.

A story went round saying that the discourses of Socrates were like the paintings of Pauson. For Pauson the painter, having undertaken from someone to paint a horse rolling, painted it running. When the man who had commissioned the picture was indignant, as it was painted contrary to the agreement, the painter answered: "Turn the picture round, and the running horse will be rolling for you." So too Socrates did not converse plainly. If, at any rate, one turned his words round, they were perfectly correct. And the reason was that he did not wish to make himself hateful to those with whom he conversed, and for this reason he made his words riddling and oblique.

When the ship had come from Delos, and Socrates had to die, Apollodorus, the companion of Socrates, came to the prison bringing him a costly, finely-woven tunic of wool and a cloak to match. He begged him to put on the tunic and wrap himself in the cloak, and so drink the poison. For he said that Socrates would not lack for a fine shroud if he died in such garments; and indeed his body would lie in state, with its adornment, not without some dignity. So Apollodorus pressed Socrates; but Socrates would not consent, and said to Crito and Simmias and Phaedo and the rest: "And how well does this Apollodorus think of us, if he has come to believe that after the parting from the Athenians he will still see Socrates? For if he supposes that I, who a little while hence will be flung down at his feet and lie there, am to be myself, plainly he does not know me."

This too of Phocion, son of Phocus, I know to be a fine thing. Coming forward before the Athenians at an assembly, when he had some reproach to make against them for their folly, he said, very wisely and tellingly: "I had rather suffer some harm at your hands than myself do you any harm."

Which, then, was the better general, Demetrius the Besieger or Timotheus the Athenian? I will tell the manner of both; and it is for you to prefer the one. Demetrius took cities by force and greed, doing the greatest harm and wrong, bringing up engines and shaking down and undermining the walls; but Timotheus by persuading and teaching with argument that it was more profitable to obey the Athenians.

Solon son of Execestides, being now an old man, suspected that Pisistratus would set himself up as tyrant, when Pisistratus came forward in the assembly of the Athenians and asked for a bodyguard. Seeing that the Athenians listened carelessly to his own words but gave heed to Pisistratus, he said that he was wiser than some and braver than others: than those who do not understand that, once he has obtained a guard for his person, he will be tyrant — wiser than these; and than those who understand it yet keep silent — braver than these. But Pisistratus, having received the force, was tyrant. Then Solon, sitting before his house with his shield and spear laid beside him, said that he had armed himself and was aiding his country as he could, being no longer a general because of his age, but loyal in his judgment. Yet Pisistratus, whether out of respect for the man and his wisdom, or out of remembrance of their youth — for the man is said to have been his favourite — did Solon no harm at all. And so Solon, a little later, being very old, ended his life, leaving behind a great reputation for wisdom and courage. They set up a bronze statue of him in the marketplace, and they buried him too at public expense beside the gates near the wall, on the right as one enters, and his tomb was walled about.

Italy was first inhabited by the Ausones, a people sprung from the soil. The most ancient of them, they say, was a certain Mares, whose forward parts were like a man's, but his hinder parts like a horse's; and the name itself, they say, means in Greek "horse-mingled." It seems to me that he was the first to mount a horse and put a bit upon it, and that from this he was believed to be of double nature. They tell in legend that he lived a hundred and twenty-three years, and that having died three times he came back to life three times; but to me these things seem unworthy of belief. They say that very many peoples settled Italy, more than any other land. The reason is the temperate climate, the excellence of the soil, its abundance of water, its fertility, its good pasturage, the fact that it is watered by rivers and that a good sea lies beside it, fringed on every side with harbours and with plentiful landing-places and anchorages. And the gentle and mild temper of its inhabitants moved many to settle there. And they say that long ago a thousand one hundred and ninety-seven cities settled Italy.

When Antisthenes was urging many to philosophy, but they paid no heed to him, at last in vexation he received no one. And so he tried to drive Diogenes too from his company. But when Diogenes grew more persistent and pressed on, then indeed he threatened to strike him with his staff; and once he even struck him on the head. But Diogenes did not depart, but pressed on still more eagerly, thirsting to hear him, and said: "Strike, if you wish, but I will offer my head; and you will not find a staff hard enough to drive me away from your discourses." And Antisthenes welcomed him warmly.

Alexander son of Philip is said to have been most jealously disposed toward his companions, and to have envied them all, though not for the same reasons. For he was vexed with Perdiccas because he was warlike, with Lysimachus because he seemed a good general, with Seleucus because he was brave; Antigonus's ambition pained him, with Antipater he was vexed for his capacity to command, Ptolemy's cleverness he viewed with suspicion, Tarrias's unruliness he feared, and Pithon's revolutionary spirit.

The Apolloniatae inhabit a city near Epidamnus on the Ionian gulf. And in the places near it there is asphalt that is dug up, and pitch springing from the earth in the same way as do most of the springs of water. Not far off the immortal fire too is shown. The burning place is small and does not extend far and has no great circuit, and smells of sulphur and alum. And about it are flourishing trees and green grass; and the fire blazing nearby does no harm either to the growth of the plants or to the flourishing grass. The fire burns both by night and by day, and never ceased, as the Apolloniatae say, until the war with the Illyrians befell them. The Apolloniatae practised the expulsion of foreigners according to the Lacedaemonian law, but the Epidamnians allowed anyone who wished to visit and settle among them.

Hipponicus the son of Callias wished to set up a statue as a dedication to his country. When someone advised him to have the statue made by Polyclitus, he said he would not attend to such a dedication, the glory of which would belong not to the dedicator but to the maker. For it was plain that those who saw the work would admire Polyclitus and not him.

These, then, are the admired little works of Myrmecides of Miletus and Callicrates of Lacedaemon. They made four-horse chariots that could be covered by a fly, and on a grain of sesame they inscribed an elegiac couplet in letters of gold. Of these, to my mind, the serious man will praise neither; for what are they but a squandering of time?

The wisdom of the Magi among the Persians knows, among the other things it is permitted them to know, also how to prophesy. These men foretold the savagery and bloodthirstiness of Ochus toward his subjects, having discerned it through certain secret signs. For when, upon the death of his father Artaxerxes, Ochus came to the kingship of the Persians, the Magi ordered one of the eunuchs standing near to watch which of the dishes set before him Ochus would attack first, when the table was laid. And while the eunuch stood watching this, Ochus stretched out his hands, took with his right one of the knives lying by, and with the other drew toward him the largest of the loaves, and laying meat upon it, then cut and ate without stint. Hearing this, the Magi prophesied these two things: abundance from the seasons and good harvests during the time of his reign, and many murders. And they were not deceived.

Philosophers too engaged in public life, and did not, having become good merely in mind, live out their days in quiet. For Zaleucus set right the public affairs in Locri, and Charondas those in Catana and those in Rhegium, when he was in exile from Catana. To the Tarentines Archytas was a good man, and Solon to the Athenians, and Bias and Thales benefited Ionia greatly, and Chilon the Lacedaemonians, and Pittacus the Mytilenaeans, and Cleobulus the Rhodians. And Anaximander led the colony from Miletus to Apollonia. Moreover Xenophon was a good soldier and a better general, when he went up with Cyrus; and when Cyrus and those with him had died, and need called for one who would be able to save the Greeks and lead them back to their homes, this was that man. And Plato, son of Ariston, brought Dion back to Sicily, and through the things he counselled and taught him, by these he overthrew the tyranny of Dionysius. Socrates was not pleased with the Athenian constitution; for he saw the democracy to be tyrannical and monarchic; and for this reason he neither put to the vote for the Athenians the death of the ten generals, nor shared in the impieties of the Thirty. But where it was necessary to fight for his country, there he was a soldier who made no excuse. He served, at any rate, at Delium, and at Amphipolis, and at Potidaea. Aristotle raised up his own country again, fallen — as the saying goes — not merely on its knees, but flat on its face. Demetrius of Phalerum governed most illustriously at Athens, until the envy familiar to the Athenians drove him out; and in Egypt, being with Ptolemy, he took charge of legislation. And who will deny that Pericles, son of Xanthippus, was a philosopher, and Epaminondas, son of Polymnis, and Phocion, son of Phocus, and Aristides, son of Lysimachus, and Ephialtes, son of Sophonides, and, lower still in time, Carneades and Critolaus, if indeed they came to Rome as ambassadors on behalf of the Athenians, and found safety for them? These so abashed the senate that they said: "The Athenians sent as ambassadors not men to persuade us, but men to force us to do whatever they wish." And I would call it statesmanship too, the work of Persaeus, if indeed he educated Antigonus, and that of Aristotle, since he too was plainly philosophizing with Alexander, the son of Philip, when he was young. And Lysis, the disciple of Pythagoras, he too educated Epaminondas. If, then, anyone calls philosophers men of no action, well, these words of his are silly and senseless; for I, for my part, would seize upon the freedom from public affairs that goes with them, and the love of quiet, even at a run.

Scythes of Inycum, the sole ruler of the Zanclaeans, went up into Asia to King Darius. And Darius judged him the most just of all the men who had come up to him from Greece, because, having asked the king's leave, he went to Sicily and from Sicily back again to the king. This Democedes of Croton did not do, and for this reason Darius spoke ill of him, calling him a cheat and a most worthless man. So Scythes, living in great prosperity among the Persians, ended his life in old age.

This account seems to charge Demosthenes with vanity, the one that says that even the water-carriers used to fill him with conceit, if ever, as he passed by, they whispered something about him. For one who was elated even by them, and plainly puffed up, what must he have been if ever he was applauded by the assembly?

Critias says that Themistocles son of Neocles, before he began to take part in public life, had a patrimony of three talents; but when he had taken the lead in public affairs and then went into exile, and his property was confiscated, he was found to have an estate of more than a hundred talents. Likewise Cleon too, before he came forward into public life, had nothing of his own free of debt; but afterward he left a house worth fifty talents.

Demetrius, though he ruled over so many nations, used to go to Lamia the courtesan with his arms and wearing his diadem. It was shameful enough for him even to send for the woman to his house; but he would go to her openly. For my part, I would prefer Theodorus the flute-player to Demetrius, since when Lamia sent for Theodorus, he disdained the summons.

"Phrynichus cowers like a cock" — a proverb said of those who suffer some ill. For when Phrynichus the tragedian was performing The Capture of Miletus, the Athenians, bursting into tears, expelled him as he cowered and crouched in fear.

Socrates said that Archelaus spent four hundred minae on his house, hiring Zeuxis of Heracleia to decorate it, but nothing on himself. Therefore those who wished to see the house came from afar with great eagerness; but for Archelaus's own sake no one journeyed to Macedon, unless he should persuade and lure someone with money — by which a man of worth would not be won.

How could the women of old fail to be ruined by their luxury? For upon their heads they set a tall crown, they shod their feet in sandals, from their ears hung long earrings, and the parts of their tunics about the shoulders down to the hands they did not sew together, but caught up with golden and silver brooches set close together. So much for the very ancient women; as for the luxury of the Attic women, let Aristophanes tell of it.

Timotheus, son of Conon, the general of the Athenians, once, having withdrawn from those costly dinners and those generals' banquets, was taken by Plato to the symposium in the Academy and entertained simply and after the manner of the Muses; and returning home he said to his household that those who dine with Plato are well even on the morrow. From this Timotheus disparaged costly and vulgar dinners as not pleasing at all on the day after. There is another story, brother to the one just told and meaning the same thing, though not telling it in the same words, that goes about: that on the next day Timotheus, meeting Plato, said: "You, Plato, dine better for the morrow than for the present day."

Theopompus relates a certain meeting of Midas the Phrygian and Silenus. This Silenus was the son of a nymph, lower in nature than a god, but higher than a man, since he was also immortal. They discoursed of many other things with each other, and among them Silenus said this to Midas: that Europe and Asia and Libya were islands, around which Ocean flowed in a circle; and that the only mainland was that one outside this world of ours. And he described its size as boundless. It nourished other animals, large ones, and men of double the stature of those here, and these lived a time not so long as ours, but that too doubled. And there were many great cities and peculiar ways of life, and laws were established among them set in opposition to those held among us. There were, he said, two cities greatest in size, and resembling one another in nothing; and the one was named Warlike, the other Pious. The Pious, then, pass their lives in peace and deep wealth, and take the fruits from the earth without ploughs and oxen, and tilling and sowing are no labour to them.
