And they continue, he said, healthy and free of sickness, and end their lives laughing heartily and rejoicing. And they are so unquestionably just that even the gods do not often disdain to visit them. The men of the Warlike city, on the other hand, are most warlike themselves, and are born with arms, and are always at war, and subdue their neighbours, and this one city rules over very many nations. Its inhabitants are not fewer than two million. They die, for the rest, of sickness; but this is rare, since for the most part they are struck down in wars by stones or by wood; for they are unwounded by iron. They have an abundance of gold and silver, so that gold is held in less honour among them than iron is among us. He said too that these once attempted to cross over to these our islands, and, sailing across Ocean with ten thousand thousand men, came as far as the Hyperboreans. And learning that these were the happiest of all among us, they despised them as faring poorly and meanly, and on this account scorned to go any further. And he added something still more wonderful. Certain men called Meropes, he said, dwell among them in many great cities, and at the extremity of their country there is a place called Anostus ("No-Return"), resembling a chasm, held neither by darkness nor by light, but with an air lying over it mingled with a murky redness. Two rivers flow about this place, the one called the river of Pleasure, the other of Grief; and beside each of them stand trees of the size of a great plane-tree. The trees that grow beside the river of Grief bear fruits of such a nature that if anyone tastes them, he sheds so many tears that he wastes away all the rest of his life in mourning, and so dies. But the others, that grow beside the river of Pleasure, bring forth fruit of the opposite kind. For whoever tastes of these ceases from his former desires, and even if he was in love forgets it, and becomes little by little younger, and takes back the years that have passed and those already gone. For, casting off old age, he returns to his prime, then withdraws to the age of young men, then becomes a child, then an infant, and after that is wholly consumed. And these things, if the Chian seems to anyone worthy of belief, let them be believed; but to me he seems a clever teller of tales, both in these matters and in others.

Euthymus the Locrian, of those in Italy, was a good boxer, and he is believed to have been most marvellous in bodily strength; for the Locrians show a stone of the greatest size, which he carried and set before his doors. And the hero in Temesa, who was exacting tribute from the neighbouring people, he made to cease; for, coming to the hero's shrine, which was forbidden ground to most men, he fought it out with him, and forced him to pay back more than he had plundered. From this, indeed, the proverb spread, said of those who profit by something to no good end, that "the hero in Temesa will come to them." They say that this same Euthymus, going down to the river Caecinus, which is before the city of the Locrians, vanished.

Themistocles son of Neocles likened himself to the oaks, saying that men take shelter under them too, and have need of them when it rains, longing for the roof their branches give; but when fair weather comes and they pass by, they pluck them and break off their boughs. So, he said, he himself suffered the same at the hands of the people. The same man said: "If someone were to show me two roads, one leading to Hades and the other to the speaker's platform, I would more gladly take the one that goes straight to Hades."

Daphnis the cowherd some say was the beloved of Hermes, others his son; and that he got his name from what befell him. He was born of a Nymph, and at his birth was exposed among the laurels. The cattle he herded, they say, were sisters of the cattle of the Sun, of which Homer makes mention in the Odyssey. As Daphnis was herding in Sicily, one of the Nymphs fell in love with him, and consorted with him, fair and young as he was and just getting his first beard, when youth is at its most charming in beautiful young men, as Homer says somewhere. She made a compact that he should come near no other woman, and threatened that it was fated for him to be deprived of his sight if he transgressed; and they had a sworn agreement with each other about this. Some time later, when a king's daughter fell in love with him, he, made drunk, broke the agreement and consorted with the girl. From this the bucolic songs were first sung, and they had as their subject the affliction of his eyes. And it was Stesichorus of Himera who first composed this kind of song.

Phaon, who was the fairest of men, Aphrodite hid among the lettuces. Another tale is that he was a ferryman and had this occupation. Aphrodite once came, wishing to cross over, and he received her gladly, not knowing who she was, and with much care brought her wherever she wished. In return the goddess gave him an alabaster jar, and it held an ointment, with which Phaon, anointing himself, became the fairest of men; and the women of Mytilene fell in love with him. At the last, however, he was slain, caught in adultery.
Dionysius the tyrant of Sicily embraced and praised tragedy, and indeed worked at composing tragic dramas, but was disposed unfavourably toward comedy, because he was not fond of laughter.

A man of Chios, angry with his servant, said: "I will not throw you into the mill, but I will take you to Olympia." For he thought, naturally, it was a far harsher punishment for that man to be roasted by the sun's rays while watching at Olympia than to grind, handed over to the mill.

The common account, which has gone out to all, says that for the Sybarites and for Sybaris itself the cause of their ruin was their great luxury. But what is not known to most, this I will relate. They say that the Colophonians too perished through their excessive luxury; for they too gave themselves up to costly clothing, and indulged riotously and beyond all need in the wantonness of the table. And the rule of the Bacchiadae at Corinth, which had advanced to great power, was nevertheless dissolved through luxury exceeding all measure.

Alexander, when he had conquered Darius and gained the empire of the Persians, thinking great things of himself and made a god by the good fortune that had then encompassed him, sent word to the Greeks to vote him a god. Absurdly. For what nature had not given him, this he gained nothing by demanding from men. So various peoples voted various things, but the Lacedaemonians voted this: "Since Alexander wishes to be a god, let him be a god" — thus in their laconic and native fashion the Lacedaemonians convicting Alexander of folly.

They say that the first quarrel of Aristotle with Plato arose from this. Plato was not pleased with his manner of life nor with his attention to his body. For Aristotle used elaborate dress and footwear, and had his hair cut in a fashion unwonted to Plato, and prided himself on wearing many rings; and there was a certain mockery about his face, and an unseasonable garrulity when he spoke, and this too accused his character. All these things, that they are foreign to a philosopher, is plain. Seeing them, then, Plato did not admit the man, but preferred to him Xenocrates and Speusippus and Amyclas and others, treating them with honour in other ways and especially with a share in his discourses. Now once, when Xenocrates went abroad to his country, Aristotle set upon Plato, gathering about him a band of his own followers, among whom were Mnason the Phocian and others of the same sort. Speusippus was ill at that time, and for this reason was unable to walk with Plato. And Plato had reached eighty years, and through his age his memory had in some part failed him. So Aristotle, setting upon him and plotting against him, and very ambitiously putting his questions, and in a manner aiming at refutation, was plainly both unjust and ungracious; and for this reason Plato withdrew from his walk outside, and walked within with his friends. When three months had passed, Xenocrates returned from abroad, and finds Aristotle walking where he had left Plato. Seeing that he, with his acquaintances, was not withdrawing toward Plato from the walk, but going off by himself into the city, he asked one of those in the walk where in the world Plato was; for he suspected that he was ill. And the man answered: "He is not ill, but Aristotle, troubling him, has made him give up the walk, and, withdrawing, he philosophizes in his own garden." Xenocrates, on hearing this, went at once to Plato, and found him conversing with those about him; and they were many, and worthy of mention, and the youths who seemed most distinguished. When he had ceased from his discourse, he greeted Xenocrates, as was natural, with kindness, and Xenocrates in turn greeted him likewise. When the gathering had broken up, Xenocrates, neither saying anything to Plato nor hearing anything, gathered his companions and rebuked Speusippus very strongly for having given up the walk to Aristotle; and he himself set upon the Stagirite vigorously, and went so far in his rivalry that he drove him out and gave back the accustomed place to Plato.

This is the epitaph inscribed for Anaxagoras: "Here, having passed to the utmost bound of truth concerning the heavenly cosmos, lies Anaxagoras." And there is an altar set up to him, and on it is inscribed by some "To Mind," by others "To Truth."

Diogenes was once lunching in a tavern, and seeing Demosthenes passing, he called to him. When Demosthenes paid no heed, he said: "Are you ashamed, Demosthenes, to come into a tavern? Yet your master comes in here every day" — meaning the common people, both as a body and one by one; showing that the demagogues and orators are slaves of the multitude.
Eurydamas of Cyrene won a boxing match, although his teeth had been knocked out by his opponent; he swallowed them, that his adversary might not perceive it.
The poetess Sappho, daughter of Scamandronymus — her even Plato son of Ariston records as wise. I learn that there was also another Sappho in Lesbos, a courtesan, not a poetess.

Cleomenes said, in the Laconian manner after the local fashion, that Homer was the poet of the Lacedaemonians, since he tells how one must make war; but Hesiod the poet of the Helots, since he tells how one must farm.

Archytas was temperate in other ways, and indeed he guarded against unseemly words. When once he was forced to say something improper, he was not overcome, but kept silent about it, and wrote it upon the wall, showing what he was forced to say, yet not forced to say it.

Dionysius plundered the treasures from all the temples in Syracuse. From the statue of Zeus he stripped the robe and the ornament, which they say was of gold worth eighty-five talents. When the workmen shrank from laying hands on it, he himself was the first to strike the statue. He also plundered the statue of Apollo, which likewise had golden locks, ordering someone to shear them off. Sailing to the Tyrrhenians, he plundered all the treasures of Apollo and of Leucothea, ordering the silver table that stood beside Apollo to be taken away, saying that he was giving the god a toast to the Good Spirit.

They say that King Antigonus was of the people and gentle. Whoever has leisure to know the particulars about him and to examine each detail of the man will learn them elsewhere; but I will tell what I am about to say, which is very gentle and unassuming of him. This Antigonus, seeing his son treat his subjects too violently and too boldly, said: "Do you not know, my son, that our kingship is a glorious slavery?" Now Antigonus's words to his son are very mild and humane; but if anyone thinks otherwise, then that man, it seems to me, does not know a kingly or statesmanlike person, but is rather suited to living with a tyrant.

To Lysander the Spartan, when he came to Ionia, the foreigners in Ionia sent many other things, and among them an ox and a cake. He, looking at the cake, asked: "What is that pastry meant to be?" And the one who brought it answered that it was made of honey and cheese and certain other things. And Lysander said: "Give this to the Helots; for it is no food for a free man." But the ox he ordered to be prepared after the manner of his fathers, and he dined on it gladly.

As Aristippus was sailing, a storm came on and he was very greatly troubled. One of his fellow voyagers said: "Aristippus, are you too afraid, like the common folk?" And he replied: "Yes, and with good reason; for your concern, and the present danger, is over a wretched life, but mine over a happy one."

The Persian king wrote to Agesilaus, asking to have him as his friend. But Agesilaus wrote back that it was not possible for him to be the king's friend privately; but if the king were a friend to the Lacedaemonians in common, then clearly he would be a friend to him also; for in that case he too would be counted among them all.

Hesiod says that the nightingale alone of birds has no share in sleep and is wakeful throughout; but that the swallow does not keep wholly wakeful even she, but has lost half her sleep. They pay this penalty for the suffering committed in Thrace, that lawless dinner.

A man of Megalopolis from Arcadia, Cercidas by name, as he was dying said to his kinsmen, who were downcast, that he was leaving life gladly; for he had hope of consorting, among the wise, with Pythagoras, among the historians with Hecataeus, among the musicians with Olympus, among the poets with Homer. And with these words, the story goes, his soul left him.

A Sybarite man, a tutor — for indeed, along with the other Sybarites, these too lived in luxury — when the boy he was leading along the road came upon a dried fig and picked it up, rebuked him most severely; but most ludicrously he himself snatched the find from the boy and gobbled it down. When I read this in Sybaritic histories, I laughed; and I gave it to memory, not grudging out of love of mankind that another too should laugh.

I would not conceal the clever and truly Greek deed of Ismenias the Theban. While serving as ambassador on behalf of his country to the king of the Persians, he arrived, and wished himself to obtain audience of the Persian concerning the matters for which he had come. The chiliarch, who carried in messages to the king and brought in those who sought audience, said to him: "Theban stranger" — he spoke thus in Persian through an interpreter, and the chiliarch's name was Tithraustes — "there is a native custom among the Persians, that whoever comes into the king's sight must not partake of speech until he has done him obeisance. If, then, you wish to meet with him in person, it is time for you to do what the custom requires; but if not, this same end will be accomplished for you through us, even though you do not perform the obeisance." So Ismenias said, "Lead me in." And going forward and coming into the king's sight, he slipped off his ring and let it fall, unseen, beside his feet, and quickly stooping down, as if doing obeisance, he picked it up again. Thus he gave the Persian the appearance of obeisance, yet did nothing that brings shame among the Greeks. So he accomplished everything he wished, and met with no failure at the Persian's hands.

Pausanias of the deme Ceramus loved the poet Agathon. This is much talked of; but what has not gone out to all, I will tell. They once came to the court of Archelaus, this lover and his beloved. Now Archelaus was no less amorous than fond of the Muses. Since, then, he often saw Pausanias and Agathon quarrelling with each other, thinking that the lover was being slighted by his favourite, Archelaus asked Agathon what he meant by so frequently falling out with the man who loved him above all. And Agathon said: "I will tell you, king. For I am neither quarrelsome toward him, nor do I do this out of boorishness; but if I too understand anything of human character, both otherwise and from poetry, I find it most pleasant for lovers to be reconciled with their beloveds after a quarrel, and I am convinced that nothing so delightful befalls them. So I often give him a share of this pleasure by quarrelling with him repeatedly; for he rejoices whenever I am continually ending my quarrel with him, whereas if I approached him evenly and as a matter of habit he would not know the difference." Archelaus, the story goes, praised this. They say too that the poet Euripides also loved this same Agathon, and that he composed his drama Chrysippus as a favour to him. Whether this is certain I cannot declare; but I know that it is said by most.

Once, while still a boy, Themistocles was returning from school. Then, as Pisistratus was approaching, his attendant told Themistocles to give way a little from the road, the tyrant drawing near. But he answered very freely: "Is this road not wide enough for him?" So noble and high-minded a thing showed itself in Themistocles even then.

Theramenes happened to be staying in a certain house, and then, when he had gone out of it, it at once fell down. The Athenians, crowding round him from all sides, congratulated him on his unexpected escape; but he, against all expectation, answered: "O Zeus, for what occasion are you keeping me?" And not long after he was put to death by the Thirty, being condemned to drink hemlock.

Perictione was carrying Plato in her arms; and while Ariston was sacrificing on Hymettus to the Muses or the Nymphs, the rest were busy with the rite, but she laid Plato down among the myrtles nearby, which were thick and dense. As he slept, a swarm of bees settled on his lips and sang, foretelling thereby the eloquence of Plato.

The mothers of the Lacedaemonians, all who learned that their sons lay slain in battle, came and inspected their wounds, both those in front and those behind. And if the wounds in front were more, they, exulting and looking at once proud and stern, carried their sons off to the ancestral tombs; but if it was otherwise with the wounds, then, ashamed and lamenting and eager to escape notice as much as possible, they went away, leaving the dead to be buried in the common grave, or carried them secretly to the family tombs.
In Celaenae, if anyone plays upon the flute, before the skin of the Phrygian, the Phrygian mode, the skin moves; but if the mode is for Apollo, it stays still and seems deaf.
There was a certain Oeagrus, a poet after Orpheus and Musaeus, who is said to have been the first to sing the Trojan War, having taken up a very great subject and ventured upon it.

The gifts given by the king to the ambassadors who came to him, whether they arrived from the Greeks or from elsewhere, were these. To each a Babylonian talent of coined silver, and two silver bowls of a talent's weight. The Babylonian talent is worth seventy-two Attic minae. He also gave bracelets and a dagger and a collar, worth a thousand darics, and besides these a Median robe; the name of the robe was the "gift-bearing" robe.

I hear that the Mantineans too were among the best-governed peoples, no less than the Locrians or the Cretans or the Lacedaemonians themselves or the Athenians; for a grand thing too was the work of Solon, even if afterward the Athenians little by little corrupted some of the laws he had written for them.

When Ilium was taken, the Achaeans, pitying the fortunes of the captured and doing this in truly Greek fashion, made this proclamation: that each of the free men should carry off, taking it up, one thing of his own that he wished. So Aeneas, taking up his fathers' gods, carried them, disdaining all else. The Greeks, then, pleased at the man's piety, granted him to take a second possession; and he, taking up his father, who was very aged, carried him on his shoulders. Astonished at this too, not least, they gave up to him all his own possessions, agreeing that toward men who are pious, and who hold the gods and their parents in reverence, even those who are by nature enemies become gentle.
They say that the Pythagoreans were very greatly devoted to the art of medicine. And Plato too gave it the greatest attention, and Aristotle the son of Nicomachus, and many others.

Dioxippus, in the presence of Alexander and the Macedonians, took a club, and fighting in single combat against Corragus the Macedonian heavy-armed soldier, struck aside his spear, seized the man with his full armour, and stepping on the neck of the fallen man, snatched the sword that hung at his side and killed the soldier. But he was hated by Alexander. And in despair, hated as he was by Alexander, and downcast, he took his own life."

They say that Milo of Croton, who was proud because of his bodily strength, met Titormus the cowherd. Seeing, then, that Titormus was great of body to look upon, he wished to make trial of his strength. But Titormus said that he had no great strength, and going down to the Evenus and stripping off his cloak, he took a very large stone, and first drew it toward himself, then pushed it away, and did this twice and three times, and after that raised it as far as his knees, and finally lifting it onto his shoulders carried it some eight fathoms and threw it; but Milo of Croton could barely move the stone. Then Titormus went to the herd, and standing in the midst he took the largest bull, which was wild, by the foot; and the bull was eager to escape, but could not. And as another passed by, he seized it likewise by the foot with his other hand and held it. Milo, seeing this, stretched his hands to heaven and said: "O Zeus, have you not begotten for us a second Heracles in this man?" From this, they say, the proverb arose: "This is another Heracles."

Ptolemy Philopator, having built a temple to Homer, set him fairly seated and beautiful, and set in a circle around the statue all the cities that lay claim to Homer. And Galaton the painter painted Homer himself vomiting, and the other poets drawing up what he had vomited.

A certain tyrant, Tryzus, wishing to root out conspiracies and plots against himself, ordered the inhabitants that no one should converse with anyone, neither in public nor in private. And the thing was impossible and grievous. So they outwitted the tyrant's command, and nodded to one another and made gestures to one another, and looked now fiercely and again calmly and cheerfully; and at sorrowful and incurable things each of them was plainly knit of brow, showing to his neighbour the affliction of his soul from his face. This too troubled the tyrant, and he believed that even their silence would surely breed him some harm, through the variety of their gestures. So he put a stop to this too. One of those distressed at the impossibility of their plight, and chafing, and thirsting to dissolve the monarchy, came to the marketplace, then stood and wept with many and abundant tears. So the crowd stood round him and gathered about, and they too were seized with lamentation. News came to the tyrant that none of them used the nod any longer, but that tears were now in fashion among them. And he, eager to put a stop to this too — not only condemning the tongue to slavery, nor the nods alone, but now shutting off from the eyes too their natural freedom — came as fast as his feet would carry him with his bodyguards, that he might check the tears. But no sooner had they seen him than, snatching the weapons of the bodyguards, they killed the tyrant.

Among the Greeks of old, Gorgias of Leontini, son of Philolaus, and Protagoras, son of Democritus, stood out for their great reputation, yet in wisdom they fell as far short as children fall short of men. For reputation, it seems, neither sees nor hears quite accurately; and so it is mistaken in many things, granting some by favour and falsifying others.

Nicodorus the boxer, having been among the most renowned of the Mantineans, late in his life and after his athletic career became their lawgiver, and so governed his country far better than by his proclamations in the stadiums. They say that Diagoras of Melos, who was his lover, composed the laws for him. I had something further to say about Nicodorus; but lest I should seem to be also taking up the praise of Diagoras, let my account go only so far. For Diagoras was hateful to the gods, and it is no pleasure to me to make much mention of him.

Fine, then, are Alexander's deeds at the Granicus and at Issus, and the battle at Arbela, and Darius defeated and the Persians enslaved to the Macedonians; fine too the conquest of all the rest of Asia, and the Indians as well obeying Alexander; fine too the affair at Tyre, and the events among the Oxydracae, and the rest of his deeds. For what need is there now to take in within the narrow bounds of speech so great a valour of the man in arms? And let it be granted, too, that Fortune loved Alexander in most things, if anyone wishes to be contentious. Fine, then, is Alexander when not overcome by Fortune, nor giving out against her eagerness toward him. But these other things of Alexander are no longer fine. On the fifth of the month Dios, they say, he drank at Medius's; then on the sixth he slept off the drinking, and lived of that day only so much as to rise and transact business with his officers about the next day's march, saying that it would be early. And on the seventh he feasted at Perdiccas's, and drank again, and on the eighth he slept. On the fifteenth of the same month he drank on this day too, and on the day following did the usual things that follow drinking. He dined at Bagoas's on the twenty-fourth — and Bagoas's house was ten stades distant from the palace — then on the twenty-fifth he slept. One of two things, then: either Alexander wrongs himself by losing so many days of the month to wine, or those who recorded these things lie. And one may infer from these that they say like things of the rest of the time as well — among whom is Eumenes the Cardian.

Aristotle was once ill. The physician prescribed him a certain regimen. And he said: "Do not treat me as you would a ploughman or a digger, but first teach me the reason, and then you will find me ready to obey" — teaching by this that nothing should be applied without a reason.

Of men I hear that the Celts are the fondest of danger. At any rate they make the subjects of their songs the men who have died nobly in war. They fight crowned with garlands, and they raise trophies too, at once taking pride in their deeds and leaving behind memorials of their valour in the Greek manner. So shameful do they think it to flee, that they will not run away even from their houses when these are sliding and collapsing, nor even when they are on fire and they are surrounded by the flames. Many even stand fast against the flooding sea. There are some too who, taking up their arms, fall upon the waves and receive their onset, brandishing their naked swords and spears, as though they could either frighten or wound them.

Lycurgus the Lacedaemonian, the son of Eunomus, wishing to make the Lacedaemonians just, drew for this no fine wages. For it befell him to have his eye knocked out by Alcander, as some say, struck with a stone out of a plot, or, as another story goes about, suffering the injury from a staff. The saying is applied to those who wished for one thing but obtained another. And Ephorus says that he died in exile, having held out against hunger.

Cleinias was a man earnest in character, and a Pythagorean in his wisdom. Whenever he was provoked to anger and perceived himself being carried away to wrath, at once, before his anger was full and it became plain how he was disposed, he tuned his lyre and played it. To those who asked the reason he answered fittingly: "I am calming myself." And it seems to me that Achilles too in the Iliad, who sang to the lyre and brought to his own memory through the music the glories of men of old, was lulling his wrath; for, being musical, he took the lyre first from the spoils.

Of Caucon, son of Poseidon, and Astydameia, daughter of Phorbas, was born a son Lepreus, who advised Augeas to bind Heracles when Heracles demanded from him the wages for the labour. So Lepreus was, as one would expect, an enemy of Heracles because of this counsel. But in time the son of Zeus came to Caucon's house, and at the entreaty of Astydameia Heracles dissolved his enmity toward Lepreus. Yet a youthful rivalry fell upon them, and they contended with each other over the discus, and the drawing of water, and which of them would devour a bull first; and in all these Lepreus was beaten. They had a contest over hard drinking as well, and there again Heracles prevailed. Stung by this, Lepreus took up arms and challenged Heracles to single combat. And so he paid the penalty for his dealings with Augeas; for he died in the fight.

Some have already cast down the famous strength of Milo of Croton, telling such things about him. The pomegranate of this Milo, which he held in his hand, none of his opponents could pull out; but his beloved drew it out very easily, contending with him often. From this one may understand that Milo was strong in body, but not brave in soul.

Xenophon cared, among other serious things, also to have fine arms. For he said that to one who conquered the enemy the fairest array was fitting, and that to one who died in battle it was a fine thing to lie nobly in fine armour; for to a noble man these are the funeral adornments that truly adorn him. They say, then, that the son of Gryllus had an Argolic shield, an Attic breastplate, a Boeotian-made helmet, and an Epidaurian horse. And I, for my part, would say that such things belong to a man who loves what is fine and thinks himself worthy of fine things.

Smindyrides the Sybarite ran aground in such luxury — for indeed all the Sybarites made it their business to live in luxury and dissolve their lives in it, and Smindyrides still more — that, having lain down upon rose petals and slept upon them, he rose up saying that he had blisters from the bed. Hardly would such a man have lain down on a hard bed, or a mattress of straw, or grass growing on a hillside, or a bull's hide, as Diomedes did, fitting for a hardy and noble soldier: "beneath was spread the hide of an ox of the field."

They say that Smindyrides the Sybarite ran aground in such luxury that he came to Sicyon as a suitor of Agariste the daughter of Cleisthenes, and brought with him a thousand cooks, as many fowlers, and a thousand fishermen.

Lycurgus the orator proposed that women should not drive in carriages at the mysteries, or that a penalty be imposed on her who did this, which he thought sufficient when he fixed it. The first to disobey the decree was his own wife, and she paid the penalty, being condemned. And Pericles proposed that no one should be an Athenian who was not born of two citizens. Then, having lost his legitimate sons, he was left with the bastard Pericles. It is plain that Pericles too wished for one thing but obtained another. And Cleisthenes the Athenian, who first proposed that men should be ostracized, was himself the first to incur the sentence. Zaleucus the lawgiver of the Locrians ordered that an adulterer caught should have his eyes put out. So things he had not even expected the divine power brought upon him contrary to his judgment and his hope; for his own son, caught in adultery, was then about to suffer what the ancestral law required. There, that what had once been ratified might not be undone, the proposer himself submitted to give his own eye in exchange for one of his son's eyes, that the young man might not be wholly blinded.

They despised wealth and showed greatness of soul, seeing their fellow-citizens in poverty while they themselves were rich: in Corinth Theocles and Thrasonides, and in Mytilene Praxis. And they advised others too to lighten for the destitute the constraint of poverty. When they could not persuade them, they at least remitted the debts owed to themselves, and they profited not in money but in their very lives; for those who were not released, attacking their creditors, putting forward the weapons of their wrath and the most reasonable plea, the irresistible compulsion of their straits, killed the moneylenders.

Alexander, son of Philip — or, if anyone prefers, of Zeus, for it makes no difference to me — to Phocion alone, the general of the Athenians, is said to have added the greeting "rejoice" when he wrote to him: so completely had Phocion won over the Macedonian. He even sent him a hundred talents of silver, and named four cities, of which he asked Phocion to choose whichever one he wished, that he might enjoy the revenues from it. The cities were these: Cius, Elaea, Mylasa, Patara. Now Alexander did this magnanimously and magnificently; but Phocion acted still more magnanimously, accepting neither the silver nor the city. Yet, that he might not seem to scorn Alexander altogether, he honoured him in this way. He asked Alexander to set free for him the men bound in the citadel at Sardis: Echecratides the sophist, Athenodorus of Imbros, Demaratus and Sparton. These last were two brothers, Rhodians.

They say that the sixth of the month Thargelion was the cause of many good things, not only to the Athenians but to many others as well. For instance, Socrates was born on this day; and the Persians were defeated on this day; and the Athenians sacrifice to Artemis Agrotera the three hundred she-goats, doing this in accordance with the vow of Miltiades. On the sixth of the same month they say too that the battle of Plataea took place and that the Greeks were victorious; for their earlier defeat, which I mentioned, occurred at Artemisium. And the victory of the Greeks at Mycale is agreed to have been the gift of no other day than this, since on the same day they were victorious both at Plataea and at Mycale. And Alexander the Macedonian, the son of Philip, they say destroyed the many myriads of the barbarians on the sixth too, when Alexander overthrew Darius. And all agree it was in the same month. And Alexander himself is believed both to have been born and to have departed from life on the same day.

Leonidas the Lacedaemonian and the three hundred with him chose the death prophesied for them at Thermopylae, and, contending well and finely for Greece, met a glorious end, and left to themselves undying glory and good fame through all time.

Pisistratus, when he became master of the rule, would send for those idling in the marketplaces, and inquired what was the reason of their loitering. And he would add: "If your yoke of oxen has died, take a pair from me and go and work; and if you lack seed, let it be given you from me" — fearing that their idleness might breed a plot.

Odysseus profited from Alcinous, and Achilles from Chiron, and Patroclus from Achilles, and Agamemnon from Nestor, and Telemachus from Menelaus, and Hector from Polydamas, in the matters in which he gave heed to him, and the Trojans from Antenor. And the Pythagoreans, the disciples of Pythagoras, profited, and the Democriteans, having associated with Democritus, enjoyed many benefits. And if the Athenians had given heed to Socrates, they would all have become happy. Hiero son of Deinomenes profited from Simonides of Ceos, and Polycrates from Anacreon, and Proxenus from Xenophon, and Antigonus from Zeno. And that I may make mention of those who belong to me no less than the Greeks belong — for this concerns me too, since I am a Roman — Lucullus profited something from Antiochus of Ascalon, and Maecenas from Areius, and Cicero from Apollonius, and Augustus from Athenodorus. And Plato, though wiser than I, says that even Zeus had a counsellor; who, and how, let us learn from him.
Pindar the poet, competing in Thebes and falling among ignorant hearers, was defeated by Corinna five times. Exposing their want of culture, Pindar called Corinna a sow.

The Chians once fell into faction with one another, suffering most manfully this most grievous disease. So a man among them, of a statesmanlike nature, said to his companions who were eager to expel all their opponents: "By no means; but since we have prevailed, let us leave some behind, that as time goes on, having no rivals, we may not begin to make war on ourselves." And in saying this he persuaded them; for he seemed to speak well, since he spoke thus.

I hear of a woman who played the trumpet and made of this both her work and her art, named Aglaïs, the daughter of Megacles. She wore false hair and a plume upon her head. Posidippus too agrees with this. Her dinner, it seems, was twelve minae of meat and four choenices of bread; and she drank a chous of wine.

Aristotle says that by the Crotoniates Pythagoras was called Hyperborean Apollo. And the son of Nicomachus adds this too, that once on the same day and at the same hour he was seen by many both at Metapontum and at Croton, rising up at the games, where Pythagoras also revealed that one of his thighs was of gold. The same writer says too that as he was crossing the river Cosas he was addressed by it; and he says that many heard this address.

Pindarus, son of Melas and grandson, through his mother, of Alyattes the Lydian, having succeeded to the tyranny of the Ephesians, was harsh and inexorable as regards punishments; but in other respects he seemed to be a lover of his country and temperate, and took great forethought that his country should not be enslaved to the barbarians. He showed that this was so by the following. For when Croesus, his uncle on his mother's side, in subduing Ionia sent an embassy also to Pindarus, demanding that the Ephesians become subject to him, and when he was not persuaded, Croesus besieged the city. And when one of the towers — afterward called the Traitor — was overthrown, and the danger was seen before their eyes, Pindarus advised the Ephesians to fasten cords from the gates and the walls and tie them to the columns of the temple of Artemis, as though leaving the city to be a dedication to Artemis, devising through this means a sanctuary for Ephesus; and he advised them to go forward and entreat the Lydian. When the Ephesians put forth their suppliant olive-branch, they say that Croesus laughed and, accepting the stratagem mildly, granted the Ephesians safety with freedom, but ordered Pindarus to depart from the city. He did not gainsay it, but taking those of his friends who wished to set out with him, and entrusting his son and the greater part of his property to the city, and appointing one of his intimates, Pasicles, guardian both of the boy and of the money, he set off for the Peloponnese, exchanging a tyrant's life for a self-chosen exile, that he might not make his country subject to the Lydians.

Antigonus the king held Zeno of Citium in great respect and esteem. Once, then, being overfull of wine, he came in revel to Zeno, and kissing and embracing him, as a drunken man, he begged Zeno to lay some command on him, swearing and protesting with an oath, in youthful manner, that he would not fail to grant the request. And Zeno said to him: "Go and vomit" — at once gravely and high-mindedly rebuking his drunkenness and sparing him, lest he should burst from repletion.

The hardest drinkers, they say, have been Xenagoras of Rhodes, whom they called "the Amphora," and Heracleides the boxer, and Proteas the son of Lanice, the foster-brother of King Alexander. And Alexander himself is said to have drunk the most of men.

Diogenes of Sinope was solitary and cast off alone, and no one received him because of his poverty, nor did anyone entertain him, shunning the man because of the censorious nature of his character and because he was hard to please at what was done and said. So Diogenes was downcast and ate the tips of leaves; for these he had at hand. And a mouse came and made use of the crumbs that fell from his bread. So Diogenes carefully observed what was happening, and smiling and coming to himself, more cheerful and serene, he said: "This mouse has no need of the luxury of the Athenians, but you, Diogenes, are vexed because you do not dine with the Athenians." And he procured himself a timely cheerfulness.

Antagoras the poet abused Arcesilaus of the Academy, having fallen out with him, and that too in the marketplace; but he, very high-mindedly, where he saw the most people gathered, there he walked along conversing, that the abuser might disgrace himself before more. So those who heard turned away and charged Antagoras with madness.

They say that great eaters were Lityerses the Phrygian and Cambles the Lydian and Thys the Paphlagonian and Charilas and Cleonymus and Pisander and Charippus and Mithridates the Pontic and Calamodrys the Cyzicene and Timocreon the Rhodian, the athlete and poet both, and Cantibaris the Persian and Erysichthon son of Myrmidon — whence indeed he was called Aethon. It is said that in Sicily there is a temple of Gluttony and an image of Demeter Sito (of the Corn). Alcman the poet too admits that he was a very great eater. And Anaxilas, the comic poet, says that a certain Ctesias ate much.

Anniceris of Cyrene prided himself greatly on horsemanship and the driving of chariots. And so once he wished to display his skill to Plato. Yoking his chariot, he drove many courses round the Academy, keeping so exactly to the line of the course that he did not stray beyond the wheel-tracks, but always went along them. Now all the rest, as was natural, were astonished; but Plato found fault with his excessive zeal, saying: "It is impossible for one who lays out so much care upon things so small and worthless to be in earnest about anything great; for, all his thought being given over to those things, he must necessarily neglect what truly deserves to be admired."

I have heard this story too; whether it is true, I do not know; but what I have heard is this. Plato, son of Ariston, worn down by poverty, was about to go abroad on military service; but, caught by Socrates as he was buying arms, Plato was checked in his eagerness, when Socrates had discoursed to him on what was fitting and persuaded him to desire philosophy.

A man of Laconia, but a rustic, was rebuked by someone for mourning very intensely and with great passion. And he answered without affectation: "What am I to do? For I am not the cause of this; it is my nature that flows out of me."

They say that Heracles behaved most humanely toward his own enemies; for he was the first from the beginning of time to give back the dead under truce to be buried, whereas the men of that time were wont to neglect the slain and leave them to be a meal for dogs.

The body of Socrates is believed to have been orderly and master of self-restraint, and in this way. The Athenians were sick in a general plague, and some died, others were near death; but Socrates alone did not fall sick at all. The man, then, who dwelt in such a body — what kind of soul do we think he had?

I praise most of all those who, anticipating the evils that are springing up, cut them off before they take hold of any strength. Agesilaus, at any rate, advised that those who gathered by night during the invasion of the Thebans be put to death without trial.

But I am willing to tell you a Rhodian opinion. In Rhodes they say that the man who gazes at fish and admires them and is, beyond all others, a lover of fine seafood — this man is praised by the people as a man of liberal taste; but the one who inclines toward meats they slander, the Rhodians do, as vulgar and a glutton. Whether they judge rightly or foolishly, I disdain to inquire.

After the victory over the Persians the Athenians established a law that cocks should fight publicly in the theatre one day of the year. Whence this law took its beginning I will tell. When Themistocles was leading out the citizen force against the barbarians, he saw cocks fighting; and he did not look on idly, but halted the army and said to them: "These birds suffer hardship neither for their country nor for their fathers' gods nor for the tombs of their ancestors, nor for glory nor for freedom nor for their young, but only that neither may be beaten and neither yield to the other." Having said this, he strengthened the Athenians. So the watchword that then arose for them he wished to preserve as an incitement to valour and a reminder for like deeds.

Socrates, seeing Alcibiades puffed up over his wealth and proud of his abundance and still more of his lands, led him to a place in the city where there was set up a tablet bearing a map of the earth, and bade Alcibiades seek out Attica there. When he had found it, he bade him examine his own lands. And when he said, "But they are nowhere drawn," Socrates said: "Are you proud, then, over these things, which are no part of the earth at all?"

A Spartan was praising the verse of Hesiod which says, "Not even an ox would be lost, were not your neighbour bad," while Diogenes listened. And Diogenes said: "Yet the Messenians and their oxen have been destroyed, and you are their neighbours."

The Leocorion at Athens was the name of the precinct of the daughters of Leos — Praxithea and Theope and Euboule. The story is that these were put to death for the city of the Athenians, Leos having given them up at the bidding of the Delphic oracle. For it said that the city could not otherwise be saved, unless they were sacrificed.

Diogenes, when he left his country, was followed by one of his servants named Manes, who, not bearing his way of life with him, ran away. When some urged him to seek the man out, he said: "Is it not shameful that Manes has no need of Diogenes, but Diogenes of Manes?" This servant, wandering to Delphi, was torn apart by dogs, paying the penalty for his master's name in return for his running away.

Someone reproached the orator Pytheas that he was a bad man. He did not deny it — for his conscience would not let him; but he answered this, that of those who had taken part in public life at Athens he had been bad for the shortest time — being proud, evidently, that he had not been such throughout, and thinking he did no wrong, since he did not compare himself with the most wicked. But this was foolish of Pytheas; for not only is he who does wrong bad, but also he who thinks of doing wrong, in my judgment.

The people of Cos say that in Cos a ewe in one of the flocks of Nicias the tyrant gave birth — and gave birth not to a lamb but to a lion. And this sign foretold to Nicias the tyranny that was to come to him, while he was still a private man.

Pittacus at Mytilene set up in the temples ladders fit for no use, but to be dedications for this very purpose, hinting at the shifting of fortune up and down — how, in a manner, the fortunate go up and the unfortunate come down.

Diogenes of Sinope used continually to say of himself that he fulfilled and endured the curses of tragedy; for he was a wanderer, homeless, deprived of country, a beggar, poorly clad, living from day to day. And yet over these things he was as proud as Alexander over the empire of the inhabited world, when, having conquered the Indians, he returned to Babylon.

The night being already far advanced, Socrates was once coming home from a dinner. Some licentious young men, having learned of it beforehand, lay in wait for him as he returned, holding lit torches and the masks of the Furies. It was their custom to make sport of others too, because of their leisure spent on baser things. Socrates, seeing them, was not at all disturbed, but standing still he questioned them as he would the others either in the Lyceum or in the Academy. — There being a festival among the Athenians, Alcibiades made it his ambition to send Socrates many gifts. When Xanthippe was astonished and thought Socrates ought to take them, he said: "But let us too match the ambition of Alcibiades, vying with him in not taking what was sent." And when someone said to him that it is a great thing to obtain what one desires, he replied: "But it is a greater thing not to desire it at all."

Plato son of Ariston, seeing the people of Acragas both building lavishly and likewise dining, said that the Acragantines build as though they would live forever, but dine as though they would die tomorrow. Timaeus says that they used silver oil-flasks and strigils and had whole couches of ivory.
Plato used to say that the hopes of waking men are dreams.

Lysander brought money to Lacedaemon and taught the Lacedaemonians to break the god's command, which ordered that Sparta should be untrodden by gold and silver. Some of the right-minded, then, tried to prevent it, still keeping a Laconian spirit worthy of Lycurgus and of the Pythian god; but those who admitted the money were discredited, and their original virtue little by little gave way.

King Ptolemy had a favourite named Galestes, most beautiful to look upon. But this youth's mind was even better than his form. Often, indeed, Ptolemy bore witness to this, and would say, "Good soul, you have never been the cause of harm to anyone, but to many you have procured many good things." Once the youth was riding with the king; and seeing from afar some men being led off to their death, he did not look on idly, but said to Ptolemy: "O king, since by some good fortune of those being led off we happen to be mounted on horses, come, if it please you, let us press on the pace and ride hard in pursuit, and become Dioscuri to the poor wretches — 'good saviours and noble helpers,' as the saying goes of those gods." The king, overjoyed at his kindness and loving exceedingly his compassion, both saved those men and added still more to the charm of his love for him.

Plato, son of Ariston, at first set out for poetry, and wrote heroic verses; then he burned them, despising them, when, comparing them with Homer's, he saw them far inferior. So he turned to tragedy, and indeed composed a tetralogy, and was about to compete, having already given the poems to the actors. But before the festival of Dionysus he came and heard Socrates, and once caught by that man's Siren, he not only withdrew then from the contest, but utterly cast away the writing of tragedy, and stripped himself for philosophy.

Amoebeus the lyre-singer was said to be most temperate, and, having a most beautiful wife, not to consort with her. And Diogenes the tragic actor renounced the licentious bed altogether and entirely. And Cleitomachus the pancratiast, if ever he saw even dogs coupling, would turn away; and at a symposium, if any talk of love crept in, he would rise and depart.

Anaxarchus, when he was campaigning with Alexander, learned beforehand, on the coming of winter, that Alexander meant to make his encampment in a treeless place; so, throwing away all the gear he had, he loaded his baggage-carriers with wood. When they reached the halting-place and there was a want of wood, Alexander's couches were burned that he might warm himself; but when someone reported that there was fire at Anaxarchus's, Alexander came to him and was anointed in Anaxarchus's tent. Learning of his foresight, he praised it highly, and gave him twice as much as he had thrown away, in return for the use of the fire.

The Tarentines had the custom of drinking from early morning and being drunk about the time the marketplace is full. And the Cyrenaeans ran aground in such luxury that they invited Plato to be their lawgiver. But he refused, they say, because of their inveterate indolence. Eupolis too agrees, in the Maricas, that the cheapest of them had signet-rings worth ten minae. And the engravers of the rings were also admired.

Olympias, the mother of Alexander, learning that her son remained a long time unburied, groaning heavily and lamenting very shrilly, said: "O my child, you who wished to share in heaven and were eager for this, now you cannot even share in what is common and equal to all men — earth and burial." So she pitied her own fortunes and rebuked the conceit of her son.

Hanno the Carthaginian through luxury did not deign to remain within the bounds of men, but devised to have reports sown abroad about himself greater than accorded with the nature he had been allotted. For having bought very many singing-birds, he reared them in darkness, teaching them one lesson to say: "Hanno is a god." And when those birds, hearing this one phrase, had mastered it, he let them loose, one this way and one that, thinking that the song about himself would spread abroad through the birds. But they, once they had set their wings free and gained their liberty and come to the habits natural to them, sang their own songs and made the music of birds, bidding a long farewell to Hanno and the lessons learned in slavery.

This is a Persian custom, observed by them above all others. When the king rides into the land of the Persians, all the Persians bring him gifts, each according to his means. And since they are engaged in farming and labour upon the land, and are by nature workers of their own soil, they offer nothing extravagant or excessively costly, but either an ox or a sheep; some bring grain, and others wine. As he passes by and rides along, these things are set before him by each man, and they are called gifts, and are so regarded by him. Those still poorer than these in their living offer him milk and dates and cheese, and ripe fruits for eating, and the other first-fruits of their region.

And who would not praise the wisdom of the barbarians? Seeing that none of them fell into atheism, nor do they doubt about the gods whether they exist or not, or whether they care for us or not. None of them, at any rate, conceived such a notion as Euhemerus of Messene, or Diogenes the Phrygian, or Hippon, or Diagoras, or Sosias, or Epicurus — no Indian or Celt or Egyptian. Rather, the aforesaid barbarians say both that there are gods and that they have forethought for us and signify beforehand things to come, through birds and through omens and through entrails and through certain other lessons and teachings — which are instructive to men, coming from the gods' forethought toward them. And they say too that many things are foreshown through dreams and through the stars themselves. And, having a strong belief about these matters, they sacrifice in purity and keep themselves holy and pure, and perform rites and observe the law of the mysteries, and do the other things from which it is agreed that they strongly revere and honour the gods.
Nicias the painter had such earnestness about painting that often he forgot to take food, so wholly absorbed was he in his art.
An athlete of Croton, an Olympic victor, as he was going to the Hellanodicae to receive his crown, was seized by an epileptic fit and died, falling in a convulsion.

Come, let me recite to you the names of the Greek wines that were sought after in old times. One they called Pramnian, and this was sacred to Demeter. And there was Chian wine from the island, and another Thasian, and Lesbian. Besides these there was one called "Sweet," fitting its name in taste, and another Cretan. And in Syracuse there was Pollian; it was named after a certain local king. They drank Coan wine too, and so called it; and Rhodian, naming it in the same way. And what of this? Was it not a proof of luxury among the Greeks? For they mixed wine with myrrh and so drank it, and greatly delighted in such a mixture; and the wine was called "Myrrhine." Philippides the comic poet mentions it.

Xenocrates of Chalcedon, the companion of Plato, was both compassionate in other ways and not only a lover of mankind but also pitied many of the irrational animals. So once, as he was sitting in the open air, a sparrow, hotly pursued by a hawk, flew into his bosom. He gladly received the bird, and kept it hidden until the pursuer had gone away. When he had freed it from fear, opening his bosom he let the bird go, saying that he had not betrayed a suppliant.

Ptolemy, called Tryphon — for this they called him from his way of life — when a beautiful woman wished to meet with him, said: "My sister has forbidden me to receive a proposal from a beautiful woman." And she, very unabashed and fittingly, said: "Could you receive one from a beautiful man?" And he, hearing it, praised her.

Here too is a Persian story. They say that a Persian man, whose name was Sinaetes, met Artaxerxes, called Mnemon, far from his own farmstead. Caught off guard, he was thrown into confusion by fear of the custom and awe of the king. Not knowing what to do in his predicament, and unable to bear being outdone by the other Persians, nor to seem dishonoured by not bringing the king a gift — this man went to the river flowing nearby, whose name is Cyrus, in haste and as fast as his feet could carry him, and stooping down, he drew up water with both his hands and said: "King Artaxerxes, may you reign through all the ages. For now I honour you in whatever way and by whatever means I can, that you may not pass by, so far as in me lies, without a gift. I honour you with water of the river Cyrus. But when you arrive at your halting-place, I will honour you from my own home with the best and most costly things I have, and so I shall be no less than any of the others who have already greeted you with gifts." At this Artaxerxes was pleased, and said: "I gladly accept the gift, my man, and I value it among the most costly, and reckon it equal to those: first, because water is the best of all things, and second, because it bears the name of Cyrus in itself. And do you by all means appear before me when I halt at my station." Saying this, he ordered the eunuchs to take the gift from him; and they ran up with all speed and received the water from his hands into a golden bowl. And when the king had come to where he was lodging, he sent the Persian man a Persian robe and a golden bowl and a thousand darics, and ordered the one who carried these to say to the recipient: "The king bids you gladden your own soul with this gold, since you too gladdened his, leaving him neither unrewarded nor unhonoured, but honouring him in this way according to your present means. And he wishes you to draw with this bowl and drink of that water."

Certain Pythian accounts say that Heracles, the son of Zeus and Alcmene, was from birth called Alcaeus, but that later, coming to Delphi for some reason to seek an oracle, he not only did not fail of the things for which he had come, but heard besides, privately from the god, these words: "Phoebus names you Heracles for your surname; for, bringing glory to men, you shall have undying fame."

Alexander, son of Philip, while a boy not yet come to manhood, was learning to play the lyre. When his teacher bade him strike a certain string with a melody, the one the music required, he said: "And what difference will it make if I strike this one?" — pointing to another. But the teacher said it made no difference to one who was to be king, but to one who was to play the lyre as a craft. And this man, it seems, feared the fate of Linus. For Linus taught Heracles, while he was still a boy, to play the lyre; and when Heracles handled the instrument too unmusically, Linus was vexed with him. And Heracles, in his indignation, struck Linus with the plectrum and killed him.

The Greeks set up Phryne the courtesan at Delphi upon a very lofty column. I will not say simply "the Greeks," lest I seem to bring under blame all of those whom I love above all men, but rather the more intemperate among the Greeks. The statue was of gold. And Cimon's mares too, in bronze, stood at Athens, made to resemble Cimon's mares as closely as possible.

Pythagoras of Samos wore white clothing, and a golden crown, and trousers. Empedocles of Acragas used purple and bronze sandals. And the report goes that Hippias and Gorgias went about in purple robes.

Xenophon says that Socrates came to converse with Theodote the courtesan, who was a most beautiful woman. And he came to converse with Callisto too, who said: "I, son of Sophroniscus, am stronger than you; for you cannot draw away any of mine, but I, if I wish, can draw away all of yours." And he said: "Yes, and with good reason; for you lead them down the easy path, but I force them to come to virtue; and the way up is steep and unfamiliar to most."

A Lacedaemonian man, Timandridas by name, going abroad, left his son as caretaker of his house. Then, returning some time later and finding that the son had made the estate greater than he had left it, he said that the son was wronging many — gods and kinsmen and guests; for the surplus of these things is spent upon them by free men. But to appear poor while living and to be found rich at death — this is the most shameful of things among men.

Omises brought to King Artaxerxes, as he was riding through Persia, a very great pomegranate upon a winnowing-fan. Astonished at its size, the king said: "From what garden did you take this gift that you bring me?" And when the man said that it was from his own home and his own farming, the king was overjoyed, and sent him royal gifts, and added: "By Mithra, this man, from such diligence, will in my judgement be able to make even a city great out of a small one." And this account seems to confirm that all things, through diligence and unceasing care and unflagging zeal, working with nature, may become better than they are.

We see the nature of rivers and their streams; yet those who honour them and make their images, some set them up in human form, while others gave them the shape of bulls. To bulls, then, the Stymphalians liken the Erasinus and the Metope, the Lacedaemonians the Eurotas, the Sicyonians and Phliasians the Asopus, the Argives the Cephisus; in the form of men, the Psophidians honour the Erymanthus, the Heraeans the Alpheus, and the Chersonesians from Cnidus likewise honour the same river in the same way. The Athenians represent the Cephisus as a man in profile, with horns just showing. And in Sicily the Syracusans likened the Anapus to a man, but honoured the spring Cyane with the image of a woman; the Egestaeans honour the Porpax and the Crimisus and the Telmessus in the form of men. The people of Acragas, likening the river that gives its name to the city to a youth in his bloom, sacrifice to it. These same people also dedicated at Delphi a statue carved of ivory, and inscribed on it the name of the river. And the statue is of a boy.

Satyrus the flute-player often listened to Ariston the philosopher, and, charmed by what was said, would add: "Were it not that I might cast these bows into the bright fire" — hinting at his flutes, and in a manner disparaging his own art by comparison with philosophy.

A youth of Eretria attended on Zeno for a long time, until he came to manhood. Later, then, he returned to Eretria, and his father asked him what wise thing he had learned in so long a stay. And he said that he would show him, and before long he did so. For when his father grew angry with him and at last laid blows upon him, he, keeping quiet and enduring it, said that this was what he had learned: to bear a father's anger and not be indignant.

Cineas, the physician of Pyrrhus, they say, wrote secretly to the council of the Romans, and asked for money, and promised to kill Pyrrhus by poisons. But they did not accept the offer; for the Romans know how to be good through virtue, not to overcome their enemies through craft and villainy and treachery. They even revealed to Pyrrhus himself the design of Cineas.

They say that the Egyptian tales tell of Rhodopis, a most beautiful courtesan. Once, as she was bathing, fortune, which loves to do strange and unexpected things, procured for her something worthy not of her judgment but of her beauty. For as she was bathing and her maids were guarding her clothing, an eagle swooped down, snatched one of her sandals, and went off; and it carried it to Memphis, where Psammitichus was sitting in judgment, and dropped the sandal into his lap. Psammitichus, marvelling at the shape of the sandal and the grace of its workmanship and at what the bird had done, ordered the woman whose sandal it was to be sought throughout all Egypt; and finding her, he made her his wife.

Plato was discoursing on certain matters, and Diogenes, who was present, paid little heed to him. So the son of Ariston was indignant at this and said: "Listen to the discourse, dog." And he, in no way disturbed, said: "But I have not gone back there whence I was sold, as dogs do" — hinting at Plato's journey to Sicily. And Plato, they say, was wont to say of Diogenes that this man was a Socrates gone mad.

A man of the Mardian race, named Racoces, had seven sons. The youngest of these was called Cartomes, and he did much wrong to the others. At first his father tried to instruct and discipline him with words; but when he would not obey, the judges of the region having come to where the young man's father lived, the father seized the child, bound his two hands behind him, and led him before the judges, and accused him precisely of all that he had dared to do, and asked the judges to put the young man to death. They were astonished, and would not themselves take it upon them to cast the condemning vote, but led them both before Artaxerxes, the king of the Persians. When the Mardian said the same things, the king broke in and said: "Then will you dare with your own eyes to endure your son's dying?" And he said: "Above all things; for when in my garden I break off and remove the bitter shoots that grow upon the lettuces, their mother plant is in no way grieved, but rather flourishes and grows larger and sweeter. So I too, O king, seeing the one who harms my house and the life of his brothers destroyed, and his wrongdoing against them ended, shall myself increase, and shall live together with the rest of my kin, who will fare as well as I." When Artaxerxes heard this, he praised Racoces and made him one of the royal judges, saying to those present that one who passed so just a judgement upon his own children would certainly be an exact and incorruptible judge in the affairs of others; and he released the young man from his present punishment, threatening him with a most grievous kind of death if he should be caught wronging others after what had gone before.

They say that Epicharmus, being very old indeed, sitting with some men of his own age in a club-room, when each of those present said — one, "Five years is enough for me to live," another, "Three for me," and a third said, "Four for me" — Epicharmus broke in and said: "My good friends, why do you wrangle and dispute over a few days? For all of us who are gathered here are, by some chance, at our setting; so it is time for all of us to be off as quickly as possible, before any of us comes to suffer some evil of old age."

Among the Laconians and the Romans there was a law that it was not permitted to anyone to buy provisions either of whatever kind he wished or in whatever quantity he wished; for they ordered the citizens to be temperate both in other ways and not least through the table.

Diogenes, coming to Olympia and seeing at the festival some young men of Rhodes expensively dressed, laughed and said: "This is vanity." Then meeting with some Spartans in coarse and dirty smocks, he said: "This is another kind of vanity."

Many loves of the ancients have been handed down to our memory, and these not least. Pausanias loved his own wife, and Apelles the concubine of Alexander, whose name was Pancaste, and who was Larissaean by birth. With her, they say, Alexander first consorted.

Dionysius, after the order against Leon, having found him, three times bade the bodyguards lead him away, and three times changed his mind, and at each summons kissed him, weeping and cursing himself for having taken up the sword. At the last he was overcome by fear, and ordered him to be slain, saying: "Leon, it is not possible for you to live."

The Egyptians say that they were instructed in their laws by Hermes; thus each people chooses to glorify what is their own. The judges in old times among the Egyptians were the priests. The eldest of these was their head, and judged all. And he had to be the most just of men and the most unsparing. He wore too an image of sapphire stone about his neck, and the image was called Truth. But I should think it right that the judge should carry Truth not made of stone and fashioned, but should have her in his very soul.

Gorgias of Leontini, being at the end of his life and very aged, was seized by some weakness, and lay slipping little by little into sleep. When one of his friends came to look in on him and asked how he did, Gorgias answered: "Now sleep is beginning to hand me over to his brother."
There is an Attic story current that formerly in the Academy it was not even permitted to laugh; for they tried to keep the place untrodden by insolence and idleness.
Socrates, seeing that Antisthenes was always making the torn part of his cloak conspicuous, said: "Will you not stop showing off to us?"

There were two Perianders, the one a wise man, the other a tyrant. And three Miltiadeses: the one who founded the Chersonese, and the son of Cypselus, and the son of Cimon. Four Sibyls: the Erythraean, the Samian, the Egyptian, the Sardian. Some say there were six others, so that there were ten in all, of whom were the Cumaean and the Jewish. Three Bacides: the one of Eleon, the one of Athens, the one of Arcadia.
Men learned in nature say that the deer, when it needs purging, eats seseli, and when troubled by the bites of spiders, eats crabs.
Lais was also called the Axe. This surname convicted her of the savagery of her character, and that she charged much, and still more from foreigners, since they departed sooner.

Socrates too, being very far advanced in age and then falling sick, when someone asked him how he was, said: "Well, as regards either outcome; for if I live, I shall have the more to envy me, and if I die, the more to praise me."

Aristotle, when he left Athens for fear of the trial, said to one who asked him, "What sort of city is that of the Athenians?": "A very fair one; but in it pear ripens upon pear, and fig upon fig" — meaning the informers. And to one who asked why he left Athens, he answered that he did not wish the Athenians to sin twice against philosophy — hinting at the fate of Socrates and the danger to himself.

A harpist was performing before Antigonus. When the king kept saying, "Tighten the top string," and again, "the middle one," the harpist grew indignant and said: "May it never go so ill with you, O king, as to know these matters better than I."

The ancients seem not to agree with one another about the number of Niobe's children. Homer says six sons and as many daughters; Lasus says twice seven; Hesiod nineteen — unless indeed the verses are not Hesiod's, but, as many other things, are falsely ascribed to him. Alcman says ten; Mimnermus twenty; and Pindar as many.
Olympias sent to Eurydice, the daughter of Philip — she had been born to Philip by an Illyrian woman — hemlock and a noose and a sword; and she chose the noose.

One may laugh at those who are proud because of their fathers and their ancestors, seeing that we do not know the father of Marius, yet we admire him for his deeds; and so too with Cato and Servius and Hostilius and Romulus.

Of Zaleucus the Locrian there are many other laws too, laid down most finely and as need required, and this not least. If any of the Epizephyrian Locrians, being ill, drank unmixed wine without the physician's prescribing it, even if he recovered, death was his penalty, because he drank what had not been prescribed to him.

There is a law of the Ceans: those among them who are very aged, as if inviting themselves to a feast or to some festal sacrifice, come together and, crowning themselves, drink hemlock, whenever they are conscious that they are useless for the works that profit their country, their judgement by now somewhat failing them through age.

Anaxarchus, surnamed "the Happy," used to laugh at Alexander for deifying himself. When Alexander once fell ill, and the physician prescribed that a broth be made for him, Anaxarchus laughed and said: "The hopes of our god, then, lie in a soup-bowl."

Alexander, when he was pursuing Bessus, finding himself in want of food, took to eating the camels and other beasts of burden, both he and those with him. And when their firewood failed them, they ate the meat raw. The silphium, which was plentiful, helped them, so as to digest the flesh. And in Bactria the soldiers found the villages, learning that they were inhabited by the smoke, and clearing the snow away from the doors.

Gelon the tyrant of the Syracusans held the establishment of his rule most gently; but some seditious men plotted against him. Learning of this, Gelon called the Syracusans together into an assembly and entered armed, and going through all the good he had done them, he uncovered the plot and stripped off his armour, saying to all: "See, then, I stand before you in a tunic, naked of arms, and I give you to do with me whatever you wish." And the Syracusans admired his judgment, and some even handed over the plotters to him to punish, and gave him the rule. But he allowed even these to be punished by the people. And the Syracusans set up a statue of him in an ungirt tunic; and this was a memorial of his popular rule and a lesson to those who should rule in the age to come.

I love to look neither at the statues which the plastic art shows us, nor at the images, idly; for there is something wise in the handiwork even in these. And one can recognize many other things in them, and among them this. None of the Muses did any painter or sculptor ever prove able to present to us with most false and counterfeit and alien forms of the daughters of Zeus. Or who was ever so madly daring a craftsman as to make them armed? This confirms that the life among the Muses ought to be at once peaceful and gentle and worthy of them.

This too is a Massiliot law: that women should have nothing to do with wine, but that women of every age should drink water. Theophrastus says that this law is in force among the Milesians too, and that the women of Miletus obey it. And why should I not tell the Roman law too? And how should I not justly be charged with unreason, if I have set down in memory the laws of the Locrians and the Massiliots and the Milesians, but leave aside those of my own country? Among the Romans, then, this law was in force above all others. Neither a free woman nor a serving-woman would drink wine, nor would those of good birth who were in their youth, up to thirty-five years of age.

They say that at Athens the olive and the fig were first found, which the earth also first gave up. And the Athenians were the first to learn to give and receive justice. And they first devised the contest of the body, and stripped and anointed themselves. And Erichthonius was the first to yoke horses.

Alexander came to Ilium. As he was studying it diligently, one of the Trojans approached and showed him the lyre of Paris. But he said: "I would rather see that of Achilles." This was a noble word of Alexander's; for he longed for the possession of a good soldier, to which that man had sung the glories of brave men. But what did the lyre of Paris ever sing, except adulterous songs, such as catch and bewitch women?

The horses of the Sacae, if one throws his master, stand still for him to mount again. If anyone wishes to marry a maiden, he fights in single combat with the girl. And if she wins, she leads him captive and has power and rule over him; but if she is beaten, she is ruled. They fight in single combat to victory, not to death. The Sacae, when they mourn, hide themselves in certain caverned and shady houses.

Alcibiades greatly admired Homer, and once, coming to a boys' school, asked for a rhapsody of the Iliad. When the teacher said he had nothing of Homer, he struck him a very hard blow with his knuckles and passed on, showing that the man was uneducated and made the boys such. This man, summoned from Sicily by the Athenians to a capital trial, did not obey, saying: "It is foolish for one who has a lawsuit to seek to escape acquittal when he can escape by flight." When someone said, "Do you not trust your country with the judgment about you?" he said: "Not even my mother; for I fear that, not knowing and missing the truth, she might cast the black pebble instead of the white." So learning that death had been decreed against him by his fellow-citizens, he said: "Let us then show that we are alive," and rushing to the Lacedaemonians he kindled the Decelean war against the Athenians. He used to say that the Lacedaemonians did nothing strange in dying fearlessly in war; for, fleeing the hardship of their laws, they gladly exchanged death for the toils they had. And he was wont, they say, to add of his own doings that he lived the life of the Dioscuri, dying and coming back to life on alternate days; for when he prospered with the people he was thought equal to the gods, but when he fared ill he differed not at all from the dead.

Of Epaminondas the Theban I know many other fine things, and among them this. He used to say to Pelopidas that he should not leave the marketplace before he had won over some younger man as a friend to the older.

The Cretans bade their freeborn children learn the laws to a kind of melody, that they might be charmed by the music and take them more easily into memory, and that, if they should do anything forbidden, they might not have the excuse of having acted in ignorance. As a second lesson they appointed them to learn the hymns of the gods; as a third, the encomia of good men.

The Arcadians had acorns for their food, the Argives wild pears, the Athenians figs, the Tirynthians wild pears, the Indians reeds, the Carmanians dates, the Maeotians and Sauromatae millet, the Persians terebinth and cress.

How could one not call these loves at once ridiculous and strange? That of Xerxes, in that he fell in love with a plane-tree. And a youth of good birth at Athens fell most ardently in love with the statue of Good Fortune that stood beside the Prytaneum. He would kiss the statue and embrace it; then, driven mad and stung by desire, he came before the council and entreated them, ready to buy the statue for the greatest sum of money. When he could not persuade them, he bound the statue with many fillets and crowned it and made sacrifice to it and put costly adornment about it, and then killed himself, after weeping countless tears beforehand. As for Glauce the harpist, some say a dog fell in love with her, others a ram, others a goose. And in Soli in Cilicia a dog fell in love with a boy named Xenophon, and in Sparta a jackdaw with another beautiful youth.

Perdiccas the Macedonian, who campaigned with Alexander, was so daring that he once went alone into a cave where a lioness had her lair; and the lioness he did not find, but he came out carrying her cubs, and for this Perdiccas was thought to be admired. It is believed, not only among the Greeks but also among the barbarians, that the lioness is the boldest and hardest to fight of beasts. They say, at any rate, that Semiramis the Assyrian was not proud if ever she took a lion or killed a leopard or any such thing, but only if she got the better of a lioness.
When someone reproached Ephialtes the general with his poverty, he said: "And why do you not mention the other thing, that I am just?"

The king of the Persians — for I wish to tell you something cheerful too — dipping a crown in perfume — and the crown was woven of roses — sent it to Antalcidas, who was on an embassy to him for peace.
