And he said: "I accept the gift and praise the kindness, but you have destroyed the scent of the roses and the fragrance of nature through the counterfeit of art."

Everything irrational is by nature ill-disposed toward wine, and especially those animals which become drunk when overfilled with husks or grape-stones. Ravens too, when they eat the herb called oenutta, and dogs themselves as well, become frenzied. And if an ape and an elephant drink wine, the elephant forgets its strength, the ape its cunning; and they are very easily caught.

The fellow-dancers of Dionysus were the Satyrs, called by some Tityri. They got the name from the warblings in which they delight. The Satyrs are named from their grinning, the Sileni from their mocking; and "sillos" they call a reproach made with vexatious jesting. The dress of the Sileni was tunics shaggy on both sides. The robe hints at the planting given by Dionysus and the thickets of vine-shoots.

The Carthaginians used to put two helmsmen aboard a ship, saying it was absurd that a ship should have two rudders, while he who was most useful to those sailing and who had the command of the vessel should be left alone and without a successor or partner.

Among the other supplies that followed Xerxes, full of extravagance and ostentation, there followed also water from the Choaspes. And when in some desert place he was thirsty, his attendants not yet having come, it was proclaimed to the army that, if anyone had water from the Choaspes, he should give the king to drink. And someone was found who had a little, and that putrid. So Xerxes drank it, and considered the giver his benefactor, because he would have perished of thirst, had not that man been found.

As a Persian gold necklace lay on the ground, Themistocles, standing by his son, said: "Will you not pick up this find, boy?" — pointing to the necklace — "for you are surely not Themistocles." When the Athenians once dishonoured him, then summoned him again to office, he said: "I do not praise such men, who use the same vessel for chamber-pot and wine-jug." To Eurybiades the Lacedaemonian he said something contrary, and Eurybiades raised his staff against him. And he said: "Strike, but listen." For he knew that what he was about to say would benefit the common good.

Alexander the tyrant of Pherae was thought to be among the most savage of men. When Theodorus the tragic poet was acting Merope very passionately, he burst into tears and then rose up and left the theatre. Excusing himself, he said to Theodorus that he had gone not out of contempt or disdain for him, but out of shame, that he should be able to pity the sufferings of actors, but not those of his own citizens.

Lovers of drink are said to have been Dionysius the tyrant of Sicily, and Nysaeus, who was also a tyrant, and Apollocrates the son of Dionysius the tyrant, and Hipparinus, son of Dionysius, and Timolaus the Theban, and Charidemus of Oreus, and Arcadion, and Erasixenus, and Alcetas the Macedonian, and Diotimus the Athenian. This last was even nicknamed "the Funnel"; for, putting a funnel into his mouth, he would let the wine poured in pass down without ceasing. Cleomenes the Lacedaemonian they say was not only a great drinker, but they ascribe to him besides that Scythian vice, that he became a drinker of unmixed wine. And Ion of Chios, the poet, they say was himself intemperate about wine. And Alexander the Macedonian, in honour of Calanus the Brahman, the Indian sage, when that man burned himself, held a contest of music and horsemen and athletes. And, gratifying the Indians, he reckoned in among the prizes mentioned a contest native to them, in honour of Calanus. He set up a contest of wine-drinking, and the prize for the one who came first was a talent, for the second thirty minae, and for the third ten. The one who bound on the crown of victory among them was Promachus. And under Dionysius, at the festival of the Pitchers, a golden crown was set as a prize for whoever drank most. And Xenocrates of Chalcedon won, and taking the crown, when he was returning after the dinner, he set it upon the Hermes standing before the doors, according to the custom of the days before; for he laid up and left there the garlands of flowers and of myrtle and of ivy and of bay as well. And Anacharsis too, they say, drank a great deal at Periander's, bringing this provision with him from home; for it is characteristic of the Scythians to drink unmixed wine. And Lacydes and Timon the philosophers, these too they say drank a great deal. And Mycerinus the Egyptian, when the oracle from Buto came to him foretelling the shortness of his life, then wished to outwit the prophecy, doubling the time and adding the nights to the days, and continued himself sleepless and drinking at once. Set down with these also Amasis the Egyptian, if Herodotus is sufficient to bear witness for anyone. And Nicoteles the Corinthian must not be left out of these, nor Scopas, son of Creon. And King Antiochus they say was a lover of wine; for which reason Aristus and Themison the Cyprians governed the kingdom for him, while he, through his hard drinking, held the rule only in name. And Antiochus surnamed Epiphanes, who was given to the Romans as a hostage, he too thirsted intemperately to drink wine. And his namesake Antiochus, who in Media made war on Arsaces, he too was a slave to drink. And Antiochus called the Great, let him too be ranked with these. And Agron, king of the Illyrians, the unjust craving for wine killed, and worked pleurisy in him. And another king of the Illyrians, Gentius, he too was used to drink intemperately. As for Orophernes, king of the Cappadocians, shall we leave him out, who also became a terrible drinker? And if one must mention women too — a woman fond of drink is monstrous, and one given to much drinking still more so, but let it be said of these too. Cleo, they say, entering into contest not with women only but with the men who were her fellow-drinkers, was most formidable at drinking, and overcame them all, carrying off, in my judgement, a most shameful prize of victory.
The ancients called bearing much fruit "phlyein." Hence they called Dionysus Phleon and Protrygaeus and Staphylites and Omphacites, and in various other ways besides.

At a certain dinner, they say, there were present Simonides of Ceos and Pausanias the Lacedaemonian. Pausanias bade Simonides say something wise, and the Cean, laughing, said: "Remember that you are a man." This Pausanias at once made light of and set at nothing, already smouldering with the longing to take the Persians' side, and high-minded over his guest-friendship with the king, and perhaps also carried away by wine. But when he was at the temple of the Lady of the Brazen House, and was wrestling with hunger and about to die the most painful of deaths, then he remembered Simonides and cried out three times: "O Cean stranger, your word was indeed a great matter, but I in my folly thought it nothing."

Protogenes the painter, they say, completed his Ialysus, painting it over seven years. When Apelles saw it, at first he stood speechless, astounded at the marvellous sight, then said: "Great is the labour and great the craftsman; yet his handiwork lacks the grace which, if the man should attain it, his labour would touch heaven itself."
When one of those about to die with Phocion was lamenting, Phocion said: "What, Thudippus, are you not content to die with Phocion?"

Apollodorus, who drank the most wine of men, did not conceal his own vice, nor did he try to cloak his drunkenness and the evils that came from it, but, kindled and inflamed by the wine, he became more murderous, having, besides his nature, the drink too as a stimulus.

The reputation of Plato and the report of the virtue that was his reached even the Arcadians and the Thebans, and so they entreated him, sending ambassadors with the utmost earnestness, that the man should come to them — not merely for the oversight of their young men, nor that he might join them in philosophical discussion, but, what is still greater than these, they called him to be their lawgiver. They were not, then, likely to fail of the man; for the son of Ariston was pleased at the invitation, and was indeed going to comply. He asked, however, of those who had come, how they stood toward all having an equal share. But when he learned from them that they were quite ill-disposed to it, and that he would not persuade them to honour equality before the law, he refused to visit them.

Elege and Celaene were daughters of Proetus. The queen of Cyprus made them wanton, and they ran, they say, naked and raving over a part of the Peloponnese, and went out into other lands of Greece as well, distraught with the disease. I hear too that a kind of bacchic frenzy fell upon the women of the Lacedaemonians and those of the Chians. And that the women of the Boeotians raged most divinely, tragedy too proclaims. They say that the daughters of Minyas alone — Leucippe and Arsippe and Alcithoe — held back from this dance of Dionysus. The reason was that they longed for their husbands, and for this cause they did not become maenads of the god. He was angered, and while they were at their looms and labouring very zealously over the work of Ergane, suddenly ivy and vines crept about the looms, and serpents lodged in the wool-baskets, and from the roofs dropped drops of wine and milk. But not even these things persuaded them to come to the worship of the god. There, indeed, they wrought a deed off Cithaeron no less than the one on Cithaeron; for the daughters of Minyas, beginning their madness, tore apart the son of Leucippe, still tender and young, like a fawn, and then from there rushed against the maenads who were maddened from the first; and these pursued them because of the pollution. From this they became birds, and one changed her form to a crow, another to a bat, another to an owl.
When Artaxerxes had put to death his elder son Darius for plotting against him, the second son, at his father's bidding, drew his scimitar and killed himself before the palace."

Cyrus, the son of Mandane, was reared, they say, by a dog; Telephus, the son of Auge and Heracles, by a hind; Pelias, the son of Poseidon and Tyro, by a horse, and so too the son of Alope. Alexander son of Priam, they say, was reared by a bear, and Aegisthus, the son of Thyestes and Pelopia, by a goat.

Epaminondas was on trial for his life, having returned from Laconia, for having added four months to his Boeotarchy contrary to the law. He bade his fellow-magistrates lay the blame on him as having been compelled, but he himself, coming forward into the court, said he had no words better than his deeds; if otherwise, he asked them to put him to death, but to inscribe on the pillar that Epaminondas had compelled the Thebans against their will to burn Laconia, which had been unravaged for five hundred years, to found Messene after two hundred and thirty years, to organize and gather the Arcadians into one, and to restore to the Greeks their independence. And the judges, out of respect, acquitted him. As he returned from the court, a little Maltese dog fawned on him. So he said to those present: "This creature repays me thanks for a kindness, but the Thebans, having often been well treated by me, have condemned me to death."

Xenocrates the companion of Plato said that it makes no difference whether one sets one's feet or one's eyes in another's house; for he sins in the same way who looks at places where he ought not, and who passes into places where he ought not.

The poorest of men were the best of the Greeks: Aristides, son of Lysimachus, and Phocion, son of Phocus, and Epaminondas, son of Polymnis, and Pelopidas the Theban, and Lamachus the Athenian, and Socrates, son of Sophroniscus, and Ephialtes, son of Sophonides, he too.

At Sybaris, while a lyre-singer was singing in the contest which they celebrated in honour of Hera, the Sybarites, falling into faction over him and taking up arms against one another, the lyre-singer in his fear, in his very robes, fled for refuge to the altar of Hera; but they did not spare the lyre-singer even there. And a little later blood seemed to gush up in the temple of Hera, no less than an ever-flowing spring; and the Sybarites sent to Delphi. And the Pythia answered: "Go forth from my tripods; still much blood about your hands, dripping from the stone threshold, holds you back. I will not give you oracles. The Muses' servant you killed at Hera's altars, not shunning the gods' vengeance. For those who do evil the end of justice comes not slow nor to be turned aside, not even if they be the offspring of Zeus; but it whirls about their own heads and upon their own children, and woe upon woe comes upon their houses." And justice did not tarry; for, taking up arms against the Crotoniates, they were driven from their homes by them, and their city was wiped away.

I hear that Darius the son of Hystaspes was a quiver-bearer of Cyrus. And the last Darius, who was defeated by Alexander, was a slave. Archelaus the king of the Macedonians was the son of a slave-woman, Simiche. Menelaus the grandfather of Philip was reckoned among the bastards. His son Amyntas was believed to be the servant and slave of Aeropus. Perseus, whom Paulus the Roman overthrew, was Argive by birth, the son of some obscure man. Eumenes is believed to have been the son of a poor father and a grave-flute-player. Antigonus son of Philip, who had but one eye and was therefore called Cyclops, was a man who worked with his own hands. Polysperchon was a brigand. Themistocles, who defeated the barbarians at sea and alone understood the voices of the gods in the oracles, was the son of a Thracian woman, and his mother was called Abrotonon. Phocion, surnamed the Good, was the son of a man who made pestles, and Demetrius of Phalerum, they say, was a home-bred slave from the house of Timotheus and Conon. As for Hyperbolus and Cleophon and Demades, although they became leaders of the Athenian people, no one could easily say who their fathers were. Callicratidas and Gylippus and Lysander in Lacedaemon were called Mothakes. This was the name for the slaves of the wealthy, whom their fathers sent out with their sons to share their training in the gymnasia. And Lycurgus, who allowed this, granted a share in the Laconian citizenship to those who kept to the rearing of children. And Epaminondas was the son of an obscure father. And Cleon the tyrant of the Sicyonians was a pirate who threw men into the sea.

Timotheus the Athenian general was believed to be fortunate; and they used to say that fortune was the cause, and Timotheus the cause of nothing, mocking him on the stage. And the painters depicted him asleep, and then, hovering over his head, Fortune standing and drawing the cities into a net. When someone asked Themistocles in what he had most delighted in his life, he answered: "To see the theatre at Olympia turning toward me as I passed into the stadium."

A certain Ptolemy — which one he was, let it pass — sat at dice and kept gaming; then one standing by him read out the names of those condemned and added their sentences, that the king might mark which were worthy of death. But Berenice his wife, taking the document from the page, then would not allow it to be read through entirely any more, saying that one ought to give very careful thought concerning a man's life and not be at play while doing so; for the fall of the dice and the fall of human lives were not alike. At this Ptolemy was pleased, and never afterward, while gaming, did he hear a man's judgment.

Of Theon the painter many other works besides attest that his craftsmanship was good, and so too does this picture. There is a hoplite rushing to the rescue, the enemy having suddenly burst in and at once laying waste and ravaging the land; vividly and most ardently the young man seems like one hurrying into battle, and you would say he was inspired, as though driven mad by Ares. His eyes look fierce, and snatching up his arms he seems to dart against the enemy as fast as his feet can carry him. From here he already thrusts forward his shield, and brandishes his bared sword, looking like one bent on bloodshed and gazing on slaughter, and threatening through his whole bearing that he will spare none. And Theon laboured at nothing more — no file-leader, no captain, no centurion, no horseman, no archer — but this single hoplite was enough for him to fulfil the demand of the picture. The artist, however, did not uncover the painting nor show it to those gathered for the viewing before he set a trumpeter beside it and ordered him to blow the rousing strain, piercing and as loud as could be, and such as wakens men to battle. So at the same moment the strain was heard, harsh and fearful, such as trumpets sound for the sally of hoplites swiftly rushing to the rescue, and the painting was uncovered, and the soldier was seen, the strain making the image of the man rushing to the rescue still more vivid to the mind.

Three young men, fellow-citizens, coming to Delphi as sacred envoys, fell in with evildoers. One, then, fled from the robbers; the second of them grappled with the last of the brigands, the others having perished first, and missed the robber but drove his sword into his friend. To the one who fled the Pythia gave this answer: "Being near at hand while your friend was dying, you did not help him. I will not give you oracles; go forth from the beautiful temple." But to the other: "You killed your comrade in defending him; blood did not stain you, but your hands are purer than they were before."

The quarries in Sicily were near Epipolae, a stade in length and two plethra in breadth. And there were men who had spent so much time in them that they had even married there and begotten children. And some of those children, never having seen a city, when they came to Syracuse and saw horses yoked and oxen being driven, fled crying out; so astonished were they. The fairest of the caverns there was named after Philoxenus the poet, in which, they say, he composed, while spending time there, the fairest of his songs, the Cyclops, setting at nothing the vengeance and condemnation of Dionysius, but making music, Philoxenus, in the very midst of his misfortune.

Themistocles and Aristides the son of Lysimachus had the same guardians, and for this reason they were reared together and educated under a common teacher. Yet they were at variance even while still boys, and the rivalry remained with them from earliest youth to extreme old age.

A Laconian youth bought a piece of land very cheaply; then he was brought before the magistrates and fined. And the cause of the condemnation was this, that being young he loved gain too keenly. For it was among the most manly traits of the Lacedaemonians, this too: to be arrayed not only against enemies but also against money.

They say that an oracle came forth to Philip in Boeotia, at the shrine of Trophonius, that he must beware the chariot. And so, for fear of the oracle, the story goes that he never mounted a chariot. There is, then, a double account current about this. The one says that the sword of Pausanias, with which he did Philip to death, had a chariot carved in ivory upon the hilt; the other, that as he was going round the Theban lake called Harma ("Chariot") he was slain. The first account is the common one; the other has not gone out to all.

The Phrygian tales sing these things too. That while Midas the Phrygian was still an infant sleeping, ants crept into his mouth, and most laboriously and industriously carried in grains of wheat. And that bees made a honeycomb in the mouth of Plato. And to Pindar, exposed from his father's house, bees became nurses, providing honey in place of milk.
Dionysius killed his mother with poisons; and though able to save his brother Leptines in the sea-battle, he looked on while he perished.

Among the women of the Greeks we praise Penelope, Alcestis, and the wife of Protesilaus; among the Romans, Cornelia and Porcia and Caestilia. I could have named others too, but I do not wish to name few of the Greeks and flood the rest with the names of the Romans, lest anyone should think I am gratifying myself because of my country.
This is a law of the Stagirites, and altogether a Greek one: "What you did not lay down," it says, "do not take up."

Dionysius the son of Hermocrates, they say, was crossing a river; a horse was carrying him. And the horse slipped into the mire, and he leaped off and caught hold of the bank and went away, leaving the horse as though it were no longer his. But the horse followed and, with a whinny, turned him back. And he caught hold of its mane and was about to mount, when a swarm of bees fell upon his hand. The Galeotae, then, when Dionysius asked them about this, said that these things signified monarchy.

Patrae is a city of Achaea. A boy among them bought a small snake and reared it with much care. When it grew, he talked to it as to one who heard, and played with it and slept with it. When the snake reached its greatest size, it was driven by the citizens into the wilderness. Later the boy, having become a young man, was returning from some spectacle, and fell among robbers with his companions; and when a cry arose, behold the snake. And it scattered some, and killed others, and saved him."

The Magnesians who dwell along the Maeander, when they were at war with the Ephesians, each of the cavalrymen brought with him as fellow-soldier a hunting-dog and a javelin-throwing servant. And when they had to engage, then the dogs, leaping forward, threw the enemy's array into confusion, being fearful and savage and implacable to meet; and the servants, leaping forward before their masters, hurled their javelins. And so, upon the disorder caused first by the dogs, the deeds of the servants too took effect. Then, in the third place, the men themselves advanced.

At first the Athenians praised Timotheus; but when he was thought to have erred in what he was thought to have done, his foregoing valour did not save him even a little, nor yet the virtues of his ancestors. And Themistocles gained nothing either from the sea-battle off Salamis or from the embassy to Sparta — I mean the one on which he served as ambassador while stealing the walling of the Athenians. For he too was exiled, not from Athens only, but from all Greece. And Pausanias the Lacedaemonian gained nothing from the victory at Plataea; but for what he did anew at Byzantium, on account of these things he destroyed even the gratitude owed him for his first deeds. And Phocion the good repute that called him "the Honest" helped not at all, nor his seventy-five years, which he lived through wronging the Athenians in no respect at all; but when he was thought to be betraying the Piraeus to Antipater, the Athenians condemned him to death.

Dionysius drove Dion out of Sicily, but kept his wife Arete and his son by him under guard. Later he gave the wife, against her will, in marriage to Timocrates, his bodyguard, who was of all men his greatest attendant; he was a Syracusan by birth. But Dion, when he took over Syracuse, Dionysius having fled to the Locrians, then Aristomache the sister of Dion greeted him. And Arete followed, veiling herself for shame and not daring to greet him as her husband, since, forced, she had not kept faith with the bed she shared with him. When Aristomache had pleaded for her, recounting the compulsion laid on her by Dionysius, Dion took back his wife and child and sent them to his house.

Zeuxis of Heracleia painted Helen. So Nicomachus the painter was struck by the picture, and was plainly amazed at the painting. Someone, then, coming up, asked him what had come over him that he so admired the art. And he said: "You would not have asked me, had you possessed my eyes." And I would say this of words too: but only if one has educated ears, just as the craftsmen have skilled eyes.

The Indians, having translated the verses of Homer into their own native tongue, sing them — not they alone, but also the kings of the Persians, if one is to believe at all those who relate these things.

Philip, taking the sons of the most esteemed men in Macedon, kept them about his own service, in no way, they say, insulting them or making them cheap, but on the contrary training them to endurance and making them ready to do what was needful. But toward those of them who were luxurious and slack at what was commanded he was, they say, hostile. At any rate he flogged Aphthonetus, because, leaving his post, he turned off the road, being thirsty, and went into an innkeeper's. And he killed Archedamus, because, though Philip had ordered him to keep himself in his armour, he stripped it off; for he had hoped, through flattery and fawning, to win over the king, being a man too weak to resist gain."

Phocion the son of Phocus, who had often been general, was condemned to death, and was in prison and about to drink the hemlock. When the executioner held out the cup, his kinsmen asked if he had anything to say to his son. And he said: "I charge him to bear the Athenians no grudge for this loving-cup which I now drink." Whoever does not praise and greatly admire this man seems to me to have no great thought in him.

The Lacedaemonians had no experience of music; for their care was for gymnastics and arms. But if ever they needed help from the Muses, whether falling sick or going mad or suffering some other such thing publicly, they would send for foreign men, like physicians or purifiers, according to the Pythian oracle. They sent, indeed, for Terpander and Thales and Tyrtaeus and Nymphaeus of Cydonia and Alcman. And Thucydides too admits that they were not zealous for culture, where he speaks of Brasidas. For he says that he was not even incapable of speaking, for a Lacedaemonian.

Menecrates the physician advanced to such a pitch of conceit that he called himself Zeus. He once sent to Philip the king of the Macedonians a letter of this kind: "Menecrates Zeus to Philip, greeting." And Philip wrote back: "Philip to Menecrates, health. I advise you to take yourself off to the regions about Anticyra." He hinted by this that the man was mad. Philip once gave a magnificent feast, and indeed invited this man to the banquet, and ordered a separate couch to be prepared for him, and when he had reclined, set before him a censer and burned incense to him; while the rest feasted, and the dinner was magnificent. So Menecrates at first held out, and rejoiced in the honour; but when little by little hunger came over him, and he was shown to be a man, and a foolish one at that, he rose up and went off, and said he had been insulted — Philip having very fittingly uncovered his folly.

Isocrates the orator used to say of the city of the Athenians that it was like the courtesans. For those who are captivated by their beauty wish to be with them, yet no one is so cheaply foolish as to endure to live with one of them. And so the city of the Athenians is most pleasant to visit, and in this surpasses all the cities in Greece; but to dwell in is no longer safe. He hinted by this at the informers who haunted it and the plots of the demagogues.

It has not escaped me that the beginnings of the greatest wars seem somehow to have been contemptible. For they say that the Persian war took its beginning from the quarrel of Maeandrius of Samos with the Athenians, and the Peloponnesian from the decree against the Megarians, and the one called Sacred from the exaction of fines by the Amphictyons, and the war at Chaeronea from the Athenians' contention with Philip and their refusal to come to terms.

Aristotle, wishing to soothe Alexander when he was angry and to stop him from being harsh with many, wrote thus to him: "Wrath and anger arise not against inferiors, but against superiors; and to you no one is equal." Aristotle, by giving Alexander the needful counsel, became a benefactor to many, by which means he restored his native city, which had been razed by Philip.

Those who are killed by elephants, whether in the hunts or in the battles, the Libyans bury with distinction, and sing certain hymns. The burden of the hymns is this: it says that they were brave men who fought against so great a beast; for they say that a glorious death is a burial-honour for the one buried.

Diogenes of Sinope said many things in disparagement of the ignorance and lack of culture of the Megarians, and said he would rather be a Megarian man's ram than his son. He hinted that the Megarians take thought for their flocks, but not for their children.

When Alexander son of Philip was leading his force against Thebes, the gods sent them signs and portents, foreshadowing the fortunes that all but immediately awaited them; but they, thinking that Alexander had died among the Illyrians, cast many blasphemies against him. For the lake at Onchestus gave forth a fearful and continuous sound, and was like the bellowing of a bull; and the spring called Dirce, flowing by the Ismenium and the very walls, which all the time before had flowed with clear and sweet water, suddenly and beyond expectation was filled with blood. The Thebans believed that the divine power was threatening the Macedonians. And in the temple of Demeter in the city a spider wove its web over the face of the statue. And the statue of Athena called Alalcomeneis was burned of itself, no fire being applied; and many other things.

Dioxippus the Olympic victor, the athlete, the Athenian, was riding into Athens according to the custom of athletes. So the crowds streamed together, and people, hanging from this place and that, gazed at him; and among them a woman of outstanding beauty met the spectacle. Dioxippus, seeing her, was at once overcome by her beauty, and kept gazing at the woman and turning round and changing his face to many colours. From this it became plain to many that he had not looked at the woman idly. Above all Diogenes of Sinope marked his condition, and said to those near him: "See your great athlete thrown by a slip of a girl."
Pythagoras used to say that these two finest things were given to men by the gods: to speak the truth and to do good; and he added that each of them resembled the works of the gods.

There was once a meeting between Dionysius the Second and Philip the son of Amyntas. Many other topics, as was natural, came up; and among them Philip asked Dionysius how it was that, having received so great a rule from his father, he then did not preserve it. And he answered, not out of tune: "My father left me everything else, but the fortune by which he gained and kept these things, that he left me no longer."

Dionysius sailed against Thurii, and brought against them three hundred ships filled with soldiers; but a north wind blowing against him shattered the vessels and destroyed his naval force. From this the Thurians sacrificed to the North Wind, and decreed that the wind should be a citizen, and allotted him a house and a portion of land, and every year performed rites to him. So not only did the Athenians consider him their kinsman by marriage, but the Thurians too inscribed him as their benefactor. And Pausanias says that the Megalopolitans did so too.

This too is a Persian law. If anyone is about to advise the king on some secret and disputed matter, he stands upon a golden brick. And if he seems to advise what is needful, he takes the brick and goes away with it as a reward for his counsel; but he is nonetheless flogged, because he has contradicted the king. To a free man, in my judgment, the insult is no fit counterweight to the reward.

A certain Archedice fell in love with the courtesan in Naucratis. But she was haughty and terribly tiresome and demanded heavy fees, and having taken them she would consort for a little while with the giver, then turn away. So the young man, in love with her, and unable to win her because he was not very rich, consorted with her in a dream, and at once ceased from his desire.

Alexander, the son of Philip and Olympias, having ended his life in Babylon, lay a corpse — he who said he was the son of Zeus. And while those about him quarrelled over the kingdom, he was without a share in burial, which even the very poor obtain, since the common nature of things demands that one no longer living be hidden away. But he was left uncared-for for thirty days, until Aristander of Telmessus, possessed by a god or held by some other chance, came into the midst of the Macedonians and said to them that Alexander had been the most fortunate of all the kings from the beginning of time, both living and dead; for the gods told him that the land that received the body, in which his soul had formerly dwelt, would be wholly blessed and unravaged through all time. Hearing this, they were filled with great rivalry, each desiring to carry off this precious freight to his own kingdom, that he might have a treasure and a pledge of secure and unshaken rule. But Ptolemy, if one is to believe it, stole the body away, and with haste carried it to the city of Alexander in Egypt. And the other Macedonians kept quiet, but Perdiccas set about pursuing him. It was not so much that he cared for the honour of Alexander and the rites due to the dead, as that the words spoken beforehand by Aristander inflamed and kindled him. When he overtook Ptolemy, a most fierce battle arose over the corpse, sister in a way to that over the phantom at Troy, which Homer sings, telling how Apollo cast a phantom of Aeneas into the midst of the heroes. But Ptolemy checked the onset of Perdiccas; for making a phantom like Alexander, he adorned it with royal dress and enviable burial-trappings. Then setting this up upon one of the Persian wagons, he furnished the bier upon it magnificently with silver and gold and ivory; and the real body of Alexander he sent forward plainly and as it chanced, by hidden and untrodden roads. And Perdiccas, overtaking the phantom of the corpse and the decked-out wagon, was checked in his course, thinking he had the prize; but too late he learned that he had been deceived, when he could not pursue."
